10.title: "The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Tale of Hope and Redemption"
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" stands as a testament to the enduring power of storytelling in cinema, weaving a narrative that transcends its prison setting to become a profound exploration of hope, friendship, and the resilience of the human spirit. Adapted from Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," the film directed by Frank Darabont remains a modern-day classic cherished by audiences worldwide.

At its heart, "The Shawshank Redemption" is the story of Andy Dufresne, portrayed with quiet strength by Tim Robbins. Convicted of a double murder he did not commit, Andy finds himself sentenced to life at Shawshank State Penitentiary. Robbins's performance is a masterclass in understated acting, capturing Andy's transformation from a man shattered by injustice to one who finds inner peace and purpose within the confines of the prison walls. His portrayal resonates deeply, portraying resilience and hope against insurmountable odds.

Opposite Robbins is Morgan Freeman as Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding, a fellow inmate known for his ability to procure goods within Shawshank. Freeman's narration throughout the film lends a contemplative and introspective tone, drawing viewers into the complexities of life behind bars. Red's journey mirrors Andy's in many ways, as both men navigate their existence within the rigid structures of the prison system while grappling with personal demons and searching for meaning.

The chemistry between Robbins and Freeman is palpable, anchoring the film's emotional core. Their friendship evolves over decades, built on mutual respect, trust, and a shared belief in the possibility of redemption. The camaraderie they depict on screen is both poignant and uplifting, illustrating the profound impact human connection can have even in the bleakest of circumstances.

Central to the narrative is Warden Samuel Norton, portrayed by Bob Gunton, whose character embodies the complexities of authority and morality within Shawshank. Norton's authoritarian rule and manipulative tendencies provide a stark contrast to Andy and Red's quest for justice and personal growth. Gunton's portrayal is chilling yet compelling, adding layers of tension and moral ambiguity to the story.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is renowned for its thematic depth and narrative craftsmanship, skillfully blending elements of drama, suspense, and introspection. Frank Darabont's direction ensures that each scene serves a purpose, whether illustrating the harsh realities of prison life or exploring moments of quiet reflection and resilience. The film's pacing is deliberate yet engaging, allowing the audience to immerse themselves fully in the characters' journeys and emotional arcs.

Visually, the film is a testament to Roger Deakins' exceptional cinematography. His use of light and shadow captures the stark contrasts of hope and despair within Shawshank, emphasizing the characters' emotional states and the passage of time. The prison's imposing architecture becomes a metaphor for confinement and liberation, underscoring the film's themes of imprisonment and eventual redemption.

Thomas Newman's evocative score further enhances the film's emotional resonance, complementing the narrative with themes of melancholy, yearning, and ultimately, triumph. Newman's compositions evoke a sense of nostalgia and longing, reinforcing the characters' inner struggles and their quest for freedom-both physical and spiritual.

"The Shawshank Redemption" received widespread acclaim upon its release in 1994, yet it faced stiff competition at the Academy Awards, where it was nominated for seven Oscars, including Best Picture, Best Actor for Morgan Freeman, and Best Adapted Screenplay. Despite not winning in any category, the film's enduring legacy has only grown stronger over the years, solidifying its status as one of cinema's greatest achievements.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" continues to resonate with audiences for its timeless themes, exceptional performances, and profound storytelling. It is a film that transcends its genre, offering a universal message of hope and resilience that speaks to the human condition. Tim Robbins, Morgan Freeman, and the entire cast deliver performances that linger in the mind long after the credits roll, while Frank Darabont's direction ensures that every frame is imbued with emotional depth and narrative significance.

Bravo to this timeless masterpiece, a beacon of cinematic excellence that continues to inspire and uplift audiences around the world.

The Shawshank Redemption is a timeless masterpiece that has rightfully earned its place among the greatest movies ever made. Directed by Frank Darabont, the film is based on a novella by Stephen King and stars Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman in the lead roles. Released in 1994, the film received seven Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, and has since become a cultural phenomenon.

The story revolves around Andy Dufresne (Robbins), a young and successful banker who is wrongfully convicted of the murder of his wife and her lover. Sentenced to life imprisonment at Shawshank State Penitentiary, Andy finds himself struggling to adjust to life behind bars. He is subjected to abuse from the other inmates, including the sadistic Captain Hadley (Clancy Brown), and becomes the target of the corrupt and tyrannical warden Norton (Bob Gunton). But despite the brutal conditions, Andy refuses to let go of his hope for freedom and redemption.

What makes The Shawshank Redemption such a powerful film is the way it explores themes of hope, perseverance, and the human spirit. Andy's journey is one of resilience and determination, as he uses his intellect and resourcefulness to make the best of a bad situation. He befriends Red (Freeman), a fellow inmate who is known for his ability to smuggle in contraband, and the two form a bond that transcends the boundaries of race and social status. As the years go by, Andy becomes an indispensable figure in the prison, helping the guards with their financial matters and even creating a library for the inmates. But all the while, he is secretly working on a plan to escape, using his knowledge of finance to launder money for the corrupt warden.

The relationship between Andy and Red is the heart of the film, and the performances by Robbins and Freeman are nothing short of incredible. Robbins portrays Andy as a quiet and introspective man who is always thinking several steps ahead, while Freeman brings a sense of warmth and wisdom to the role of Red. The chemistry between the two actors is palpable, and their scenes together are some of the film's most memorable.

The supporting cast is also excellent, with standout performances from Brown as the sadistic Captain Hadley, Gunton as the corrupt warden Norton, and William Sadler as Heywood, one of the inmates who befriends Andy. The film is also notable for its beautiful cinematography, with Roger Deakins capturing the bleakness of prison life while also finding moments of beauty and hope.

One of the most iconic scenes in the film is the escape sequence, which is executed with precision and suspense. The build-up to the escape is masterfully handled, with Andy's plan unfolding gradually and the tension mounting as the day of the escape draws near. The actual escape itself is a tour de force of filmmaking, with Darabont using every trick in the book to keep the audience on the edge of their seats.

But perhaps the most memorable aspect of The Shawshank Redemption is its message of hope. Even in the darkest of places, there is always a glimmer of light that can guide us through the toughest of times. Andy's story is a testament to the human spirit, showing us that no matter how dire the circumstances, we can always find a way to persevere.

In conclusion, The Shawshank Redemption is a masterpiece of filmmaking that deserves every bit of its reputation as one of the greatest movies ever made. It is a timeless tale of hope and redemption that speaks to audiences of all ages and backgrounds. With its unforgettable characters, stunning cinematography, and powerful message, it is a film that will stay with you long after the credits have rolled.

10.title: An Epic that will Leave you Speechless
10.content:
What an experience. Because that's what this is, more of an experience than a film. Just sensational in so many ways. So visceral, real, emotional, rewarding. Shawshank has it all. The cast, the story, the set, costume, direction, script, soundtrack... everything was sublime. Numerous touching moments, comedic moments, dramatic moments, sombre moments and heart warming moments combine to make this a goliath of film making.

The entire cast were great, not a single dud performance, but the performances of Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman were stellar. Robbins as Andy Dufresne gave such a powerful, varied and nuanced performance. As soon as I'd finished watching I wanted to dive straight into a second viewing to appreciate it one more time. Freeman as well was superb, tying the film together so perfectly with his narration and overall presence.

What I really loved about Shawshank was how it didn't dwell on the crimes of the men, but treated them as very real and human people. Despite being set in a prison this wasn't a film about crime and punishment, but about life and hope. It was because of this that the film has so much heart. Sombre, yes, often bleak, but always with a vein of hope running through it.

The way that prison life was presented felt quite real and gritty. The costume, set design, and sinister portrayals of Warden Norton and Captain Hadley brought the film to life, creating a dangerous and brutal atmosphere for proceedings.

What Shawshank also did very well was transcend time so effortlessly and effectively. As mentioned earlier, this film managed to feel like an epic novel crammed into two hours twenty minutes. There is so much to digest and pick through, yet that time manages to absolutely fly by.

Intricate. Detailed. Rich. Rewarding. The Shawshank Redemption most definitely earns its position at the top of IMDb's highest rated films list.

10.title: Tied for the best movie I have ever seen

The only other movie I have ever seen that effects me as strongly is To Kill a Mockingbird. Both movies leave me feeling cleaner for having watched them.

I didn't intend to see this movie at all: I do not like prison movies and I don't normally watch them. I work at a branch library and one day as I was checking The Shawshank Redemption out to one of our older patrons, she said to me, "Whenever I feel down or depressed, I check out this movie and watch it and it always makes me feel better." At the time, I thought that was very strange. One day there was nothing on TV except things I absolutely would not watch under any circumstance or things that I had seen too many times already. I remembered what she said, so I watched it. I have watched it many many times since then and it gets better with every showing.

No action, no special effects - just men in prison uniforms talking to each other.

10.title: A marvel of filmmaking...
10.content:
As near to perfect as a movie can get, "The Shawshank Redemption" is absolutely superlative entertainment. I keep wondering at those who claim the movie is too long (as many also did for the fantastic "Green Mile"). I wonder if MTV, television newscasts, commercials and other things have destroyed the attention span of several generations of people. Nobody seems to be able to stick with anything for more than an absolute maximum of two hours anymore. It's a disappointing trend, because often a great story cannot be told in the usual 120-minute maximum alloted to most films.

If you have the attention span to watch a film longer than two hours, movies just don't get any better than this one does. Don't look for realism (try PBS or any documentary for that), look for plot, acting talent and (above all): Simply a good, satisfying tale! The Shawshank Redemption has it all, in spades, and Frank Darabont is on his way to an absolutely stellar directing career. Kudos to Stephen King as well for his excellent novella, "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," which obviously helped make this film possible. 10/10.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic masterpiece that tells a poignant and powerful story about the human spirit. Directed by Frank Darabont, the film is based on a Stephen King novella and features outstanding performances from its lead actors, Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman.

The film is set in a conservative prison in the mid-20th century, and it explores themes of hope, redemption, and the resilience of the human spirit. The characters are complex and multifaceted, and their journeys are both inspiring and heart-wrenching. The film's pacing is deliberate and thoughtful, allowing the story to unfold in a way that is both satisfying and emotionally resonant.

The cinematography and production design are top-notch, creating a gritty and realistic world that draws the viewer in and immerses them in the story. The musical score is also notable, perfectly complementing the film's tone and mood.

Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a must-see film that will leave a lasting impression on anyone who watches it. It is a timeless classic that has earned its place in the pantheon of great American films, and it is a testament to the power of cinema to move and inspire us.

10.title: "Remember Red, hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies."
10.content: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a 1994 drama directed by Frank Derabont starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman in the leading roles. Movies based on the novels and stories of mastermind Stephen King enjoyed massive popularity for now almost half a century, some as critically acclaimed masterpieces ("The Shining", "The Green Mile") and some as mediocre but cult classic flicks ("Pet Semetary", "Christine"). Although they never fail to entertain it's not always easy to predict where an adaptation ranges. In this case though, it's obvious. I mean, could 2.2 Million other cinephiles be totally wrong? I guess not. This film definitely deserves the first spot. As a bookwork who loves the original short story it's satisfying to see how well adapted it is and how true it is to its source material. It had slightly different changes, but they were all for the better. I know, in the novella Red is a red-headed Irish man, but who would dislike a story narrated by Morgan Freeman? Additionally, he and Robbins performed outstandingly and acted together so well. This film is a melancholic and simultaneously hopeful journey of a falsely convicted banker and depicts how he manages to fulfill his dream of freedom. It's wonderfully filmed by the legendary and somewhat underappreciated cinematographer Roger Deakins and he really knows how to capture the devastation and the depressing tone of the story. Each and every brilliantly written character was spectacularly portrayed by their respective actor. Unlike other prison break movies this film addresses the dramatic and philosophical aspect of a lifetime sentence: What distinguishes an inmate from a human being? Of course most people commited a crime, but is it really necessary to take them in for a whole life? This film sensitively tries to answer these questions and shows us that although everything they have done, the inmates are still human beings. It's social criticism at it's finest, extremely emotionally shown through the story of Brooks. The ones who served their whole life in prison never get the chance to rehabilitate and reintegrate into society. It's simply devastating to see at times, sometimes the brutality shows itself by violence and sometimes by unexplainable human behaviour. Despite all those prominent aspects this film also depicts the hopes and dreams of a man and inspiringly tells us that it's never to late to dream and that we as humans should never give up. All in all, this cinematic masterpiece lives up to its reputation and gives us an unforgettable experience that gives you goosebumps by its packing narrative and outstanding performances. This one of the best dramas ever made and will always be a milestone achievement in the history of cinema. Brilliant!

10.title: Cinema at its very best
10.content:
Once again, a DVD purchase gives me an excuse to write about a film I first saw years ago - and, by happy chance, it's a truly magnificent piece of work.

Stephen King's work, itself uneven in quality, also has a spotty history when transferred to the screen, whether in the form of a movie or a TV drama. Neither version of "The Shining" was very good, while "The Stand" was converted into a TV drama that flowed better than the novel itself, but was unable wholly to overcome or conceal that book's very real flaws.

This film is based on King's short story "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption" - a good story that makes a superb film. It DOES drag somewhat in places, but what else can you expect in a film describing events that stretch over decades, but are confined to a very small physical space? For the rest, the acting is flawless, the music is subtle and appropriate, while the photography and script are both excellent. I particularly liked the characterization and portrayal of relationships - not just the Robbins-Freeman interaction, but also the other characters, even the minor ones, who cross our field of vision as the film progresses.

There are a number of enjoyable high points and thought-provoking low points along the way - not too many, that would destroy the film's main impact - and the conclusion rates as one of the most gratifying I've ever seen in a movie.

In short, unless you demand lots of action of the explosions and chases type, you're going to be enthralled by this one.

Rating: 10/10 - the only film I've seen so far to deserve this rating.

10.title: Best Movie Ever.
10.content:
A monumental celebration of resiliency, The Shawshank Redemption explores eternal themes of hope and friendship through the story of a banker convicted of murder adjusting to a brutal new life behind bars.

It's 1947 in New England, and young bank vice president Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. He is sent to the sprawling Shawshank State Penitentiary to serve two consecutive life sentences. The prison is run by warden Samuel Norton (Bob Gunton), who believes in discipline and the Bible, and ruthless chief guard Byron Hadley (Clancy Brown). Andy initially sticks to himself and has to fend off the unwanted advances of a group of pathologically violent rapists. He then befriends resourceful long-timer Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), a leader among the prisoners and legendary for being able to secure any item from outside the prison walls - for a standard 20 percent mark-up.

Andy finally establishes his reputation by helping Hadley save on his taxes. Norton then appoints Andy as his personal banker and chief tax-evader. Over the years, Andy uses his elevated position within the prison community to dramatically enhance the prison library, and helps several convicts to finish their high school education. But a shocking confession from a prisoner in another facility sets Andy on a collision course with Norton. 19 years into his sentence, Andy's determination to hang onto hope faces its ultimate challenge.

A generally faithful adaptation of a Stephen King novella, The Shawshank Redemption is a dazzling achievement. Director and screenwriter Frank Darabont constructs a deeply moving essay on the adaptability of the human spirit, and the conflict between hope and despair when the future appears uniformly grim.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless classic that continues to captivate audiences over two decades after its release in 1994. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," the film tells the poignant story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is wrongfully convicted of a double murder and sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary.

At the heart of the film is the indomitable spirit of Andy Dufresne, brilliantly portrayed by Tim Robbins. When we first meet Andy, he arrives at Shawshank with a quiet demeanor and a steadfast refusal to let the brutality and injustice of prison life crush his spirit. Through his intelligence, resilience, and unwavering belief in hope, Andy emerges as a beacon of light in the dark confines of Shawshank.

Central to the narrative is Andy's unlikely friendship with Ellis "Red" Redding, a lifelong inmate played with depth and nuance by Morgan Freeman. Red serves as the film's narrator, providing poignant reflections on life, freedom, and the enduring power of hope. Their bond transcends the confines of Shawshank's walls, offering solace, companionship, and a glimmer of humanity in a place defined by despair and cruelty.

One of the most compelling aspects of "The Shawshank Redemption" is its exploration of themes such as redemption, resilience, and the enduring power of the human spirit. Andy's journey serves as a testament to the resilience of the human soul in the face of adversity. Despite being unjustly imprisoned and subjected to unimaginable hardships, Andy never wavers in his commitment to maintaining his dignity and sense of self-worth. His unwavering resolve to seek redemption and justice is a powerful reminder of the triumph of the human spirit over adversity.

Through the character of Red, the film also delves into the complexities of guilt, forgiveness, and the possibility of redemption. Red's initial skepticism and cynicism gradually give way to hope and renewal as he witnesses Andy's unwavering commitment to his principles and his refusal to be broken by the harsh realities of prison life. Red's own journey towards redemption parallels Andy's quest for freedom, highlighting the transformative power of friendship, compassion, and the belief in second chances.

Beyond its powerful themes and character dynamics, "The Shawshank Redemption" is also a masterclass in storytelling and filmmaking. Frank Darabont's direction is understated yet masterful, allowing the emotional weight of the narrative to shine through without the need for excessive theatrics. The film's pacing is deliberate and measured, drawing viewers into the world of Shawshank and immersing them in its atmosphere of oppression and camaraderie.

The cinematography by Roger Deakins is evocative, capturing the stark beauty of the prison's architecture juxtaposed with the bleakness of life behind bars. The use of light and shadow, symbolic imagery, and subtle visual cues enhance the film's emotional impact, subtly reinforcing its themes of darkness giving way to light, despair yielding to hope.

Moreover, the performances in "The Shawshank Redemption" are nothing short of extraordinary. Tim Robbins delivers a nuanced and deeply affecting portrayal of Andy Dufresne, embodying the character's intelligence, integrity, and quiet strength with remarkable authenticity. Morgan Freeman's performance as Red is equally exceptional, infusing the character with warmth, wit, and a sense of wisdom that anchors the film's emotional core.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" stands as a cinematic masterpiece that endures as a timeless classic. Its rich tapestry of themes, unforgettable characters, and masterful storytelling continue to resonate with audiences around the world, reminding us of the enduring power of hope, friendship, and the indomitable human spirit. As Andy Dufresne famously states, "Hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies."

Going to prison is never easy and almost an unimaginable experience for most people. It's even worse if you are sentenced for fifty years despite being innocent.

Shawshank Redemption is an incredible movie. Not only because of its fantastic narration and storytelling technique. Not only because of the emotional yet inspirational performances put on by each and every actor/actress. Not even the spectacular filming and perfect settings. No, what makes Shawshank Redemption a truly excellent film is the complete story and the very relatable tale that is the life of Andy Dufresne.

This movie focuses on the lives of minor characters, life in and out of prison, and how the system has changed so many men and women drastically. And it's these individual stories that make Andy's even more special. He was able to stay strong, to manage without friends or support in the worst times. He was a man no one would have looked at twice. No one special. Just another person like you and me. Yet, his story is one that we can all imagine ourselves in. Where bad circumstances meet inexplicable motives, and it's being capable of imagining ourselves in Andy's shoes that makes Shawshank Redemption such a beautiful movie.

This movie stands for a lot of things. Love, respect, peace and friendship among other things. More so than the rest, Shawshank Redemption is a story about hope. Having faith in the future, secretly knowing good will overcome bad.

No one knows what our future holds. But if we could all live like Andy, optimistic and ever so kind in the most dire of situations, holding up true justice, this world would be a better place.

10.title: Shawshank Redemption
10.content:
It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

From Andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - Red, who becomes his best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy Yaşamak' or get busy Dine'."

At its core, this movie is a poignant exploration of the resilience of the human soul in the face of adversity. It follows the journey of Andy Dufresne, a man unjustly convicted of murder, as he navigates the harsh realities of Shawshank State Penitentiary. The themes of friendship, the pursuit of freedom, and the enduring power of hope resonate with audiences of all ages and backgrounds.

The cinematography, led by Roger Deakins, beautifully captures the contrasting worlds within the prison and the lush landscapes that symbolize freedom. 10.title: All Time Great Movie
10.content:
All Time Great Movie - rom Andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - Red, who becomes his best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'."

The key to the film's structure, I think, is that it's not about its hero, but about our relationship with him - our curiosity, our pity, our admiration. If Andy had been the heroic center, bravely enduring, the film would have been conventional, and less mysterious. But we wonder about this guy. Did he really kill those two people? Why does he keep so much to himself? Why can he amble through the prison yard like a free man on a stroll, when everyone else plods or sidles?

People like excitement at the movies, and titles that provide it do well. Films about "redemption" are approached with great wariness; a lot of people are not thrilled by the prospect of a great film - it sounds like work. But there's a hunger for messages of hope, and when a film offers one, it's likely to have staying power even if it doesn't grab an immediate audience.

"The Shawshank Redemption" premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September 1994, and opened a few weeks later. It got good reviews but did poor business (its $18 million original gross didn't cover costs; it took in only another $10 million after winning seven Oscar nominations, including best picture).

The performances are spectacular. From the leads on down. Definitely my favorite Morgan Freeman performance of all time (and there a lot of good ones to choose from.) Tim Robbins was born to play this role. He shines so bright and his arc is amazing to watch. The supporting cast is also excellent.

Another interesting side note is that Morgan Freeman's character of "RED' was named that in the book because he was an Irishman with red hair. 10.title: Film Analysis
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a film that plays out the story of Red's, Morgan Freemans, experiences, encounters, and friendships while imprisoned for murder. Red begins with his first encounter of Andy Dufresne, Tim Robbins. Andy was quit peculiar in the way in which he carried himself and his quietness, which intrigued Red. Andy requested a rock hammer from Red, from then on Andy and Red's friendship began to grow. The film shows the hardships prisoners experience, including being jumped and raped by the "Sisters." But the film also displays what good can be done within the prison, such as Andy, an experience banker, volunteering to do taxes and give financial advice to the guards in return for a better life behind bars for him and his friends. Andy uses his privilege to rejuvenate the prison's library and offering assistance to prisoners to obtain there high school equivalency. The film is spanned out over 40 years, showing the long term sentences these men have served. There are several themes as work in this film, but the most prominent one is the power of hope. Throughout the movie, glimmers of hope are expressed by the men but then soon shattered. The beginning scene of the bet of which "New fish" would cry was soon realized to be cruel and led to a prisoner's death. Throughout the movie, Red (Freeman) had lost all hope. Red displayed this loss of hope with his uncaring attitude displayed at his parole hearings. He had no motivation to express to the board that he was a changed man and was ready to return back to society. He said the same speech at almost every hearing which lead to his denial until he later regained hope for a brighter future and spoke of his regret to the parole board. Hope was also displayed through music, the singing French woman and the harmonica. A glimmer of hope was displayed for Red when his friend escaped prison, this hope grew when he was unexpectedly granted parole. Through Red's narrative, it seemed as his Red's fate was to be the same as Brooks, "Institutionalized," but Red prevailed and pursued his long lost friend, Andy. The letter that Andy left for Red under the lava glass near the oak tree stated, "Hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies." This changed Red, he now understood the saying "Either get busy living, or get busy dying," and he chose life. Symbols used throughout the film were rocks and pinup posters of iconic women. Rocks were used ultimately to hide the true purpose of the rock hammer, but they were also a symbol of hope and normalcy. The posters of the iconic women, such as Rita Hayworth and Marilyn Monroe, were posters to cover up Andy's true desire which was to escape this unjust imprisonment and return to his normal life.

An example of good sound effects is the scenes leading up to Brooks' demise. The sound effects create a sense of understanding and realism; soft music is played as her narrates his final letter to his friends back at prison. Shots of the hustle and bustle of the city, cars whizzing by and honking at Brooks, the noisy and bossy grocery manager. In the final scene of him committing suicide, the noise of his pocket knife is very prominent and creak of the chair as he mounts it to carve his name in the rafter, and the sound of the chair being kicked away and the tension on the rope is heard. This is very realistic and somber. The music is soft which created an emotion of sadness and does not drown out the important subtle noises.

A movie that shares some of the same themes and motifs is Green fried Tomatoes, this film portrays a significant amount of time and displays the power of hope as well.

In conclusion, this film displays the power of hope and how it effects people when hope is lost. Andy's unwavering hope brings "light" to others around him, possibly saving their lives.

10.title: "The Shawshank Redemption" (1994)
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences with its powerful storytelling and unforgettable performances. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, this film transcends the prison genre, delving into themes of hope, friendship, and the resilience of the human spirit.

Set in the confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film follows the journey of Andy Dufresne (played brilliantly by Tim Robbins), a banker who is wrongly convicted of murder and sentenced to life behind bars. Within the harsh and unforgiving walls of Shawshank, Andy forms an unlikely friendship with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (portrayed with depth by Morgan Freeman), a seasoned prisoner known for his ability to smuggle contraband into the prison.

What sets "The Shawshank Redemption" apart is its meticulous attention to character development and its ability to evoke raw emotions from its audience. As Andy navigates the brutal realities of prison life, his unwavering hope and determination to maintain his dignity serve as a beacon of light amidst the darkness. The bond between Andy and Red is the heart of the film, showcasing the transformative power of friendship in the most dire circumstances.

The cinematography is masterful, capturing the stark contrast between the claustrophobic confines of the prison and the vastness of the outside world. The haunting score by Thomas Newman complements the film's tone perfectly, further immersing viewers into its world.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is not just a film; it's an experience that leaves a lasting impact. It reminds us of the enduring power of hope, redemption, and the indomitable human spirit. Even after multiple viewings, its message resonates deeply, making it a true classic of cinema.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a triumph of storytelling, acting, and direction. It stands as a testament to the resilience of the human spirit and continues to be celebrated as one of the greatest films ever made.

10.title: Fantastic, brilliant and memorable.
10.content: This is with out doubt one of the best film ever made, it shows how the best of human nature can triumph in the darkest hour. The script is flawless and the acting is sublime. I've seen it more times than i can count and it never gets tired. Brilliant! The opening aerial shots of the prison are a total eye-opener. This is an amazing piece of architecture, strong and Gothic in design. Immediately, the prison becomes a character. It casts its shadow over most of the film, its tall stone walls stretching above every shot. It towers over the men it contains, blotting out all memories of the outside world. Only Andy (Robbins) holds onto hope. It's in music, it's in the sandy beaches of Zihuatanejo; "In here's where you need it most," he says. "You need it so you don't forget. Forget that there are places in the world that aren't made out of stone. That there's a - there's a - there's something inside that's yours, that they can't touch." Red (Morgan Freeman) doesn't think much of Andy at first, picking "that tall glass o' milk with the silver spoon up his ass" as the first new fish to crack. Andy says not a word, and losing his bet, Red resents him for it. But over time, as the two get to know each other, they quickly become the best of friends. This again, is one of the film's major strengths. Many movies are about love, many flicks have a side-kick to the hero, but Shawshank is the only one I can think of that looks honestly at the love between two best friends. It seems odd that Hollywood would skip this relationship time and again, when it's a feeling that weighs so much into everyone's day to day lives. Perhaps it's too sentimental to seem conventional, but Shawshank's core friendship hits all the right notes, and the film is much better for it. It's the kind of friendship that is honest, truthful and brings you back to the time in your life when the world was new and you and your friend owned it and in that sense it makes you think of another classic "Stand by me" by Stephen King. And it is this friendship and how the author, scriptwriters, director and cast manage to paint in colors that ring true to our heart that truly makes this film stand out.

10.title: The best prison movie
10.content: If there were any actor I would choose to narrate my life. It would be Morgan Freeman. Shawshank Redemption stars Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. Tim Robbins plays Andy Dufresne, a lawyer who gets framed for killing his ex wife and her lover. He is sent to Shawshank to where he meets Morgan Freeman and the two become friends. This is one of those movies where its good from start to finish that made me want to watch this movie again. This is the godfather of all prison movies. There are some prison movies that are great to watch, but nothing will ever come nowhere near as this. This is one of those prison movies where I felt bad for the prisoners and I also liked them as the movie progresses. Maybe not all of them, but the ones they focus on that's a different story. Shawshank Redemption is an adaptation of a Stephen King book and its fun to see a Stephen King book that doesn't involve a supernatural force being transformed into a movie. I'm not a big fan of prison movies because some of them try too hard to make us feel sympathetic towards the main character, but this one doesn't. It focuses on Andy who is shy at first, but as time passes he makes friends and he becomes more and more confident. And it shows that we as an audience actually and physically care about him that its not shoved in our faces where we can relate to him in some way. It's got heart and soul with fantastic acting, directing, music, and a script that's not rushed or a scene was thrown so it can add drama or intensity to it. The movie is two and a half hours long by the way, but it was so great and well written that I forgot I was watching a two and a half hour movie. What I liked about it was it wasn't trying to be the next big hit or be the next blockbuster. It told a beginning, middle, and an end that flowed perfectly that didn't feel pressured by Stephen King or Warner Bros. Everyone involved in Shawshank Redemption took Stephen King's book, sat down and all agreed that this is how we should make it, and that's all you need.

10.title: Hope overcomes everything
10.content:
This subtitle might sound a little cheesy, but in fact the movie presents us with a story of having to cope with a harsh reality, and in the end, managing to move on from it. The Shawshank Redemption always gives to me the feeling that it is separated between two very different acts. Although this separation isn't balanced in the runtime, it is, in a way, the manner in which the film is constructed.

At the beginning, we are introduced to Andy Dufresne (Robbins), a man accused of murdering his wife and her lover. He is sent to Shawshank Prison for life, and there he meets Red (Freeman), the man who can get you anything you want. Over the years, Andy will become good friends with Red, be brutally abused by a group of aggressive homosexuals, and participate in a series of scams orchestrated by the warden. All the time Andy spends in incarceration seems like a living hell, thus setting up the dark, absorbing environment of most of the movie's runtime. By the time we get to the last part of the film, we see a pleasant payoff that presents itself in a different tone, one that while sometimes present in the movie's gritty prison setting, lashes out fully in the last few scenes.

Directed masterfully by Frank Darabont, and with career defining performances from Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman, Shawshank lives on as a cinematic landmark. It's a movie that captures the essence of good storytelling and lives up to its legacy through that, while also being a competently made film, with a diverse soundtrack and a beautifully planned production design.

For me, The Shawshank Redemption represents assuming responsibility and coming to terms with a complicated situation, while also having the strenght to triumph over adversity. As Andy says, hope is what keeps a man mentally stable and in my estimation the most powerful feeling in a movie like this.

Rating 10/10

10.title: Great Movie
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption follows Andy Dufresne, a banker accused of the murder of his wife and her lover. In prison, he meets an inmate Ellis "Red" Redding, who Dufresne befriends. Redding is the narrator of the movie talking about his past experience at Shawshank. Over the 19 year period that the movie takes place, Red and Dufresne grow closer, and the tale follows tragic losses of friends, corruption of the prison's staff, and a great escape.

This movie is a great movie for those who like a 'justice served' type movie as well as a well written one. In general, foreshadowing indicates that the story is well written enough to the point where the writers can make a reference to the future about what is going to happen. In one scene, Dufresne is carving names into the walls in his cell block. The scene then shifts to Dufresne asking Red if he can acquire a poster (because Red is the guy who can 'get things' in prison). Throughout the entire movie, every scene in Dufresnes cell shows that poster. At the end of the movie it is revealed that the poster hanging on the wall was used to cover a hole that Dufresne had been digging since the night he was carving the names in the wall. He accidentally discovered how flimsy the walls were, and realized he could tunnel out. This makes the movie good because the scenes leading up to the end hinted at the fact that there was something special about the poster, however the audience was never sure. When it was revealed at the end, the audience can make the connection between that night he asked for the poster and the scene where the hole is discovered. Andy Dufresne is accused of murdering his wife and her lover, however it is never actually revealed if he did it or not. The movie goes along hinting that Dufresne is innocent and although it is never confirmed, I found myself trusting the fact that he did not do it. Throughout the movie, Dufresne is treated very poorly, such as being used to launder money for the prison due to his banking background. So when news comes in of a new inmate who confessed to Dufresne crime, Dufresne tries to convince the Warden that he is innocent and demands a retrial or probation. The Warden denies him but at a cost; Dufresne escapes and reveals the corruption at Shawshank causing the Warden to commit suicide to avoid arrest. In general, people who pity Dufresne in his position would feel that he won in the end, escaping the prison and revealing the warden's corruption. This is enjoyable because it has a sense of karma, where because the warden treated Dufresne so poorly, he got fooled in the end. Therefore, this movie is a good movie for people who enjoy social justice type movies, because Dufresne beat the Warden and escaped the prison, as well as for people who enjoy deep movies, that are well written, as demonstrated through the foreshadowing that the writers put into it.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption: A Tale of Hope and Freedom
10.content:
Few films manage to capture the essence of human resilience as masterfully as The Shawshank Redemption (1994). Directed by Frank Darabont and based on a story by Stephen King, this masterpiece immerses us in the life of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker unjustly sentenced to life in prison for the murder of his wife and her lover.

From the moment he arrives at the infamous Shawshank prison, Andy faces a harsh and unforgiving world. However, his intelligence, determination, and an unexpected friendship with Red (Morgan Freeman) make him a symbol of resilience and hope. Throughout the film, we see how his cleverness allows him to navigate the corruption of the prison system while planting small seeds of change in those around him.

One of the film's greatest strengths is its impeccable storytelling. Morgan Freeman's voice-over narration adds depth and warmth to the story, becoming an emotional pillar that guides the audience. Additionally, Roger Deakins' cinematography masterfully captures the oppressive atmosphere of Shawshank, contrasting the darkness of the prison with the light of hope that Andy represents.

But beyond its flawless technical execution, The Shawshank Redemption is a story about freedom in its purest form. Through music, books, and perseverance, Andy proves that even in the darkest places, the mind and spirit can remain unbroken. Its unforgettable climax is a reminder that patience and faith can break any wall, no matter how strong it may seem.

With unforgettable performances, a deeply nuanced script, and a powerful message, The Shawshank Redemption transcends the prison genre and stands as one of the greatest films of all time. It is a testament to the human ability to find redemption and freedom, even in the most adverse circumstances.

10.title: The Best Movie ever watched...WARNING SPOILER AHEAD
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a motivational drama which deals around the life of Andy Dufresne (starred by Tim Robbins) who has been sentenced to two life terms for the murder of his wife and lover. The main character, the hero of the film is Tim Robbins (as Andy Dufresne) who is a convicted former banker. The complete film is narrated through the point of view of another prisoner, Ellis 'Red' Redding (starring Morgan Freeman).

The complete movie revolves on how other people see Andy from the day of his arrival on the prison to the film's end. Starting with Red, who becomes Andy's best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. The film rotates around the life of prisoners. It gives an impression of how people lose hope and give up living. The life as portrayed in the movie shows how new prisoners are attacked by the previous prisoners to fulfil their need. It also shows how money can be used to get several items smuggled into the prison and bet based on the smuggled item. The key to the film's structure is that it's not about the hero but about the relationship we share with him - our curiosity, our pity and our admiration.

The movie's motive becomes clear when Brooks the librarian commits suicide after being released from prison. He committed suicide because he was lonely and adrift in freedom. It shows us the importance of hope in our life. Various examples of hope have been shown in the movie. Starting from Andy doing the accounts of the entire guards and warden to getting the government to pay for the renovation and upgradation of books in the library. The last act of the movie shows Andy's efforts and planning to escape prison. It took him approx. Twenty years to dig a tunnel in the wall hidden behind the Rita Hayworth poster. He dug the tunnel using the small rock pick. Not only did he plan his escape, he even laundered money from Warden Norton's account to a non-existing person account. Finally, when he escaped, he took the identity of that person and all the money. The final act in which Andy helps Red accept his freedom is deeply moving. This is so because Andy again operates at a distance, with letters and postcards, and is seen through Red's mind.

Overall, this movie is the best movie that I have ever seen and worthy of being called the best movie in the world. I will recommend this movie for everyone to watch at least once because it gives an impression of how one can bring the best of their abilities when people lose hope and thinking of giving up.

10.title: The Greatest Film Ever? Could Be.
10.content:
For those who have not seen The Shawshank Redemption, you have, so far, missed a genuine treat. I have seen hundreds of films. I don't think I have ever seen more than two or three that combined what I consider to be the five basic aspects requisite for consideration as a masterpiece. This is one of those films. The five basic elements are great acting--in which we the viewer see the character, feel the character, not the actor; a great score/sound-track; a cinematic quality that enables the viewer to experience the surroundings, not just view them; great dialogue and non-dialogue--the best scripts usually utilize not only the verbal abilities of actors, but non-verbal expression as well (see a film with Cary Grant or Robert De Niro to know what I mean); and most important a compelling story.

The Shawshank Redemption not only offers ALL of these, but does so at a level few films have ever reached.

The basic plot is simple enough: a man is wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and the man with whom she is having an affair. Why then is it so great? The performances, all around, but especially of Robbins and Freeman are so rich, so human, the viewer feels they are living their experiences. The film demonstrates, magnificently, how a man can create a meaningful life against horrid (mentally and physically) circumstances. The film wrenches the guts of its viewers, yet provides great satisfaction in the end. It is a great film celebrating determination, friendship, revenge (as sweet as you will ever see), education, and the basic goodness intrinsic to all people.

10.title: That's Really Called A Movie
10.content:
As a movie enthusiast, I recently had the pleasure of watching "The Shawshank Redemption" for the first time, and I must say, it left an indelible mark on me. This timeless classic, directed by Frank Darabont and based on a novella by Stephen King, is a masterful blend of drama, hope, and redemption.

Set in the 1940s, the film revolves around the life of Andy Dufresne (played brilliantly by Tim Robbins), a young and successful banker wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. Sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary, Andy must navigate the harsh realities of prison life, including corruption, brutality, and a sense of hopelessness that pervades the atmosphere.

At the heart of the story is the unlikely friendship between Andy and Red (portrayed impeccably by Morgan Freeman), a seasoned inmate who has become the institutionalized heart and soul of the prison. Their bond transcends racial and societal barriers, providing a powerful narrative thread that carries the film's emotional weight.

The film's strength lies not only in its compelling storyline but also in the exceptional performances of its cast. Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman deliver performances that are nothing short of extraordinary. Robbins captures Andy's resilience and determination, while Freeman's deep, soulful narration lends an added layer of depth to the storytelling.

"The Shawshank Redemption" masterfully weaves themes of hope, friendship, and the human spirit's triumph over adversity. The film is an emotional rollercoaster that tugs at your heartstrings and keeps you invested until the very end.

Additionally, the cinematography beautifully captures the essence of the prison environment, from the dark and oppressive cell blocks to the breathtaking moments of freedom found in the prison yard. Thomas Newman's hauntingly poignant musical score perfectly complements each scene, enhancing the film's overall impact.

Throughout the movie, the underlying message of resilience and the belief in the power of hope is exceptionally moving. It teaches us that even in the darkest of circumstances, the human spirit can prevail and find solace in the smallest acts of kindness.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is not merely a prison drama; it is a poignant tale of human endurance, friendship, and the pursuit of freedom, both within and beyond the prison walls. This timeless masterpiece has rightfully earned its place as one of the greatest films of all time.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic triumph that continues to captivate audiences worldwide, transcending generations. As a watcher, I wholeheartedly recommend this movie to anyone seeking an emotional and thought-provoking cinematic experience. Prepare to be moved, inspired, and reminded of the enduring power of hope and the strength of the human spirit.

10.title: Quite possibly the best movie of all time...
10.content:
First things first... This is my favorite movie of all time. Therefore, I was disturbed to see a few reviews claiming that this movie isn't all that great. Having only a few college credits remaining until I obtain a degree in Critical Film Analysis, I have studied this film numerous times and can tell you just why it is so great. First off, I read from another review that it was horrible because it was a first-time director. That just happens to be one reason why the film is so great to begin with. The director is passionate about the project since it is his first, and Darabont's passion is displayed magnificently in this film. The same goes for Kevin Costner (Dances With Wolves) and Sam Mendes (American Beauty). Both were first time directors and as a matter of fact both won Oscars for their Best Picture winning "first timers."

The other unlogical argument against this film that I read was about how "plain" it was. Heaven forbid that there is no computer enhanced bullets flying by a body being covered by dozens upon dozens of cameras (The Matrix) or some cheesy George Lucas characters that have no bearing on a story. The Shawshank Redemption is far from a plain movie though. The camera work IS amazing, just look at the scene where Andy is about to be pushed off of the roof that the inmates are tarring. That was pulled off WITHOUT a computer at all. Another argument that I heard: The story is too plain. Well I'm sorry that there is no Hans Solo pressing the *fill in the blank* button that will lift the *fill in the blank* to stop the *fill in the blank* from attacking the planet of *fill in the blank* that is inhabited by the *fill in the blank* race. The Shawshank Redemption is as real as it gets. Why introduce twenty million characters just for the shear joy of it? Darabont shows more emotion with Red and Andy than any other director that I have seen (possibly Sam Mendes may be better by a short bit). Without getting too much further into the film I'll just stop by saying that if you haven't seen The Shawshank Redemption there is a reason why it is #2 on the IMDB top 250 list. A good movie is enjoyable to watch, but a great movie will get you lost within the film and open a entire new world that you might never experience. You will lose yourself in the Shawshank Redemption. **I also recommend another Stephen King/Frank Darabont film: The Green Mile.

10.title: Shawshank? Redemption? A great movie with a bad title.
10.content:
When the film The Shawshank Redemption was released it was barely seen and hardly earned back its budget at the global box office. It is pretty surprising to consider this when one realizes that the story is by Stephen King, whose films based on his stories are usually well-known (if not well-reviewed).

The novella by King is part of his collection of stories found in the book Different Seasons, and the novella is entitled: Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption, subtitled: Hope Springs Eternal. Anyone who has seen the film knows that it is outstanding. The characters are realistic, the conflicts are life and death and the themes are deep and moving. One can't help feeling emotional during the last scene as the story resolves so beautifully. It was nominated for Best Picture even.

If I had one wish for this film it would be to go back in time and change the title, perhaps just using the novella's subtitle: Hope Springs Eternal. It may be a little on-the-nose, but it is so much more evocative of the themes in the film, especially since the word Shawshank has no meaning outside the story, and the word Redemption is used as a noun and begs the question, "redeemed from what?", again leaving the title as vague and uncompelling.

I can only imagine that the film would have actually won Best Picture in 1994 if it had been released with the title: Hope Springs Eternal.

You know, now that I think about it, I don't think there is more than one woman in this film.

This is interesting, because the fact is: this is a guy movie. This is the kind of movie a dad should watch with his son when he's having a hard time. This is the movie a guy would not be ashamed to feel emotional about.

It is the story of a man who goes to prison, but ends up coming out a better man because of his experiences. And it all ties together so nicely. The ending is especially touching, even as it moves from the main character (Robins) to the supporting character/narrator (Freeman). BY the way, the film was nominated for seven oscars and somehow didn't win any, which is a tragedy.

Every person in the world should see this film, even if you have to see it on TV, at least give it a shot, you will feel emotional at the end, but like the lead character, you will be better for it.

10/10

10.title: Copy From Someone
10.content: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair. The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest busload of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods. But Andy does not cry, and Red loses the cigarettes he wagered. Andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in Shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. Andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. He's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time. Red is also a lifer. From time to time, measuring the decades, he goes up in front of the parole board, and they measure the length of his term (20 years, 30 years) and ask him if he thinks he has been rehabilitated. Oh, most surely, yes, he replies; but the fire goes out of his assurances as the years march past, and there is the sense that he has been institutionalized -- that, like another old lifer who kills himself after being paroled, he can no longer really envision life on the outside. Red's narration of the story allows him to speak for all of the prisoners, who sense a fortitude and integrity in Andy that survives the years. Andy will not kiss butt. He will not back down. But he is not violent, just formidably sure of himself. For the warden (Bob Gunton), he is both a challenge and a resource; Andy knows all about bookkeeping and tax preparation, and before long he's been moved out of his prison job in the library and assigned to the warden's office, where he sits behind an adding machine and keeps tabs on the warden's ill-gotten gains. His fame spreads, and eventually he's doing the taxes and pension plans for most of the officials of the local prison system. There are key moments in the film, as when Andy uses his clout to get some cold beers for his friends who are working on a roofing job. Or when he befriends the old prison librarian (James Whitmore). Or when he oversteps his boundaries and is thrown into solitary confinement. What quietly amazes everyone in the prison -- and us, too -- is the way he accepts the good and the bad as all part of some larger pattern than only he can fully see. The partnership between the characters played by Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman is crucial to the way the story unfolds. This is not a "prison drama" in any conventional sense of the word. It is not about violence, riots or melodrama. The word "redemption" is in the title for a reason. The movie is based on a story, Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption, by Stephen King, which is quite unlike most of King's work. The horror here is not of the supernatural kind, but of the sort that flows from the realization than 10, 20, 30 years of a man's life have unreeled in the same unchanging daily prison routine. The director, Frank Darabont, paints the prison in drab grays and shadows, so that when key events do occur, they seem to have a life of their own. Andy, as played by Robbins, keeps his thoughts to himself. Red, as Freeman plays him, is therefore a crucial element in the story: His close observation of this man, down through the years, provides the way we monitor changes and track the measure of his influence on those around him. And all the time there is something else happening, hidden and secret, which is revealed only at the end. "The Shawshank Redemption" is not a depressing story, although I may have made it sound that way. There is a lot of life and humor in it, and warmth in the friendship that builds up between Andy and Red. There is even excitement and suspense, although not when we expect it. But mostly the film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything. If the film is perhaps a little slow in its middle passages, maybe that is part of the idea, too, to give us a sense of the leaden passage of time, before the glory of the final redemption.

10.title: 10 Perfect Moments From The Shawshank Redemption
10.content:
Twenty years ago this week, the film that we all know and love as The Shawshank Redemption was released in theaters. What started as a theatrical bomb that made little to no noise at the box office turned into a massive home video hit, a cable viewing staple for any good lazy weekend, and the top film on IMDB's top 250 list. What makes Frank Darabont's first motion picture in the director's chair different from any under-appreciated gem in the last 20 years of filmmaking is that for all intents and purposes, it's a perfect film.

Every line, every note, and every moment of The Shawshank Redemption hits you the exact same way that it did the first time you saw it. It's eminently quotable, memorably beautiful, and reads like an adult's bedtime story through the smooth voice of Morgan Freeman. Yet Shawshank's perfection lies not in the fact that everyone remembers a piece of it to call their own favorite moment, but it's the fact that there's such a wealth of moments to enjoy that when the film is mentioned in conversation, its genius is honored in so many different ways. In honor of the 20th anniversary of The Shawshank Redemption, here now are ten of the most iconic moments (besides the obvious choice of Andy in the rain after his escape) that make the story of Andy Dufresne a classic not only in age but also in storytelling.

This feature will contain numerous spoilers for The Shawshank Redemption. You have been warned.

Andy's Moment Of Weakness

We open The Shawshank Redemption with a good look at a drunk and desperate Andy Dufresne, played with expert style and brilliance by Tim Robbins. Drunk as all get out, and loading a gun to presumably kill his wife and her lover, we're shuttled back and forth between the night in question and the legal proceedings that will ultimately send Andy to Shawshank.

If this were any other film, those in charge would probably want us to know flat out that Andy didn't do it. Instead of taking that shortcut, Frank Darabont lets us mull over the possibility of whether Andy murdered the pair or not, so as to make it all the more rewarding when we take a shine to him, only to later find out that he is innocent.

Tommy Acquits Andy

As previously stated, the beginning of The Shawshank Redemption gives the prosecution and the audience a reasonable case to question whether or not Andy Dufrense was capable of murdering his wife and her lover. The state that he's in, matched with the icy demeanor he shows as he's put on trial work against Dufrense's defense, thus dooming him to his incarceration.

Yet one flashback/monologue ultimately acquits the character we've spent the entire film thus far identifying with, getting to know and like. In this acquittal, Frank Darabont not only acquits Andy of any wrongdoing, he acquits the audience for rooting for him. The mix of sorrow and joy is shared by both parties, and what happens after is just as equally invested between both sides of the screen.

Building The Library

Through dogged determination -- as well as a lot of paper, ink, and postage -- Andy Dufrense wages a one-man war with the government of the fine state of Maine. His endgame is to secure funds for the prison library, in hopes that the inmates will be able to enrich their minds and feel just a little bit more like free men in their time of imprisonment. Through one of the film's more comedic moments, his letters are ignored by the government, only to finally be answered.

When Andy Dufrense finds that answer (and it's monetary amount) unsatisfactory, he wages a second campaign that ultimately results in the library being given a regular amount of funding ($500 a year). Andy has proven yet again that he's a force to be reckoned with, and The Shawshank Redemption cements itself as a feel-good movie at its very core. Instead of hitting you over the head with its good deeds, it pokes some good-natured fun at them, while ultimately recognizing their importance.

Brooks' Final Days

As ultimately redeeming as The Shawshank Redemption truly is, it does have its fair share of tragic moments. One such moment is told through the eyes of Brooks Hatlen, a prisoner from the main gang we follow through Shawshank who is paroled after 49 years of institutionalization. While he makes his best effort, Hadlen ultimately can't handle the modern world and its fast paced ways.

With no support system and no help on the outside, Brooks ultimately takes his life after one last letter to his pals. At face value, this isn't a moment that would belong on a list like this; but I've chosen to include it because it develops the stakes of the film subtly. The whole time that Andy is yearning for his freedom from the walls of Shawshank, he's living among friends that fear that freedom because it could kill them faster than prison ever could.

Beers On The Roof

Morgan Freeman's role as Red is iconic for so many reasons. Chiefly among them the fact that his voiceover bathes the film's moments -- even the grimy ones -- in the glow of a bedtime story. One such moment that reflects this is the scene where, after Andy squirrels his way into the good graces of the guards on the roof of the prison, he and his compatriots enjoy an "icy cold Bohemia-style beer, courtesy of the hardest screw that ever walked a turn at Shawshank."

It's Morgan Freeman's voice over that ties this film together, both tempering the tragedy and enhancing the humor, but without going overboard on either side of the spectrum. More importantly, through this scene in particular, Red's retelling of Andy's story shows how the man he thought would crack first in his class of prisoners gave everyone he became friends with the hope and humanity that the prison experience took away from them. It's something that later saves Red's life, and in a big way.

Andy The Accountant

Andy Dufrense's usefulness as an accountant, as well as his tenacity, help keep him sane during his almost two decades in prison. In addition to keeping himself sane, it helps keep Andy in the good graces of guards that aren't even in the same prison as he is. After offering some free tax advice (that almost gets him killed), word spreads that Andy's a hell of a money man. In fact, the way that he works his tax magic for everyone and anyone, it's amazing that he wasn't already in prison on some sort of tax fraud charges.

Andy earns favor through his intelligence, and it you can see it make him so happy to be in charge of the guards that are in charge of him for once. If there's anything Andy values above all else in this world, it's his intellect; and his little accounting firm only helps keep him sharp. That sharpness comes in handy, as this not only gives him the cover for his escape, it also helps him net a huge chunk of cash to live on.

Andy Explains The Scheme

While working in his newly built prison library, Andy and Red discuss the financial scheme that he and Warden Norton are embarking upon with all of the kickbacks coming in to Shawshank Prison, courtesy of various public works projects. Red, curious as ever, wonders about the ins and outs of money laundering, as he's concerned about his friend's welfare.

With a smile on his face and a glint in his eye, Andy tells Red that it won't be he who ends up in front of a judge this time... it will be a phantom of a man that does. This moment is so infused with such child-like glee as Tim Robbins' Andy explains to Morgan Freeman's Red just how smart he is when it comes to cooking the books. Robbins' happiness is infectious, because not only does it flavor a standard moment of exposition for setting up the film's third-act twist, it's just so good to see Andy smile like a free man again.

A Day At The Opera

You know those moments where you share a movie or song you love with friends who've never experienced it before, and they turn out to be truly moved by its beauty? That's exactly what Andy attempts, and succeeds in doing, when he takes over the prison loudspeaker and plays "Duettino Sull' Aria from The Marriage Of Figaro, thus landing him in some hot water with the screws.

Andy Dufrense might be a culture vulture, but he's not above sharing with his friends inside. In fact, it helps him teach them the ultimate lesson about how to survive during their time in prison. It's the lesson that all of his actions throughout his tie in Shawshank have sprung out of: hope keeps a man alive. With art and the relative comforts of home, Andy manages to do just that for himself and all of his friends.

"His Judgement Cometh"

Throughout The Shawshank Redemption, Warden Norton (played by the always impressive "that guy," Bob Gunton) is equally a menace and a mentor to Andy. One moment he's swapping bible passages and allowing minor contraband in exchange for some minor money laundering, the next he's killing the only person that knows Dufrense is innocent in order to keep that operation going.

Yet the best moment in Warden Norton's arc has to be his attempted apprehension, and eventual suicide. Frank Darabont, in the injust and cruel world he created in the context of The Shawshank Redemption, manages to prove that even in an unfair world, the scales sometimes tip in the favor of the heroes. It is also a master class in building tension within such a fast-moving scene, especially coming off the high the audience should have experienced when they saw just how Andy escaped.

Thick As Thieves

If Red had killed himself at the end of The Shawshank Redemption, the whole film would have collapsed on itself. While a fair share of people who didn't deserve to die did just that, to have followed up the investment of all that time and energy into Red's parole hearings with a tragic suicide would have just crushed the audience like there's no tomorrow.

10.title: "Remember, Red, hope is a good thing"
10.content:
"Hope" is probably the word mentioned in many movies, many of which have inspired me with this very message. In recent years, this message has become stronger than ever in the real world. And of all the movies I've seen, this is the one that conveys this message most beautifully and completely.

I have watched this movie several times. For the first and second time, I found it to be a great movie, with a story that has depth and is perfectly developed, the characters all shine in their own way, albeit with a few forced details (like how did Andy get out of prison so fast?). The movie has a clear message, weight, and full of emotion at the end. But perhaps that is still not enough to accurately judge the quality of the film, until recently... I have experienced unexpected events, and this has severely affected the lives of me and my loved ones. Most coincidentally, I happened to re-watch the movie. It can be said that it has been a long time since my heart has been so touched by the lines in the movie.

"Remember, Red, hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies." The future is something no one can predict, but one thing is undeniable, this movie has lit up many broken and desperate souls out there, that is the power of The Shawshank Redemption, you will only be able to understand and feel the full message if the life you are living is experiencing something, a certain condition.

Andy Dufresne is probably a very good character, full of positivity, a strong desire for freedom. He's smart, hard-working, persistent, but naive enough to believe Norton will let him go when Tommy reveals the truth. This contrasts with Brooks. I'm not saying Brooks is a character filled with negativity, he's simply not as lucky as Red. It can be said that Andy is Red's hope. And people like Andy are hard to come by in real life, each of us is just Red, with reflections on life.

One day, I really want to watch this movie again, with such beautiful emotions...

10.title: Amazing
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless classic and one of the greatest films ever made. Directed by Frank Darabont and released in 1994, the film is based on a novella by Stephen King and stars Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman in lead roles.

The movie tells the story of a banker named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) who is sentenced to life imprisonment at the Shawshank State Penitentiary for the murder of his wife and her lover. Despite maintaining his innocence, Andy adapts to life in prison and eventually becomes friends with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman).

One of the things that make "The Shawshank Redemption" so powerful is its portrayal of hope and redemption in the face of despair. The film shows how even in the darkest of places, there is always a glimmer of hope that can help people survive and even thrive. The relationship between Andy and Red is a perfect example of this, as they help each other through the struggles of life behind bars.

The film also features outstanding performances from its cast, especially Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. Robbins delivers a nuanced portrayal of Andy, showing both his vulnerability and his resilience. Freeman, meanwhile, brings warmth and humanity to his role as Red, making him a character that audiences root for from start to finish. In terms of technical aspects, the cinematography, editing, and score of "The Shawshank Redemption" are all top-notch. The film's use of voice-over narration from Red adds an extra layer of depth to the story and helps to highlight the film's themes of hope and redemption.

Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece that deserves all the praise it has received over the years. It's a film that can make audiences laugh, cry, and feel inspired all at once, and it's a testament to the power of cinema to tell stories that resonate with people for decades to come.
