10.title: The Shawshank Redemption
10.content:
Classic review by R.E.

This is a film that is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman).

From Andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - Red, who becomes his best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'." The key to the film's structure, I think, is that it's not about its hero, but about our relationship with him - our curiosity, our pity, our admiration. If Andy had been the heroic center, bravely enduring, the film would have been conventional, and less mysterious. But we wonder about this guy. Did he really kill those two people? Why does he keep so much to himself? Why can he amble through the prison yard like a free man on a stroll? People like excitement at the movies, and other titles provide that. But there's a hunger for messages of hope, and when a film offers one, it's likely to have staying power even if it doesn't grab an immediate audience.

The movie premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September 1994, and opened a few weeks later. It got good reviews but did poor business ($18 million B.O.; only another $10 million after 7 Oscar noms).

There wasn't much going for it: It had a terrible title, it was a "prison drama", it contained almost no action, starred actors who were not big stars, and it was long at 142 minutes. This was a movie that needed word-of-mouth to find an audience.

Then, in one of the most remarkable stories in home video history, it found its real mass audience on tapes & TV. In five years, "Shawshank" was a phenomenon, a video best renter and seller. When the Wall Street Journal ran an article about Shawshank in 1999, it was first place in the IMDb vote of 250 best films.

Polls and rentals reflect popularity but don't explain why people value "Shawshank" so fervently. It does have entertaining payoff moments (as when Andy does all of the guards taxes). But much of the movie involves quiet, solitude, and philosophical discussions about life. The moments of violence are seen objectively, not exploited. The movie avoids lingering on Andy's suffering.

The Morgan Freeman character is carrier of the film's spiritual arc. We see him at three parole hearings, decades apart. The first hearing involves storytelling trickery; the film has opened with Andy's sentencing, and as we see the parole board we expect to listen to Andy's appeal. But, no, that's when we first see Red. In his first appeal he tries to convince the board he's been rehabilitated. In the second, he just goes through the motions. In the third, he rejects the whole notion of rehabilitation, and somehow in doing so he sets his spirit free and is released.

There's an underlying problem. Behind bars, Red is king. He's the prison fixer, able to get you a pack of cigarettes, a little rock pick or a Rita Hayworth poster. On the outside, he has no status or identity. We've already seen what happened to the old librarian (James Whitmore), lonely and adrift in freedom. The last act, in which Andy helps Red accept his freedom, is deeply moving - all the more so because Andy again operates at a distance, with letters and postcards, and is seen through Red's mind.

Frank Darabont wrote and directed the film, basing it on a story by Stephen King. His film grants itself a leisure that most films are afraid to risk. The movie is as deliberate, considered and thoughtful as Freeman's narration.

Deliberate, too, is the dialogue. Tim Robbins makes Andy a man of few words, quietly spoken. He doesn't get real worked up. He is his own man, capable of keeping his head down for years and then indulging in a grand gesture, as when he plays an aria from Mozart's "The Marriage of Figaro." (The overhead shot of the prisoners in the yard, spellbound by the music, is one of the film's epiphanies.)

Roger Deakins' cinematography is tactful, not showy. Two opening shots, one from a helicopter, one of prison walls looming overhead, establish the prison. Shots follow the dialogue instead of anticipating it. Thomas Newman's music enhances rather than informs, and there is a subtle touch in the way deep bass rumblings during the early murder are reprised when a young prisoner recalls another man's description of the crime.

Darabont constructs the film to observe the story, not to punch it up or upstage it. "When they put you in that cell," Red says, "when those bars slam home,that's when you know it's for real. Old life blown away in the blink of an eye. Nothing left but all the time in the world to think about it."

Affection for good films often grows with familiarity, as it does with music. Some have said life is a prison, we are Red, Andy is our redeemer. All good art is about something deeper than it admits.

10.title: An uplifting story of hope
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a compelling drama starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. The film is an adaptation of the novella written by Stephen King, "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption" released in 1982. In this 1994 film, we enter the dark world of Shawshank prison where monotony rules the lives of each convict found within its walls.

As we delve deeper into the dark world, we soon come to realize that corruption and violence are everyday occurrences, wielded by men in charge over those with no power.

Andy Dufresne, (Tim Robbins) was a successful banker wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. Upon his conviction, he is sent to live out his sentence behind the walls of Shawshank prison, where he befriends several other long-term inmates.

Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman) is one such inmate. Also, a convicted murderer, Red is a man who is known to be able to get things on the inside and thus spends his days making deals and bargains to get the men items they desire.

Andy and Red's lives intertwine as they build a friendship, learning from each other and their past mistakes. This film explores the power of unrelenting hope in the face of dire circumstances. Andy displays hope throughout the film as he makes himself useful to keep himself from going insane. He reminds the men of Shawshank that there are places inside that the warden and the institution cannot touch and inside prison is where keeping those places alive are the most important.

Andy finds himself working for a corrupt warden, embezzling money from the prison and in return the warden grants him some lenience's throughout his time in Shawshank. Andy is able to completely revamp the entire prison library and help several other inmates receive their GED's.

One inmate that Andy helps get his GED is a young prisoner named Tommy (Gil Bellows) who is sent to prison for burglary. Through circumstances, Tommy holds information that could potentially set Andy free, but this creates issues for the warden, as Andy is privy to all the corruption, he is behind and must prevent Andy from being released at all costs.

This film beautifully focuses on creating an environment within those prison walls through the use of slow cutting and lighting. Dark and gloomy days are created with the use of low lighting and stormy weather, but on the rare occasion of something beautiful happening within those walls, we are rewarded with bright lighting and sweeping camera angles. The script was artfully adapted for the big screen and tells an empowering story that we hold our own fates in our hands.

Another film that conveys the powerful theme of hope is The Bucket List. Another film starring Morgan Freeman that revolves around two older gentlemen from very different walks of life, who have decided they will complete all the things they wish to do before they "kick the bucket". This is an uplifting movie that reminds people that you are never too old to do new things and no matter what obstacles you face; undying hope will see you through.

This stunning, poignant, and profound film will leave you with a renewed feeling of hope that life, no matter how hard, can be overcome and we can find redemption in even the darkest of times.

The best so far I watched this movie when I was a kid and still the best for me The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest busload of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

But Andy does not cry, and Red loses the cigarettes he wagered. Andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in Shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. Andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. He's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

Red is also a lifer. From time to time, measuring the decades, he goes up in front of the parole board, and they measure the length of his term (20 years, 30 years) and ask him if he thinks he has been rehabilitated. Oh, most surely, yes, he replies; but the fire goes out of his assurances as the years march past, and there is the sense that he has been institutionalized -- that, like another old lifer who kills himself after being paroled, he can no longer really envision life on the outside.

10.title: "Shawshank" is probably the most perfect movie ever!
10.content:
What would you do if you were convicted of murdering your wife and her lover, and sentenced to two life-imprisonment terms? Would you just give up? Would you try to escape? How long would you have to live in prison before you lose hope? Writer-Director Frank Darabont (The Mist, The Green Mile) explores these situations, and the themes of integrity, hope, and freedom.

Tim Robbins portrays the character of Andy Dufresne, the man who's situation was described earlier. Andy claims he didn't commit the murders, but strong evidence overruled his claims. Did Andy really not do it? We never really know for sure until later on in the film. When Andy first arrives at Shawshank prison, he's antisocial, and goes along with the prison's routine for months. After a few months, however, Andy starts developing a friendship with Red (Morgan Freeman), a man who can get practically anything from outside the prison to inside, for a price. Andy asks him for a rock hammer. The importance of this rock hammer is evident later on in the film. But Andy's request for this rock hammer at the beginning of the film allows him to make a new friend at the prison to keep him company.

Andy's time at Shawshank prison causes it to change dramatically. Within a few years, Andy becomes an important aspect to the prison. His accounting skills help him receive benefits for himself and his friends by helping the prison guards with their taxes and other financial issues. The warden of Shawshank prison also takes interest in Andy, and soon uses him for a complex money scheme. Andy's role in the prison allows him to have a library established in the prison, as well as get beers and other things for his friends. Andy is basically making a new life for himself in the prison, but he still wants to get out. However, how many years does it take in the prison for him to give up? How many years does it take until the prison is your only way of life? This becomes a problem for many prison inmates, and even to a friend of Andy's.

One of the prisoners, Brookes (James Whitmore) is in this predicament. Brookes has lived in the prison for so long, for many decades, that it's all he knows. In the film Brookes gets released out of Shawshank prison, and is allowed to live a normal life; he has a job and a home. However, how does one live in a world that has drastically changed over the past decades? When Brookes was a little boy, cars were rare, but when he gets released from prison cars were everywhere. It's difficult to cope with, and Brookes is unable to deal with it. How long until Andy is the same way?

The film portrays two decades of Andy's sentence, with many different interesting story lines and conflicts mixed in, with many different characters. 'The Shawshank Redemption' has one important plot involving Andy's life in the prison and his hopes to escape, along with numerous side plots involving new inmates and such. The third act of the film is the quickest, and one of the most interesting parts. It involves a strong, yet completely unpredictable, resolution to the film. It also wraps up the lives of the main characters within the film in satisfying ways.

'The Shawshank Redemption' does an excellent job at portraying the themes of integrity and freedom, and how the prison can sometimes be some peoples' freedom, with the outside world being feared. Andy's integrity and hopes to escape from the prison is also a major part of the film. 'The Shawshank Redemption', adapted from the Stephen King novel, 'Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption', is a strongly-acted, well-written, and wonderfully-directed film. It's an amazing and inspirational piece of work, and probably the most perfect film I've ever seen. The plot is always at the same constant pace, and is never slowed down and boring. Every single part of the film is strong, entertaining, and thoughtful. It truly is a perfect film (this doesn't necessarily mean it's the the best film ever in the history of cinema).

PS: 'The Shawshank Redemption' came out around the same time as 'Forrest Gump' (1994). Both films are amazing and one of the best, but 'Shawshank' was overshadowed by the popularity of 'Gump.' But years later, 'Shawshank Redemption' was placed even higher than 'Forrest Gump' on AFI's 100 Years 100 Movies list. 'Shawshank' is also currently the #1 movie of all time on IMDb. Go figure.

10.title: Brooks Was Here.
10.content:
I don't know how to write this review. What I'm saying has been called and repeated like mockingbirds for the past 2 decades, and yet I feel like I must add.

I'll cut to the chase: BUY (not rent) BUY The Shawshank Redemption. And while people may call me basic and boring for saying it's my favorite movie, I don't think I love it the same way others do. I don't love this movie because of its cinematography or its cast or even its plot. I love this movie because it exists.

Some birds aren't meant to be caged. And while Morgan Freeman delightfully echoes this message into our ears, I don't even think this is close to the message of this movie.

Watching Andy escape and seeing the pure joy upon his face isn't the greatest part of this movie. Watching an old man die is. While that may sound incredibly grim, watching this harmless, near pitiful character, Brooks, become so stressed by the world around him, beautifully contrasting to Andy, is my favorite part. It makes me cry every time. And while some birds aren't meant to be caged, I think those who already have been cannot be freed. No matter how much you help them. Not Andy, not Brooks, not Red. No matter how long they spend out there, they aren't the same man as they stepped in as. No, they become such a different form of themselves that it's near impossible to put them together. Yet, you can't help but love it.

Freedom is Attained. Not given.

TL;DR: Watch this movie. Then again. And again.

10.title: The Ultimate Story of Friendship
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption (1994/Frank Darabont) **** out of ****

"I have to remind myself that some birds aren't meant to be caged. Their feathers are just too bright. And when they fly away, the part of you that knows it was a sin to lock them up DOES rejoice. Still, the place you live in is that much more drab and empty that they're gone. I guess I just miss my friend."- Red (Morgan Freeman)

This is the ultimate story of friendship. It tells the story of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a young hot-shot banker who is railroaded for a double murder in 1947. He is then sent to Shawshank Prison, where he soon befriends Red (Morgan Freeman), a man 'who can get things'. The movie spans almost 20 years, and shows the growing friendship of these two men. Joining them is the old pro James Whitmore as Brooks, who does a great job as a man who "lives in fear".

This is the best "feel good" movie of all time, and one of the best of the 90's. It is flawless in a departments. It is based on a short story by Stephen King, and is masterfully put onto the big screen. Freeman turns in his best performance, and has many great lines as the stories narrator. In fact, the film is well written and projects deep meanings of triumph and hope. Many critics have complained that the film is too long. Whomever truly believes this can not call themselves a film critic. The film is slowly paced to show the long growing friendship of Andy and Red. It's pacing is what makes it so real and excellent.

SPOILERS: The ending is the best part of the film, and has probably the best scene in motion picture history: Andy's Escape. The film's music plays a big part in this scene, showing Andy's determination and endurance. You end up rooting for him all the way. Another great scene is when Andy talks to Red after he gets out of the "hole". Red reveals his weaknesses and fears, but Andy has hope.

This film is a masterpiece of story telling, and should not be missed. Like I said in the beginning of the review, not only is the film flawless in all departments, it excels in every way. You will believe in hope.

10.title: Life Lesson Teaching Movie
10.content:
As a movie enthusiast, I have seen my fair share of films, but few have left such a lasting impression on me as The Shawshank Redemption. Directed by Frank Darabont, this movie tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a man wrongly convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison. While the premise may sound bleak, the film manages to weave together themes of hope, friendship, and redemption to create a truly unforgettable viewing experience.

The acting in The Shawshank Redemption is exceptional, with Tim Robbins giving a masterful performance as Andy, a man who is both intelligent and resourceful. He is complemented by Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, a longtime inmate who befriends Andy and helps him navigate life behind bars. Freeman's narration throughout the film adds a layer of depth to the story, as he reflects on his own experiences and provides insight into the lives of the other prisoners.

One of the most impressive aspects of The Shawshank Redemption is its ability to balance moments of humor and levity with more serious subject matter. The film deals with themes of institutionalization, corruption, and abuse of power, but it never feels overly heavy or depressing. Instead, the characters' relationships and interactions with each other provide a sense of hope and humanity in an otherwise bleak setting.

The cinematography and score of The Shawshank Redemption are also noteworthy. The film's muted color palette and use of natural lighting create a sense of realism and authenticity, while the music adds emotional depth and resonance to key moments in the story. The iconic scene in which Andy plays Mozart over the prison loudspeakers is a prime example of how the film uses music to enhance its themes and connect with its audience.

Overall, I would highly recommend The Shawshank Redemption to anyone who enjoys thought-provoking and emotionally resonant films. It is a powerful and poignant story of friendship, perseverance, and the enduring power of hope. Even after multiple viewings, the film continues to captivate me and leave me with a sense of awe and admiration for the human spirit..

It is entertainment at its best, featuring an amusing, rousing story of survival and redemption, while attaining those sincere, practical, and original qualities a "film purist" will heartily enjoy. You develop an intense bond with their struggles, and how they manage to overcome so many hardships and injustices, while still retaining confidence and hope. 10.title: A Masterfully Crafted Emotional Roller Coaster Ride
10.content:
I will not rehash the plot outline as many other reviewers have done a fine job of presenting it. Note, however, that this is not an action/adventure film. It is not fast-paced. It is grueling and harsh in part. But it evolves into a moving story of the triumph of indomitable human spirit over crushing adversity.

"The Shawshank Redemption" packs an intense and unforgettable emotional wallop. Thanks to a perfect blend of cinematography, acting, soundtrack, and plot development, the film takes the viewer on an unforgettable emotional roller coaster ride. It masterfully elicits powerful emotions running the gamut from the lowest lows to the highest highs.

I read a great number of other IMDb members' excellent comments on this film. I think it is safe to say that those of us who rate "Shawshank" among our favorite movies share one view in common --we truly FELT the impact of this film.

Some who disliked the film have argued that certain aspects of the plot are unrealistic. I must note that I thoroughly enjoyed the plot itself. Nonetheless, is every element of the story realistic? It really doesn't matter.

This is not a purely plot-driven vehicle. This is far more than a "life in prison" film. The prison serves as the framework in an ongoing struggle between hope and hopelessness under the most adverse circumstances. The beauty of "Shawshank" is the way it excels in evoking a great range of human emotions while presenting a fulfilling and moving tale of resilient human spirit.

Whether viewed as "true to life" or a parable, "Shawshank" succeeds in making us really care about the main characters. It is unsurpassed in making the viewer feel the full emotional impact of events as they unfold. It excels in making us feel fine gradations of despair and hope, cruelty and kindness, hatred and friendship, sadness and joy.

Along with the excellence of the film as a whole, I consider a certain scene among the most intense, fulfilling and memorable moments I have experienced in cinema. (I won't discuss it for the benefit of those who have not yet seen the film.)

"The Shawshank Redemption" is a true masterpiece of film making. It is unsurpassed in evoking a full range of intense human emotions as it proceeds to an unforgettable conclusion. It fully deserves its place as one of the all-time greats in film history.

10.title: Re-watch Necessary
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a film that has stood the test of time, and rightfully so. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, it is a remarkable example of storytelling on screen. The movie is centered around the life of Andy Dufresne, a successful banker who is falsely convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. He is sent to the Shawshank prison, where he meets a variety of unique and captivating characters, each with their own story to tell.

One of the most striking aspects of the film is the genuine acting displayed by the cast. Tim Robbins, who plays Andy, gives a masterful performance, perfectly capturing the character's stoicism and determination. Morgan Freeman, as Red, the prison's resident "fixer," brings a depth and authenticity to his role that is simply unmatched. The chemistry between the two actors is palpable, and their relationship serves as the emotional core of the film.

However, it is not just the two main actors who shine in this movie. Every member of the cast delivers a remarkable performance, from the corrupt warden, played by Bob Gunton, to the brutal captain of the guards, played by Clancy Brown. Each character is fully realized, with their own unique personality and motivations.

The film also tackles a number of challenging concepts, such as the corrupt nature of the prison system and the harsh realities of life behind bars. These themes are expertly woven into the narrative, creating a story that is both engaging and thought-provoking. The film also explores the idea of redemption, as Andy seeks to clear his name and find a sense of purpose in his new life.

One of the film's greatest strengths is its attention to detail. Every scene is meticulously crafted, with small details and nuances that can only be fully appreciated through multiple viewings. For example, the scene in which Andy chisels away at his cell wall using a rock hammer hidden in a Bible is a masterclass in visual storytelling. The slow, deliberate pace of the scene, coupled with the haunting music, creates a sense of tension and excitement that is hard to forget.

Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a brilliant masterpiece of filmmaking. It is a film that deserves to be watched and re-watched, with each viewing revealing new depths and nuances. The characters are unforgettable, the story is gripping, and the themes are universal. It is a movie that will leave you feeling both uplifted and contemplative, a rare combination in today's world of cinema.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a particularly good adaptation of Stephen King's work that is as close to a perfect film as one can have. It is a testament to the power of storytelling, and a reminder of the incredible talent that exists within the film industry. The attention to detail, the genuine acting, and the challenging concepts all converge to create a splendid story of triumph, defeat, adversity, and corruption. It is a film that will stand the test of time and continue to inspire and entertain audiences for years to come.

The film follows the story of Andy Dufresne, a successful banker who is wrongfully convicted of the murder of his wife and her lover and sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary.

10.title: Unraveling the Tapestry of Hope: A Shawshank Redemption Odyssey
10.content:
Frank Darabont's "The Shawshank Redemption" is not merely a film; it's an odyssey that navigates the tumultuous waters of despair and emerges on the shores of hope, leaving an indelible mark on the canvas of cinema. Released in 1994, this timeless masterpiece transcends the boundaries of its prison setting, delving deep into the human spirit and the redemption that can be found even in the darkest corners.

The film's brilliance lies in its ability to weave a tapestry of contrasting emotions with meticulous craftsmanship. At the heart of Shawshank is the story of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker convicted of a crime he didn't commit. Robbins delivers a tour de force performance, portraying the quiet resilience and unwavering hope that define his character. His journey is juxtaposed against the backdrop of Shawshank State Penitentiary, a place where brutality and despair reign supreme.

Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, the wise and weathered inmate, adds another layer of richness to the narrative. Freeman's voice, a soothing narration that guides us through the labyrinth of prison life, becomes the film's soul, resonating long after the credits roll. The chemistry between Robbins and Freeman is electric, forming the beating heart of the film.

Cinematographer Roger Deakins captures the essence of Shawshank with a visual palette that oscillates between the harsh reality of prison life and the ethereal beauty of freedom. The iconic scene of Andy's escape through the sewage pipe, underscored by Thomas Newman's haunting score, is a symphony of visual and auditory mastery.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is not a typical prison drama; it's a meditation on the human condition. It explores friendship, resilience, and the transformative power of hope. The film's emotional crescendo is reached in the final act, a revelation so profound that it reshapes the entire narrative, leaving the audience in awe of its sheer brilliance.

As the end credits roll, "The Shawshank Redemption" lingers in the mind like a cherished memory. It reminds us that even in the darkest of times, the human spirit has the power to soar. It is a timeless tale that stands as a testament to the enduring strength of hope and the possibility of redemption against all odds. Frank Darabont's magnum opus is not just a film; it's a beacon of light that continues to guide and inspire audiences on their own journeys of redemption.

10.title: A timeless masterpiece of cinema with outstanding performances, excellent writing, and beautiful visuals, exploring themes of hope, friendship, and redemption.
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a timeless masterpiece of cinema that has become a classic in its own right. Released in 1994, the film was directed by Frank Darabont and starred Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman in lead roles. Based on a novella by Stephen King, the film tells the story of a man's journey through the prison system and his eventual redemption.

The film is set in the 1940s and follows the story of Andy Dufresne, a successful banker who is wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. Andy is sentenced to life in prison and is sent to Shawshank State Penitentiary. It is here that Andy befriends a fellow inmate, Red, played by Freeman. The two men develop a close friendship, and Red becomes Andy's confidant and ally.

One of the most significant aspects of the film is its excellent writing. The screenplay was written by Darabont, who did an outstanding job of adapting King's novella for the screen. The dialogue is sharp, witty, and often poignant. The film's narrative structure is also impressive, as it weaves together multiple storylines to create a complex and compelling narrative.

Another essential element of the film is its outstanding performances. Robbins and Freeman both deliver powerhouse performances that are both nuanced and powerful. Robbins perfectly captures the character of Andy, a man who is intelligent, resourceful, and determined. Freeman, on the other hand, brings a quiet dignity to his role as Red, a man who has spent his entire life behind bars.

The film's themes are also incredibly powerful. The Shawshank Redemption explores the themes of hope, friendship, and the human spirit's resilience in the face of adversity. The film shows that even in the darkest of places, there is still hope and that it is possible to find redemption and meaning in life.

The film's visual style is also striking. The cinematography by Roger Deakins is stunning, with each shot beautifully composed and lit. The film's use of color is also noteworthy, with the drab and oppressive colors of the prison contrasting with the vibrant colors of the outside world.

Finally, the film's score by Thomas Newman is a thing of beauty. The music perfectly captures the film's themes and elevates the emotional impact of each scene.

In conclusion, The Shawshank Redemption is a cinematic masterpiece that has stood the test of time. It is a film that is both powerful and moving, with outstanding performances, excellent writing, and beautiful visuals. The film's themes of hope, friendship, and redemption are universal and will continue to resonate with audiences for generations to come.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Tale of Hope and Friendship
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of a typical prison drama. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, this film delves deep into the human spirit, exploring themes of hope, friendship, and resilience.

The story follows Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, and his journey through the harsh realities of Shawshank Prison. His friendship with Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), a long-term inmate, forms the emotional core of the film. Freeman's narration adds a layer of depth, making the audience feel intimately connected to the characters and their struggles.

What sets The Shawshank Redemption apart is its ability to find beauty and humanity in the bleakest of circumstances. Andy's unwavering hope and quiet determination inspire those around him, including the audience. The film's pacing allows for a gradual build-up of tension and emotion, culminating in a powerful and satisfying conclusion.

The performances are stellar, with Robbins and Freeman delivering some of their best work. The supporting cast, including Bob Gunton as the corrupt warden and William Sadler as Heywood, add richness to the story. The cinematography and score further enhance the film's atmosphere, making it a truly immersive experience.

Despite its initial lukewarm reception at the box office, The Shawshank Redemption has grown in stature over the years, becoming a beloved classic. Its message of hope and redemption resonates with viewers, making it a film that stands the test of time.

In conclusion, The Shawshank Redemption is more than just a movie; it's a poignant exploration of the human condition. It's a reminder that even in the darkest of places, hope can flourish, and friendships can thrive. This film is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates powerful storytelling and unforgettable characters.

I didn't intend to see this movie at all: I do not like prison movies and I don't normally watch them. I work at a branch library and one day as I was checking The Shawshank Redemption out to one of our older patrons, she said to me, "Whenever I feel down or depressed, I check out this movie and watch it and it always makes me feel better." At the time, I thought that was very strange. One day there was nothing on TV except things I absolutely would not watch under any circumstance or things that I had seen too many times already. I remembered what she said, so I watched it. I have watched it many many times since then and it gets better with every showing.

No action, no special effects - just men in prison uniforms talking to each other.

The Shawshank Redemption and To Kill a Mockingbird are the best movies I have ever seen. I do not judge it by it's technical merits - I don't really care about that. I have read that Citizen Kane or The Godfather or this or that movie is the best movie ever made. They may have the best technique or be the most influential motion pictures ever made, but not the best. The best movies are ones that touch the soul. It takes a movie like The Shawshank Redemption to touch the soul.

Set against the bleak backdrop of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film follows the life of Andy Dufresne (played brilliantly by Tim Robbins), a banker wrongly convicted of murder. As the story unfolds, we witness Andy's resilience and unwavering hope, which not only transforms his own life but touches the hearts of those around him.

Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Ellis "Red" Redding is nothing short of iconic. His narration provides a rich and insightful perspective, serving as the soul of the film. Freeman's performance is both poignant and deeply moving, capturing the essence of a man who finds redemption in the most unexpected of places.

The supporting cast delivers exceptional performances, each character contributing to the tapestry of the prison's microcosm. Bob Gunton as the ruthless Warden Norton and Clancy Brown as the brutal Captain Hadley bring an intimidating presence that contrasts starkly with the hope Andy embodies.

One of the film's most striking elements is its cinematography, expertly handled by Roger Deakins. The visuals seamlessly transition between the harsh reality of prison life and the transcendent moments of freedom and hope. The juxtaposition of light and darkness, both literally and metaphorically, underscores the film's central themes.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption, directed by Frank Darabont and released in 1994, is a critically acclaimed film based on Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption." The film stars Tim Robbins as Andy Dufresne, a banker wrongfully imprisoned for the murder of his wife and her lover, and Morgan Freeman as Ellis "Red" Redding, a long-term inmate who becomes Andy's close friend.

Set in the bleak Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film explores themes of hope, friendship, and resilience in the face of despair. Despite the harsh realities of prison life, Andy maintains his dignity and humanity. He uses his financial skills to help the corrupt warden and guards, which eventually leads to his plan for escape. Throughout the years, Andy and Red forge a deep bond, sharing stories and dreams of freedom.

One of the film's most powerful moments occurs when Andy plays Mozart's "The Marriage of Figaro" over the prison's loudspeakers, providing a brief glimpse of beauty and hope in an otherwise dark environment. This scene encapsulates the film's message: that even in the direst circumstances, the human spirit can prevail.

The Shawshank Redemption received critical acclaim upon its release, though it initially underperformed at the box office. However, it gained a massive following over the years, becoming a classic and consistently ranking among the greatest films of all time. The film's powerful performances, poignant storytelling, and exploration of themes like friendship, redemption, and the pursuit of freedom resonate deeply with audiences, making it a timeless masterpiece.

10.title: One of the greatest movies you'll ever, ever see.
10.content: BELIEVE the hype. Best film ever says IMDb ? Couldn't defend the Godfather's case if I tried, but this. This is just supreme cinema. You WILL NOT be disappointed by this, even with the seemingly excessive hype that surrounds it now, decades later. Everything is there...everything. Calling it 'perfect in every way' makes one just seem like a biased fanboy bereft of any objectivity, but really, on a number of levels, everything you will come to expect of brilliant, masterful cinema, you will find here. Its cinematography, plain but efficient; its length, just right, not one scene too long or too many. The acting, superb all-round, and the characters as vivid and efficient/relevant to the story as possible. The tension in the film: just right. We're always given compelling events to deal with, some rough and tragic, that just deepen the film more and more, while creating subplots and rejuvenating the story with newer elements, but while never straying away from the whole point of the film, which is, ladies and gentlemen, so touching and unique I'd have great difficulty to find a climax as beautifully directed, imagined and executed, and as magically cultivated scene after scene, until this utmost emotional eruption. The dialog, Freeman's narration, the complexity on so many levels and the layers of the plot, the theme of good vs evil, of never giving up, the thirst for justice, the intelligence manifested through the main character... This film is so beautiful, and masterful...it's quite possible, I'd have to admit...it's quite possibly the greatest film of all-time. 10/10 most certainly.

For those of you who rated this movie a 1/10: Shame on You! There is no way, even if you don't personally love the movie, that you can deny it's one of the best movies ever made. Just like there are some people who may not have personally loved the Godfather, Citizen Kane, Shindler's List, etc. and, therefore, gave those movies a 1/10. That's a bunch of crap. I personally didn't love the Godfather, but thats because it's not exactly my type of movie. That doesn't mean I bashed it and gave it a 1/10. I could see right away all the great qualities the movie had. So for those of you who voted 1/10 for shaw-shank, ask yourselves if it was really that bad, or was it just that you personally didn't enjoy it as much as everybody else...My guess is you would respond truthfully to the latter, so at least give it a 7, 8, or 9, not a 1. Thats all I have to say about that.

Now about the movie...The writing, the acting, the the music, the theme, etc. It's all as close to perfect as you will find in a movie. I don't want to write any spoilers, so let me just say that each and every scene of this movie is well crafted. It's the type of movie that keeps you on your toes from beginning to end. This is one of the only movies that I can remember that was so good, I forgot I was watching a movie. You can connect with the characters on such a personal level. Everything they do feels real. Nothing is under or overblown. TIm Robbins was the perfect cast for Andy Dufrane. Robbins' melodramatic personality lends itself perfectly to his character (Andy). As a viewer, you can never really tell what Andy is doing or thinking. Unlike most heroes, Andy doesn't make his objective clear to the audience. Morgan Freeman is the perfect actor for the character Red. Listening to him narrate the story is a real treat. I don't want to say anymore for those of you who haven't watched the movie yet. If you are one of those people, I wouldn't skip out on this movie. You will be doing yourself a disservice by missing this film. One of the best.

10.title: The Longest Film I've Ever Seen

This was, put simply, the longest film I've ever seen. I've spent many an hour watching movies. Some of them were good. Some of them were bad. Some of them reached me so deep inside that I spent days afterward thinking about them. But the experience, watching the film itself, always lasted between one to four hours.

With "The Shawshank Redemption," the experience lasted twenty years.

I wasn't bored. At first, I was skeptical about this film. Some movies which ranked high in the IMDb weren't worthy; for example, "Batman Begins." My skepticism was so strong that it prevented me from entering the film with awe. But after a while, I found myself completely immersed in Red's narrative.

It is useless to try and explain the experience of watching this film. But I can say one thing more.

This film was the first film that brought tears of joy to my eyes. I ended up smiling and then chuckling. And then I felt a streak of water run down my cheek. And I realized I just experienced the ultimate movie: the life story of people I wouldn't have known other wise, and as real and as good as it gets.

10.title: Great movie

After opening on 33 screens with take of $727,327, the $25M film fell fast from theatres and finished with a mere $28.3M. The reasons for failure are many. Firstly, the title is a clunker. While iconic to fans today, in 1994, people knew not and cared not what a 'Shawshank' was. On the DVD, Tim Robbins laughs recounting fans congratulating him on "that 'Rickshaw' movie." Marketing-wise, the film's a nightmare, as 'prison drama' is a tough sell to women, and the story of love between two best friends doesn't spell winner to men. Worst of all, the movie is slow as molasses. As Desson Thomson writes for the Washington Post, "it wanders down subplots at every opportunity and ignores an abundance of narrative exit points before settling on its finale." But it is these same weaknesses that make the film so strong.

I remember showing this movie to some friends after I'd seen it and a parent walked in about halfway through and asked "was it good?" they all said it was enthralling and amazing, then the parent added "what's it about?". There was a pause, because everyone realised that to summarise this movie would undermine what it is about in every way possible: every nuance and intricacy is important, and they deserve every minute of screen time that they are generously awarded. We grow into the characters so well that we aren't surprised by how they behave, because we can understand it. Even the apparently crazy antics of Brooks is wholly comprehensible. Then there's the music, amazingly visual and emotionally abundant in content. The movies so good that it doesn't need music to drive it, but when the music is of such astounding quality you begin to get a real resonance of mood, and an extra dimension of depth in the already amazing aesthetics of the cinematography. Whether everyone else is blown away by this movie doesn't bother me, because I will know how lucky I am. Lucky that I came across this movie, and lucky that I get it... that I really get it, in a way obviously not everyone in the world can. Anyone reading this should just hope they will fall into this category, and anyone who hasn't yet should just watch it again, and again, and again... (Please note, the ending is just as perfect as the rest of the package, but in-case someone hasn't seen it yet, I don't want to give it away).

10.title: One of the Greatest, Most Powerful, Uplifting, and Wonderful Pieces of Cinema Ever Conceived
10.content:
This is in my opinion, tied with Goodfellas for the greatest ever made. Masterfully conceived and directed by Frank Darabont, a powerfully adapted story from Stephen King's short story, amazing acting, and one of the best musical scores ever written made this movie one of the handful of masterpieces that will never die. Along with Goodfellas losing Best Picture, choosing Forest Gump(a great movie) over the Shawshank Redemption was the biggest mistake they ever made. The movie that makes many references to redemption and hope is like Jesus himself. The film did poorly in the box office but has enjoyed one of the greatest afterlives in the history of cinema.

Plot: The story is taken from Stephen King's short story "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption" and Frank Darabont made one of the only movies better than the source material. Masterfully crafted to start with a depressing image of everything the film goes to make one of the most uplifting, happy, and powerful endings in the history of film.

Acting: Narrating is Morgan Freeman who gives an Oscar-Worthy performance as Red a lifer for murder in The Shawshank State Prison. Tim Robbins likewise gives a powerful performance as the sympathetic Andy Dufresne a lifer for murder as well. Playing the cold and ruthless Mr. Norton the Warden is Bob Gunton who creates one of the greatest villains I've ever seen on screen.

Quality: This film is one of the greatest ever. One of the things that really made this film was probably one of the best, most uplifting and powerful musical scores I've ever heard which also deserved an Oscar. The camera work was also fantastic opening with a sky-view of the prison.

This is one of the few movies where if you don't see the genius of it I will have to question if you really seen the entire film or any of the film. This is along with Goodfellas the greatest movies ever. There are only a handful of masterpieces in history and this is one of them. Even less is the amount of films that will never die and will always stand the test of time. This is one of them. This is a film that you should just buy.

10.title: Get busy living. Or get busy dying.

Outstanding. Never has a film gripped so powerfully before. Some films are great and hold you well enough, but this absolute powerhouse of a film keeps me glued, and is a great tribute to Hollywood, the great Stephen King short story, and of course a great tribute to all the things that make hope and freedom so wonderful. Tim Robbins gives the performance of his life, as Andy Dufresne. A strong-headed man who is sent to Shawshank prison, wrongfully accused of "murdering his wife, and the fellow she was banging." With that in mind, it is excruciatingly tense and powerful, as we watch Andy adapt to prison life, form a beautiful friendship with 'Red' the convict who knows how to get things, (played brilliantly by Morgan Freeman, who in my opinion deserved to win the Best Actor Oscar) and of course see him handle himself around those out to get him, which spans from other prisoners to the warden, who he helps turn the prison into a business, due to his good experience as a banker, the occupation which he held before being convicted. But as the picture goes on, you can see the yearning to get out. He is a bird that has been caged wrongfully, and when you see how long he has been locked away for, even though he didn't do it it really makes for stunning and compelling viewing. The ending is beautifully scripted, and the mood is outstanding. Frank Darabont has created an exceptional film, with realistic talents and people we can care for. The stereotype of the prisoner is made into something better, and the overall experience of this film is magnificent, with fantastic memorable quotes, and an exchange of good to bad atmosphere, which at one point makes you feel good watching it, but then shows the awful atrocities and seriousness of the situation. This complex style of direction and storytelling is amazing, and the ending is top notch, I won't spoil this bit though. You wanna know how good it is? Then watch it and be dazzled by this truly remarkable film.

10.title: Literary ,Movie Review
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption A literary/movie review

It is often said that a book should not be judged by its movie; based/adapted on Stephen King's novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption the movie The Shawshank Redemption tries to oppose this claim. Frank Darabont, the director of the movie penned the screenplay to perfection (near about!) , having acquired the filming rights from his pen-pal Stephen King. Albeit He made some changes in the screenplay from the novella , these changes make the movie more watchable! Lets say Frank took some cinematic liberty which even bettered the movie from the novella. The strong voice of Morgan Freeman narrates the movie sequences for us. The character of Freeman is an Irish (Ellis Boyd Rankine ;called as Red in the movie whole time) in novella and Frank alludes to this fact when Freeman tells Andy Dufresne, "maybe because I'm an Irish." The story is obviously inspired from Leo Tolstoy 's story "God sees the truth, but waits." (Andy is wrongly? accused of murdering)The film also refers to Alexandre Dumas's "The Count of Monte Cristo" . Actually this scene is quite comic and funny. Heywood , a fellow convict of Dufresne's reads wrongly the name of Alexandre Dumas name as dumb-ass, then Andy corrects him and tells him that the book will interest Heywood that the book "The Count of Monte Cristo" is also about Prison break and Red (Freeman) says jokingly that the this book should also be put under Educational pile of books. Both the book and movie tells us about a smart banker (Dufresne) who is wrongly convicted through fate for the murder of his wife and her lover in cold blood. In the mid-way of novella and the movie We are told that there might be a possibility of acquitting , but while novella disperses this possibility gently , the film does something quite different and shocking, Another cinematic liberty!! Then the through the Banker or Red , we are acquainted with the hardships and cruel practices ongoing in the Shawshank Prison. How Andy Dufresne copes with the Prison environment and find new ways of amusement as in listening to opera, setting up of huge library and teaching fellow prison members. Of course his journey is not a smooth one. A major difference in physique of Andy is depicted in the movie from the novella,where Tim Robbins is Tall and strapping , Andy in the book is average height and of weak physique which makes him prone to attack of sodomites and how he fights them back. Both book and movie make us realize the price of freedom, hope and endless patience and perseverance. Andy picks up a curious habit which he used to pursue when he was free in his home which helps him a lot as we move through. Then movie shows the usual and Cruel! Prison officers and wardens, their scheming and corruption. How Andy fights them and overwhelms them is a study and pleasure to watch or read whichever you choose. P.S.-Rita Hayworth is Chekhov's Gun in both movie and novella!!!! Quotable Quotes- "Get busy living or Get Busy Dying"

10.title: It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison but its a classic.
10.content:
It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

From Andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - Red, who becomes his best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'."

The key to the film's structure, I think, is that it's not about its hero, but about our relationship with him - our curiosity, our pity, our admiration. If Andy had been the heroic center, bravely enduring, the film would have been conventional, and less mysterious. But we wonder about this guy. Did he really kill those two people? Why does he keep so much to himself? Why can he amble through the prison yard like a free man on a stroll, when everyone else plods or sidles?

People like excitement at the movies, and titles that provide it do well. Films about "redemption" are approached with great wariness; a lot of people are not thrilled by the prospect of a great film - it sounds like work. But there's a hunger for messages of hope, and when a film offers one, it's likely to have staying power even if it doesn't grab an immediate audience.

"The Shawshank Redemption" premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September 1994, and opened a few weeks later. It got good reviews but did poor business (its $18 million original gross didn't cover costs; it took in only another $10 million after winning seven Oscar nominations, including best picture).

There wasn't much going for it: It had a terrible title, it was a "prison drama" and women don't like those, it contained almost no action, it starred actors who were respected but not big stars, and it was long at 142 minutes. Clearly this was a movie that needed word-of-mouth to find an audience, and indeed business was slowly but steadily growing when it was yanked from theaters. If it had been left to find its way, it might have continued to build and run for months, but that's not what happened.

Instead, in one of the most remarkable stories in home video history, it found its real mass audience on tapes and discs, and through TV screenings. Within five years, "Shawshank" was a phenomenon, a video best seller and renter that its admirers feel they've discovered for themselves. When the Wall Street Journal ran an article about the "Shawshank" groundswell in April 1999, it was occupying first place in the Internet Movie Database worldwide vote of the 250 best films; it's usually in the top five.

Polls and rentals reflect popularity but don't explain why people value "Shawshank" so fervently. Maybe it plays more like a spiritual experience than a movie. It does have entertaining payoff moments (as when the guards from another prison, wearing their baseball uniforms, line up to have Andy do their taxes). But much of the movie involves quiet, solitude, and philosophical discussions about life. The moments of violence (as when Andy is sexually assaulted) are seen objectively, not exploited.

The movie avoids lingering on Andy's suffering; after beatings, he's seen in medium and long shot, tactfully. The camera doesn't focus on Andy's wounds or bruises, but, like his fellow prisoners, gives him his space.

The Morgan Freeman character is carrier of the film's spiritual arc. We see him at three parole hearings, after 20, 30 and 40 years. The first hearing involves storytelling trickery; the film has opened with Andy's sentencing, and then we see a parole board, and expect it's about to listen to Andy's appeal. But, no, that's when we first see Red. In his first appeal he tries to convince the board he's been rehabilitated. In the second, he just goes through the motions. In the third, he rejects the whole notion of rehabilitation, and somehow in doing so he sets his spirit free, and the board releases him. Advertisement

There's an underlying problem. Behind bars, Red is king. He's the prison fixer, able to get you a pack of cigarettes, a little rock pick or a Rita Hayworth poster. On the outside, he has no status or identity. We've already seen what happened to the old librarian (James Whitmore), lonely and adrift in freedom. The last act, in which Andy helps Red accept his freedom, is deeply moving - all the more so because Andy again operates at a distance, with letters and postcards, and is seen through Red's mind.

Frank Darabont wrote and directed the film, basing it on a story by Stephen King. His film grants itself a leisure that most films are afraid to risk. The movie is as deliberate, considered and thoughtful as Freeman's narration. There's a feeling in Hollywood that audiences have short attention spans and must be assaulted with fresh novelties. I think such movies are slower to sit through than a film like "Shawshank," which absorbs us and takes away the awareness that we are watching a film.

Deliberate, too, is the dialogue. Tim Robbins makes Andy a man of few words, quietly spoken. He doesn't get real worked up. He is his own man, capable of keeping his head down for years and then indulging in a grand gesture, as when he plays an aria from Mozart's "The Marriage of Figaro." (The overhead shot of the prisoners in the yard, spellbound by the music, is one of the film's epiphanies.) Because he does not volunteer himself, reach out to us or overplay his feelings, he becomes more fascinating: It is often better to wonder what a character is thinking than to know.

Roger Deakins' cinematography is tactful, not showy. Two opening shots, one from a helicopter, one of prison walls looming overhead, establish the prison. Shots follow the dialogue instead of anticipating it. Thomas Newman's music enhances rather than informs, and there is a subtle touch in the way deep bass rumblings during the early murder are reprised when a young prisoner recalls another man's description of the crime.

Darabont constructs the film to observe the story, not to punch it up or upstage it. Upstaging, in fact, is unknown in this film; the actors are content to stay within their roles, the story moves in an orderly way, and the film itself reflects the slow passage of the decades. "When they put you in that cell," Red says, "when those bars slam home, that's when you know it's for real. Old life blown away in the blink of an eye. Nothing left but all the time in the world to think about it." Watching the film again, I admired it even more than the first time I saw it. Affection for good films often grows with familiarity, as it does with music. Some have said life is a prison, we are Red, Andy is our redeemer. All good art is about something deeper than it admits.

10.title: My new favorite movie
10.content:
Before I saw this movie, it was hard for me to imagine why so many people liked it. I figured it must be one of those gritty movies that people like because of its harsh realism, but in truth it is so much more than that. In fact, I don't find it very gritty at all. I can now understand why it is the second highest movie on IMDb's Top 250 and why so many of my friends list it as their favorite movie. It is the most emotionally powerful movie I've ever seen and I doubt anything I see will top it.

Tim Robbins plays Andy Dufresne, a man convicted of killing his wife and her lover. Morgan Freeman plays the convicted killer Ellis Redding that befriends Andy in prison. These are two very touching and true performances. Tim Robbins should have at least been nominated for an Oscar for the quiet intensity he brought to his role. He takes on the right sense of mystery required for the role and he gives the movie the conviction it needs to reach its emotional heights. Marlon Brando claimed that some roles are actor-proof- the story is so good that no actor can mess it up. This could possibly be one of those roles, but I can't help feeling that a lesser actor would have overacted and destroyed Robbins's character. Morgan Freeman was nominated, and justly so (though it is an injustice that he was chosen above Robbins; they both are equals in this movie). He complements Robbins beautifully as a stoic man that understands prison life better than anyone else. He also narrates the movie; we see things through his eyes and experience things through his words. As in Million Dollar Baby, his voice provides the movie with its thematic focus. The supporting cast is fine, but James Whitmore stands out as the prison librarian.

The actors do not make this a great movie though. They were given a great story and they lived it for us perfectly, but it is the story that lives on after the movie is over. Stephen King may be a pop fiction author, but he has an extraordinary grasp on human nature which is brought to light in Shawshank.

Marlon Brando also said that movies are good because of what we bring to them, and I suppose there's some truth in that, though there are some movies that are good no matter what- Casablanca and Citizen Kane, for example. I don't know which category this movie belongs to and I'm afraid that because I love it so much I don't trust myself to say. I can say, however, that everyone can identify with the triumph of the human spirit, and maybe that explains why it is such a beloved movie.

It really is a shame that The Shawshank Redemption came out in 1994, the same year as Forrest Gump and Pulp Fiction. All three are great movies, and all three deserved Best Picture. But to me, Shawshank is the best of them all and will continue to resonate with me for a long time to come.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption Review
10.content: The Shawshank Redemption isn't your average movie with big explosions, gun fights, or super heroes instead its just a simple movie about a friendship that forms between two prisoners each serving a life sentence for murder. My favorite thing about the movie is all of the remember able quotes that you can take from it. Mine is a conversation between the district attorney and Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) the conversation goes like this District Attorney: "And that also is very convenient, isn't it, Mr. Dufresne"? Andy: "Since I am innocent of this crime, sir, I find it decidedly inconvenient that the gun was never found." Out of all of the amazing quotes from this movie this is my favorite because it says early in the film the this character can be funny even at his own murder trial and he can be a little sarcastic to. Another reason I really enjoyed the film was watching how the writers of the movie developed the relationship of Red (Morgan Freeman) and Andy overtime. The first time Red saw Andy he says "I didn't think much of Andy the first time I saw him", but they would develop a very strong friendship as the movie goes on. Every character in this movie is different from any other character in someway. Red is seems to be wise, nice, and doesn't ever stress out ever. Andy is clever, smart, and what seems to be a good person. Warden Norton seems to be evil, manipulative, and controlling. Something that is a bit ironic from this movie is that most the prisoners seem to nice guys while Norton and the guards seem to be the real criminals I thought it was inserting that makers of the movie decided to kind of change the ways we are used to seeing things. The thing the movie shows the best is that with time everything can change for example Andy was once just a banker until he he went to prison and meet Red which probably was the most meaningful thing he ever did in his life. Although the story may look like your same old prison movie its not it has many unexpected twist through out the whole movie. Most films you watch today just focus on action and big name actors but, this isn't one of those movies it gives real attention to the story being to told and even two friends talking in the prison yard will have you on the edge of your seat and wondering what is going to happen next. This is one of those movie you watch 5 times and still enjoyed it and catch something new you hadn't noticed before. This movie will be talked about for many many more years ahead and will never get old. The Shawshank Redemption was nominated more 7 Oscars and in my opinion has the best acting of any film I have ever seen. So if you feel like taking a break from your normal blockbuster movie and sees and movie that tells a great story of hope and friendship then I would highly recommend watching this movie.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption" (1994) stands as a masterpiece that transcends time
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" (1994) stands as a masterpiece that transcends time. Frank Darabont's adaptation of Stephen King's novella is a captivating tale of hope, resilience, and the human spirit.

Set within the walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film follows the journey of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, and his friendship with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman). The narrative navigates through years of Andy's life behind bars, showcasing his quiet determination, unwavering hope, and his profound impact on those around him.

The performances are exceptional, with Robbins delivering a nuanced portrayal of a man maintaining dignity amidst adversity, while Freeman's narration adds depth and introspection, anchoring the film's emotional core. The supporting cast, including Bob Gunton as the ruthless Warden Norton, adds layers to the narrative, creating a richly textured prison environment.

The film's cinematography captures both the bleakness of confinement and the resilience of the human spirit. The iconic scenes, from Andy's defiant escape to moments of quiet camaraderie among the inmates, resonate long after the credits roll. Thomas Newman's hauntingly beautiful score further elevates the emotional impact of each scene, enhancing the storytelling.

What makes "The Shawshank Redemption" enduring is its universal message of hope and redemption. It's a testament to the power of inner strength and perseverance in the face of adversity. The themes of friendship, survival, and the quest for freedom resonate with audiences, making it a timeless classic that continues to captivate and inspire generations.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic gem that excels in storytelling, performances, and emotional depth. It's a film that stays etched in the hearts of viewers, reminding us of the resilience of the human spirit against all odds.

10.title: Stephen King wrote an amazing story; Frank Darabont did it justice.
10.content:
This movie is amazing, no doubt about it. Forget about all the people saying it's the most overrated movie of all time, they're just bitter. Maybe Shawshank didn't have the most amazing, jaw-dropping cinematography, camera work, etc. ever from start to finish (all the things that made films such as the Godfather so great. Granted, it's not like Shawshank had a lot to work with since a majority of the film was set at the prison), but it had an enjoyable, moving, inspirational story. It also had really enjoyable characters, particularly Andy Dufresne, who is my favorite fictional character. I liked him from the start.

Anyway, I think the Shawshank Redemption is the highest rated movie on this site because it's simply a great film. Easy to understand and follow, easy to love, and easy to be moved by. As IMDb has in the FAQ for this movie, "It is perhaps worthwhile to remember that the top 250 list doesn't really measure what individuals consider the best movies of all time. It measures the collective opinion of the films in which people have the greatest positive feel when they are rating it. People are not voting for the movie against other movies. They are voting for it based on their opinion at the time have decided to rate it on IMDb." So, when people complain about how it's overrated, just think about that.

Tim Robbins, when asked about why he chose to do this movie, (in addition to saying how he was moved and inspired by the story) said, "it's not just about prison. It's about the limitations we put on ourselves and life, and the limitations, more importantly, we allow others to place on us. And if we listen to them, and we believe what these people are saying to us, then we're really building walls around ourselves. We're really building our own prison What the film is saying in a larger way is that in order to keep alive and keep living in a strong and thorough way that oftentimes you have to look beyond the walls around you. And you have to not believe in the prison and believe in that light, and that hope, and that person that you think you can be, and the person that you believe you are, and not listen to what your boss is saying, what your spouse is saying, what your leaders are saying." I don't think I can elaborate much further. The Shawshank Redemption taught me to hold onto hope and believe in myself. I'm reminded of that Emily Dickinson poem, "Hope is the Thing with Feathers," and I think it represents a lot of what Andy stood for.

10.title: Quite simply, the best story in the history of motion pictures.
10.content:
This is a story about the despair of life in prison, as well as the friendship and hope that can be found and maintained within its walls, against all odds.

As mentioned above, and as far as I am concerned, this movie is the best of all time. I have lost count of the number of times I have seen this movie, and it touches me every time I watch it. As a matter of fact, I just finished watching this movie on television, on a cable channel that cannot seem to get enough of showing this film. I'm sure you know the one I mean, because they have shown this movie dozens of times, usually back to back. If you are a fan of this film, I'm sure you watch it every time it is on, much like I do, and are always amazed, yet again, at the end of it.

This film is written so eloquently that I doubt much could top it. Having not read the original short story by Stephen King (which is titled "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption"), I cannot comment on the accuracy of the movie in relation to his telling of story. However, I'm sure that it does justice to King's writing. Frank Darabont, who wrote the screenplay and directed Shawshank, also wrote the screenplay for and directed King's other prison film, The Green Mile, which also should not be missed.

The acting here is excellent, but I doubt anybody would be surprised at that, given the cast present here. Morgan Freeman (Se7en, Deep Impact, Kiss The Girls) has shown time and time again that he is one of Hollywood's best and most underrated actors, and he certainly shines here as Red, the man who "knows how to get things." Freeman's narration is superb, I doubt a better job could have been done by anyone else. In the history of film, people such as James Earl Jones and Martin Sheen never fail to provide narration that is highly eloquent, but this film shows that Freeman deserves to be in the same category as those two actors. Tim Robbins does a great job as Andy Dufresne, an innocent man who knows he will remain in prison for a long time to come, but refuses to give up hope.

Despite excellent writing and acting, however, I believe the most poignant thing about this film is the score. Present at the best times, and lacking when it should be, the use of the score for this film helps set the tone and the mood for almost every scene. Obviously, in a film set in a prison, there isn't much happiness to go around. However, certain scenes in this film are defined by the score that goes with them, making the viewer look twice at a scene which would otherwise be quite drab and seemingly unimportant, and making them appear different than they are, thus impressing the theme of hope on the viewer in an almost subconscious fashion.

Historically, of course, this film will never be viewed with the respect and honor it deserves, especially with newer, more appealing prison-based films available, such as the aforementioned The Green Mile. It is unfortunate that Shawshank didn't win the Academy Awards it was nominated for, because it certainly deserved them. However, during its Oscar year, it was up against a little Tom Hanks vehicle called Forrest Gump, a movie which held back most others that year, and deservedly so. As often happens, seemingly to avoid one particular film taking home all the gold, Oscars were awarded to other films over Forrest Gump that year in various categories, and it's too bad that Shawshank wasn't one of them.

I guarantee that you will love the characters of Andy & Red, along with the interaction between them; hate Warden Norton and his sniveling sidekick Captain Hadley; and be moved by the eloquent ending of this fantastic and unforgettable film. It truly is an experience not to be missed.

10/10, and I'd give it an 11 if I could.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a critically acclaimed 1994 film directed by Frank Darabont, based on Stephen King's novella of the same name. It tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is wrongfully convicted of murder and sentenced to a life term in Shawshank State Penitentiary.

The film is known for its gripping storytelling, exceptional performances, and powerful themes of hope and redemption. The performances by Tim Robbins as Andy Dufresne and Morgan Freeman as Red, a fellow inmate and narrator of the story, are particularly noteworthy. Robbins brings a quiet strength and determination to his role, while Freeman delivers a commanding and heartfelt performance that has become one of his most memorable.

The film skillfully explores the harsh reality of life in prison, touching on themes of institutionalization, friendship, and finding meaning in the face of adversity. It portrays the bond that develops between Andy and Red, as well as their efforts to maintain their dignity in a brutal and dehumanizing environment.

Visually, the film is well-crafted, capturing the starkness of the prison setting while also highlighting moments of beauty and hope. The cinematography effectively conveys the passage of time and the emotional journeys of the characters.

"The Shawshank Redemption" has received widespread critical acclaim and has earned its place as one of the greatest films of all time. It was nominated for seven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, although it did not win any. Despite this, it has gained a significant following over the years and has achieved a cult status.

Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a thought-provoking and emotionally resonant film that explores the indomitable spirit of human beings in the face of adversity. It continues to captivate audiences with its powerful performances, engaging storytelling, and universal themes of hope and redemption.

10.title: Must see
10.content:
Red's narration of the story allows him to speak for all of the prisoners, who sense a fortitude and integrity in Andy that survives the years. Andy will not kiss butt. He will not back down. But he is not violent, just formidably sure of himself. For the warden (Bob Gunton), he is both a challenge and a resource; Andy knows all about bookkeeping and tax preparation, and before long he's been moved out of his prison job in the library and assigned to the warden's office, where he sits behind an adding machine and keeps tabs on the warden's ill-gotten gains. His fame spreads, and eventually he's doing the taxes and pension plans for most of the officials of the local prison system.

There are key moments in the film, as when Andy uses his clout to get some cold beers for his friends who are working on a roofing job. Or when he befriends the old prison librarian (James Whitmore). Or when he oversteps his boundaries and is thrown into solitary confinement. What quietly amazes everyone in the prison -- and us, too -- is the way he accepts the good and the bad as all part of some larger pattern than only he can fully see.
