10.title: An Analysis of "The Shawshank Redemption", Frank Darabont created a masterpiece and a film you can always go back to, it's beloved for many reasons
10.content:
The film begins with Andy Dufresne being sentenced for life because of killing his wife and her lover, a crime he had the motives for but never did. Thus begins Shawshank Redemption, a film I've seen multiple times and the first time was in high school. It was one of those films that stuck with me for a long time and when I watched it as I grew older, the film hit me much more with his emotional impact and the deep emotional depth it has. You see, Shawshank Redemption is a film you can rewatch multiple times and find something new to like, details you've never seen before, and plainly be entertained for 142 minutes. Now, it has been around 6 years since I last saw the film and I'm as impressed now since then. It's the first time watching it on 4k blu-ray and I'm even more impressed, mainly because of the musical score, I've never appreciated the soundtrack before but with the Dolby Atmos track it just hits differently. Same with the sound design, it's terrific and you truly hear the prison fence rattling and the loud crowd when Andy Dufresne enters the prison. The picture quality is truly mesmerizing, photographed brilliantly by Roger Deakins who's among the best cinematographers in Hollywood. Back to the 4k transfer, with the HDR and Dolby Vision, the color grading is just phenomenal. From a reviewer at High-Def Digest, "Though the palette remains drab for most of the movie, splashes of color make huge impressions. Bold, brassy reds, verdant greens, and cool blues grab attention, and the orange glow that bathes the picture during its final half-hour exudes a wonderful cozy warmth. Inky blacks anchor the image, the bright, crisp whites never bloom, and superior shadow delineation allows us to drink in the dank, foreboding atmosphere of the prison cells. Fine details pop off the screen - the prison's rusted metal, chipped paint, and worn wood, the checkerboard's texture, the contours and shadings of the stone walls, the weave of the prison uniforms, and the most delicate pinstripes on suits - while razor-sharp close-ups highlight stray hairs, facial blemishes, pores, tiny knicks and cuts, and hair follicles (even on hands and fingers)."

Over the course of several years, two convicts form a friendship, seeking consolation and, eventually, redemption through basic compassion.

The plot of Shawshank Redemption follows Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding (played superbly by Morgan Freeman) who does the narration for the film, narrating the story of Andy Dufresne (played brilliantly by Tim Robbins). Although the film is quite long, the pacing is perfect and you'll never get bored watching this film, following Dufresne as years go by in the prison. From being brutally beaten to using his education and work as a banker to his potential. It's one subplot which has stayed with me the longest, the character of Brooks Hatlen (a memorable character and performance from James Whitmore) who's an elderly prison librarian, imprisoned at Shawshank for over five decades. The subplot comes into play halfway through the film, with his parole being accepted and what does he do? He becomes so depressed and scared that he loses it and sees the only way for him to stay is to kill one of his friends, but he never does, a scene where Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman along with James Whitmore give superb performances. Brooks is probably the easiest character to sympathize with, how hard it must be to leave a place which has been your 'home' for the past five decades, and not getting the opportunity to stay. When Brooks lets Jake, the crow, fly away. It's like he's letting himself fly off, to somewhere better, something he does later in the climax. The climax of his subplot which goes hand in hand with the overall story, is truly heartbreaking. There's something Red says as Brooks leaves the prison, how the life sentence is the prison taking their lives away from them, what they ultimately did to Brooks. He took his own life in a heartbreaking scene which moves the rest of the story forward. The story of Shawshank Redemption is truly spectacular and memorable, the screenplay and story by Frank Darabont but I would say it's the attention to detail and every scene he crafts, the mise-en-scene. It's his vision and the camera work used in the film is beyond excellent, from the close ups and other angles like the beating inside the cinema projector room where the camera is on the ceiling and we get to see the whole room. That's one of many truly beautiful shots. You can just pause whenever and you'll see a still photo worth looking at.

Shawshank Redemption was a failure at the box-office during its theatrical release, yet went on to receive multiple award nominations, including seven Academy Award nominations. Now, it's one of the most beloved films and also among the greatest films of all time. Something I agree with, deeply. It's a film with such depth and perhaps one of the best adaptations of a Stephen King novel, along with Stand By Me. With another filmmaker and cinematographer, I'm sure this film wouldn't have been as great as it was. Frank Darabont created a masterpiece. The performances by Morgan Freeman and Tim Robbins are absolutely perfect. Thomas Newman's musical score enhances each scene and contributes so much to the film. There are also compelling themes in the film, Christianity being a major one, but also another one. Film critic Roger Ebert argued that The Shawshank Redemption is an allegory for maintaining one's feeling of self-worth when placed in a hopeless position. Andy's integrity is an important theme in the story line, especially in prison, where integrity is lacking. Roger Ebert wrote in his review, "Shawshank slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope." continuing, "Watching the film again, I admired it even more than the first time I saw it. Affection for good films often grows with familiarity, as it does with music. Some have said life is a prison, we are Red, Andy is our redeemer. All good art is about something deeper than it admits." Like Ebert, I admire it more the more I watch it. Shawshank Redemption is like I wrote, a masterpiece. Some of the best storytelling I've ever seen and worthy to be on many critics list of best movies. It also has one of the best endings I've ever seen. This is one of my all time favorites.

10.title: Shawshank Redeems Hollywood
10.content:
Shawshank Redeems Hollywood Can Hollywood, usually creating things for entertainment purposes only, create art? To create something of this nature, a director must approach it in a most meticulous manner, due to the delicacy of the process. Such a daunting task requires an extremely capable artist with an undeniable managerial capacity and an acutely developed awareness of each element of art in their films, the most prominent; music, visuals, script, and acting. These elements, each equally important, must succeed independently, yet still form a harmonious union, because this mixture determines the fate of the artist's opus. Though already well known amongst his colleagues for his notable skills at writing and directing, Frank Darabont emerges with his feature film directorial debut, The Shawshank Redemption. Proving himself already a master of the craft, Darabont managed to create one of the most recognizable independent releases in the history of Hollywood. The Shawshank Redemption defines a genre, defies the odds, compels the emotions, and brings an era of artistically influential films back to Hollywood.

The story begins with the trial of a young banker, Andy Dufrense, victimized by circumstantial evidence, resulting in a conviction for the murder of his wife and her lover. After a quick conviction, Andy finds himself serving a life sentence at Shawshank prison, with no hope of parole. He exists in this prison only in appearance, keeping his mind free from the drab walls around him. His ability to do this results in the gaining of respect from his fellow inmates, but most of all from Ellis Redding. Ellis, commonly referred to as Red, finds gainful use of his entrepreneurial spirit within the drab walls of Shawshank by dealing in contraband and commodities rare to the confines of prison. Andy's demeanor and undeniable sense of hope causes Red to take a deeper look at himself, and the world around him. Andy proves to Red and the other inmates that in the conventional walls of Shawshank prison convention will find no home in his lifestyle.

By creating the film's firm foundation, the meticulously chiseled screenplay paved the way for this film's success. Frank Darabont outdoes himself with the phenomenal adaptation of Stephen King's equally noteworthy novella, Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption. In this novella, King demonstrates that he can break free from the genre he dominates and still create a marvelous piece of modern literature. Though the film mirrors the novella in many ways, Darabont illustrates a focused objective of improving upon the areas where the novella came up short, resulting in one of the best book to film transitions ever.

10.title: Hope Unshackled: The Inimitable Mastery of The Shawshank Redemption

As a born in 2005, my earliest memories of The Shawshank Redemption are of glimpses on my dad's old squared television set, with images of the warden ripping off the poster in Andy's cell etched in my mind. I can't recall the first time I watched it, as it feels like it has been a part of my movie-watching journey for as long as I can remember. However, as I grew older and my love for films deepened, I began to truly appreciate the beauty of this movie.

I started noticing the intricate details that director Darabont planted throughout the film, such as the deliberate use of camera angles to highlight the contrasting journeys of characters like Red and Brooks as they left the prison. These subtle nuances added depth and richness to the storytelling, elevating my admiration for the film.

But it wasn't until I matured even more that I grasped the profound thematic elements that make The Shawshank Redemption a masterpiece. The film's portrayal of hope as an unstoppable force in the face of adversity resonated deeply with me. It revealed how hope can transcend the confines of imprisonment, and its portrayal in the film was truly compelling and thought-provoking.

Of course, my appreciation for The Shawshank Redemption is just the tip of the iceberg. The film's artistry, from its storytelling to its performances, is unmatched. It is a true piece of cinematic art that has stood the test of time and continues to captivate audiences. If you haven't seen it yet, I highly recommend experiencing this unmatchable masterpiece for yourself. It is a film that is truly worth your time and attention.

10.title: Best Film I've Ever seen
10.content:
*** This review may contain spoilers ***

I believe that this film is the best story ever told on film, and I'm about to tell you why.

Tim Robbins plays Andy Dufresne, a city banker, wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. He is sent to Shawshank Prison in 1947 and receives a double life sentence for the crime. Andy forms an unlikely friendship with "Red" (Morgan Freeman), the man who knows how to get things. Andy faces many trials in prison, but forms an alliance with the wardens because he is able to use his banking experience to help the corrupt officials amass personal fortunes. The story unfolds....

I was so impressed with how every single subplot was given a great deal of respect and attention from the director. The acting was world-class. I have never seen Tim Robbins act as well since, Morgan Freeman maybe (e.g. Seven). The twists were unexpected, an although this film had a familiar feel, it wasn't even slightly pretentious, it was original. The cinematography was grand and expressive. It gave a real impression of the sheer magnitude of this daunting prison.

But the one thing which makes THE SHAWSHANK REDEMPTION stand above all other films, is the attention given to the story. The film depends on the story and the way in which it unravels. It's a powerful, poignant, thought-provoking, challenging film like no other. If Andy were to comment on this film, I think he might say: "Get busy watching, or get busy dying." Take his advice.

Thoroughly recommended.

10.title: Great movie
10.content: n 1946 a young New England banker, Andy Dufresne (Robbins), is convicted of murdering his wife and her lover and sentenced to life at the Shawshank State Prison - twice over. Quiet and introspective, he gradually strikes up a friendship with the prison 'fixer', Red (Freeman), and over the next two decades wins the trust of the governor and guards, but in his heart, he still yearns for freedom. Darabont's adaptation of a Stephen King novella is a throwback to the kind of serious, literate drama Hollywood used to make (Birdman of Alcatraz, say) though the big spiritual resolution takes some swallowing - ditto the colour-blind relationships within the prison and the violent disavowal of any homosexual implications. Against this weighs the pleasure of discovering a first-time director with evident respect for the intelligence of his audience, brave enough to let character details accumulate without recourse to the fast- forward button. Darabont plays the long game and wins: this is an engrossing, superbly acted yarn, while the Shawshank itself is a truly formidable mausoleum.

10.title: Worth its number one rating
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" deserves the title of the Most Moving Movie of All Time.

Picking a list of "The Best Movies Ever" is always a ridiculous and futile practice. A look at IMDBs top 10 shows several entirely different movies, from "Star Wars" to "Schindler's List" and "The Godfather." The only characteristic shared by all 10 is that they are "worth watching." So, since Shawshank held the #1 slot for many months, it received plenty of ranting, illogical, completely undue criticism:

* That its characters were static - Simply not true. They do become moral icons by the end of the movie, but they evolve into their parts.

* That there is too much preaching/narration/"babying" - There is nothing out of place in this movie. Red doesn't labor his narration because he's pedantic, he does it because he's straightforward - this isn't a college professor speaking - and absolutely, astoundingly beautiful. Yes, there is the panoramic shot of the azure pacific at the end - but it dovetails neatly with the story - "Something that big would scare me." (Not verbatim).

* That there are perhaps 15 minutes at the end of the movie in which the fate of the characters is clear and 5 after questions have been resolved - This is absolutely necessary. "The Shawshank Redemption" attempts to leave the viewer thinking about ideas, not plot twists. Though this is only ever argued on scholastic (rather than aesthetic) grounds, even Star Wars' ending would have seemed abrupt without a brief, ceremonial resolution.

* That its foreshadowing or narration cuts drama - missing the point. I shutter to think of this film if told entirely from the present - it would loose its beauty. There's deliberately a lot of "time passing" sequences. The real reason this movie has its high ranking is that it grapples with "hope" - and hope, like all abstract notions, becomes concrete with introspection, and introspection takes time. This is not a "prison escape" movie.

See this movie. Think about this movie. Talk about this movie. The Shawshank Redemption thinks and feels more than other works of popular cinema, and demands that viewers do the same. I almost envy anyone who hasn't seen it yet; the first viewing is absolutely magical.

10.title: Get busy living get busy dying!
10.content:
The Shawkshank Redemption's - Review Get busy living get busy dying! Is merely one of the many great messages this 1994 masterpiece has to offer. Originally written as a short story by Stephen King 'The Shawkshank Redemption' has come to be one of the greatest movies of all time being nominated for 7 Oscars, and winning 11 various other awards. Directed by Frank Darabont it stars Tim Robbins as 'Andy Dufresne' and Morgan Freeman as 'Red'. This earlier 19th century film is delivered to its audience directly through the eyes of 'Red' giving us a strong one mined impersonation of the prison and the people who make up its walls.

The life that Andy once had drastically changed when he is charged guilty for the murder of his wife and her lover. Made to serve 2 life sentences Andy soon got to grips with his new surroundings. But one day he pushes aside all moral judgement on one decision that almost as him killed but his heroism and sheer courage gains him respect from other inmates at which point he slowly becomes good friends with 'Red' the man who can get you things. With 'Hope' on his side Andy goes on to do great things! The movie rests deeply on the persona built up around Andy. To some respect the filmmakers regarded him as a religious symbol and used brief yet powerful references to reflect on this. He would take up massive challenges helping out the majority all so that I could simply create a sense of freedom or retained hope in his life. He conveys a particular demeanour that people tend to associate with 'Christ' and as 'red' quite rightly says, "He strolled. Like a man in a park without a care or worry".

'Character Development' is a complete different term altogether in this movie, taking us as far into the unknown. Darabont encouraged something different, with twists and turns in the story we are continually struck with new surprises. By pushing boundaries of modern day cinema, Darabont exercised in presenting us with new, interesting but most importantly feel-good and exiting Characters. This would have never been possible without the powerful and striking performances from both 'Tim Robbins' and 'Morgan Freeman', as individuals they play there separate roles with a convincing harmony. But as a pair they pitch together as if you were husband and wife, the acting is flawless there chemistry works in perfect balance and there absolute ability to grasp the audience in continuous narrative is something that is rarely witnessed in a movie.

While the characters are unbelievably amazing and the script is excellent, it's the extraordinary way this movie uses cinematography to give us a hardened view into the reality of this film. Thick walls, large inescapable fences, and confined spaces all remind us of this place we have been brought to. This is spanned onwards with the common use of relentless Guards marching and the heavy cell bars slamming open and shut. In a way reinforcing the dull existence these men have to live with. This is all backed by outstanding crane and helicopter shots from the Coen Brother arguably some of the best camera work to date, the lighting brought not only outstanding quality from the work but it helped to create meaning and build layers deep into the story. Finally the editing was set at a perfect pace and even with regular leaps into future the team manages to maintain a high standard from beginning to end.

It is considered as a feel-good classic. But in hindsight thoughts four walls hold a more grime, corrupt and depressing existences. But it is the exultance of Writer/Director Frank Darabont who unlike most directors forces on the real human issues head on, dealing the problems of male rape, assault, murder, and abuse in a very effective way. But by encouraging more enthuses on the strong emotional relationships created between you and the characters Darabont was able to stray audiences away from this harsh reality into uplifting portrayals of Andy and his great achievements.

Its quite amazing to think how such a great movie would fail to make an impact on the big screen and would only pick up fame after it was realised to video in 1995. But its success was well received and people soon began to understand what they had been missing. But its only now 10 years on that we begin to see how its success continues to be harvested and filtered through into many modern day movies.

My Personal Rating for this Movie 9/10

10.title: Beautiful in its restraint.
10.content:
Being the cynic that I am, it's my inclination to look for the weaknesses of films that ultimately detract from their overall quality. How refreshing it is that, on occasion, a film is so masterfully crafted that I can simply take in all that it has to offer. Such is the case with _The Shawshank Redemption_.

And with _The Shawshank Redemption_, it isn't an issue of the excellence of the different components of the film; instead, it's an issue of the way that all of the elements of this movie-- the writing, directing, and acting-- are so vastly superior to those of most every other film.

It's difficult to imagine two things more cliched than "Prison Dramas" and films about "The Triumph of the Human Spirit." Though _The Shawshank Redemption_ certainly qualifies as both of those cinematic cliches, there's nothing about the film that seems even the least bit tired. The unique characters of Red and Andy Dufrense bring an unexpected liveliness to a film that could have easily been both obvious and trite-- such as _The Green Mile_.

Because of the intelligently-written screenplay, with its engaging plot twists and historically appropriate dialogue, coupled with truly remarkable performances by both Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman that convey all of the depth and honesty of their challenging characters, _Shawshank_ improves upon the repeated viewings that are necessary to take in all that it has to offer. The unparalleled depth of this movie allow the viewer to gain something new-- and something ultimately positive-- from each additional viewing.

Perhaps the greatest achievement of _The Shawshank Redemption_ is the restraint that director Frank Darabont uses in unfolding this multifaceted story. When approaching a film with even a fraction of the thematic load of this one, most directors simply succumb to the too-easy temptation to tack a didactic, heavy-handed morality statement onto the last sequence. Darabont attains a rare closure; he _doesn't_ moralize. He allows the viewer to make his/her own judgments about each of the characters and the fate that he ultimately meets over the course of the film.

RATING: 10 out of 10. In a decade, _The Shawshank Redemption_ will be grouped into the cinematic canon alongside such triumphs as _Citizen Kane_ and _Dr. Strangelove_. It's not an unmerited distinction. An example of truly flawless filmmaking.

10.title: Best film ever!

I am aware that by now almost everyone knows the plot of this film, but since this is my first reviewed title on IMDb, I'll do my part in explaining it.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is based on the Stephen King's short story "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption". Set in New England, the film tells the story of a young banker named Andy Dufresne (played by Tim Robbins), who is wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. In prison he befriends Ellis Boyd Redding (Morgan Freeman), nicknamed "Red" by his friends, and his gang. But he also catches the eyes of "The Sisters", a gang of rapists and bullies led by Bogs (Mark Rolston). He then must make up his escape plan, while aiding the guards and most importantly the warden (Bob Gunton) to cheat on their taxes.

I was deeply impressed by this film since the first time I watched it, and has remained my favorite film ever since. All of the main actors play their parts beautifully (Freeman in particular), and the ending is the most powerful I have ever seen.

A must-see for everyone.

10.title: Best Movie
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is written and directed by Frank Darabont. It is an adaptation of the Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption. Starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman, the film portrays the story of Andy Dufresne (Robbins), a banker who is sentenced to two life sentences at Shawshank State Prison for apparently murdering his wife and her lover. Andy finds it tough going but finds solace in the friendship he forms with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Freeman). While things start to pick up when the warden finds Andy a prison job more befitting his talents as a banker. However, the arrival of another inmate is going to vastly change things for all of them.

There was no fanfare or bunting put out for the release of the film back in 94, with a title that didn't give much inkling to anyone about what it was about, and with Columbia Pictures unsure how to market it, Shawshank Redemption barely registered at the box office. However, come Academy Award time the film received several nominations, and although it won none, it stirred up interest in the film for its home entertainment release. The rest, as they say, is history. For the film finally found an audience that saw the film propelled to almost mythical proportions as an endearing modern day classic. Something that has delighted its fans, whilst simultaneously baffling its detractors. One thing is for sure, though, is that which ever side of the Shawshank fence you sit on, the film continues to gather new fans and simply will never go away or loose that mythical status.

It's possibly the simplicity of it all that sends some haters of the film into cinematic spasms. The implausible plot and an apparent sentimental edge that makes a nonsense of prison life, are but two chief complaints from those that dislike the film with a passion. Yet when characters are this richly drawn, and so movingly performed, it strikes me as churlish to do down a human drama that's dealing in hope, friendship and faith. The sentimental aspect is indeed there, but that acts as a counterpoint to the suffering, degradation and shattering of the soul involving our protagonist. Cosy prison life you say? No chance. The need for human connection is never more needed than during incarceration, surely? And given the quite terrific performances of Robbins (never better) & Freeman (sublimely making it easy), it's the easiest thing in the world to warm to Andy and Red.

Those in support aren't faring too bad either. Bob Gunton is coiled spring smarm as Warden Norton, James Whitmore is heart achingly great as the "Birdman Of Shawshank," Clancy Brown is menacing as antagonist Capt. Byron Hadley, William Sadler amusing as Heywood & Mark Rolston is impressively vile as Bogs Diamond. Then there's Roger Deakins' lush cinematography as the camera gracefully glides in and out of the prison offering almost ethereal hope to our characters (yes, they are ours). The music pings in conjunction with the emotional flow of the movie too. Thomas Newman's score is mostly piano based, dovetailing neatly with Andy's state of mind, while the excellently selected soundtrack ranges from the likes of Hank Williams to the gorgeous Le Nozze di Figaro by Mozart....

It is a movie that focuses on principals and fundamental values of humans beings, such as freedom. It is a movie about dreams, and how to achieve them. About how someone can be a free man while prisoned. About how someone can be a prisoner, while living in open space. Indicating that you must first change yourself internally to what you want to become and then gradually achieve it. Difficulties are to come but nothing hurts unless you get your eyes off your dream.

Institutionalization, is something that many people have been infected with, but they seem not to be able to understand it. You don't have to be in a prison to get institutionalised. Look around you and you will see a race of slaves fighting every day to defend their slavery.

Watch the "MATRIX" and don't focus on the fighting scenes, but on the meanings spoken out by Morpheas during the first part of the movie. You will then notice the similarities between the two movies, both concentrating on freedom from a slightly different view angle.

All the above are wooven around a firm and perfect cinematographic structure of excellent performances, brilliant shooting and atmosphere.

If art is to cultivate people, meaning the focusing of people on principles and fundamental values, then "The Shawshank Redemption" is sure one of the best tools to fulfill this task.

To me it is one of the few movies that justify the existance of film making. Without such movies cinema would have been a mean of erosion of human personalities.

I have seen this movie 7 times and i keep watching it to remind me of things that everyday routine makes you forget. Things that give happiness to your soul, not your mind. Things that set worthwhile goals for someone. I believe that everyone needs such tools to help him go after his godgiven rights which are neglected everyday due to the soul devastating slavery, our minds put us through. 10.title: masterpiece!
10.content:
At its core, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a story of hope, resilience, and the indomitable human spirit. The screenplay, based on a Stephen King novella, skillfully weaves together multiple narratives, creating a tapestry of characters and events that contribute to the film's emotional depth. The script not only explores the harsh realities of prison life but also delves into the psychological impact of incarceration and the quest for redemption.

Tim Robbins delivers a standout performance as Andy Dufresne, portraying a character whose quiet strength and determination inspire those around him. Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is equally remarkable, providing both narration and a nuanced portrayal of a man who finds redemption through his friendship with Andy.

The cinematography by Roger Deakins is nothing short of breathtaking. The film captures the oppressive atmosphere of Shawshank while simultaneously highlighting moments of beauty and liberation. The iconic scene of Andy escaping through a tunnel of sewage is a testament to both the film's visual prowess and the resilience of the human spirit.

Thomas Newman's score is hauntingly beautiful, perfectly complementing the emotional nuances of the story. The soundtrack enhances the film's atmosphere and contributes to its enduring impact on the audience.

10.title: Amazing film
10.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a 1994 American drama film written and directed by Frank Darabont and starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman.

Adapted from the Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption, the film tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who spends 19 years in Shawshank State Prison for the murder of his wife and her lover despite his claims of innocence. During his time at the prison, he befriends a fellow inmate, Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding, and finds himself protected by the guards after the warden begins using him in his money laundering operation.

Despite a lukewarm box office reception that barely recouped its budget, the film received multiple award nominations and favorable reviews from critics for its acting and realism. It has since enjoyed a remarkable life on cable television, VHS, DVD, and Blu-ray. It was included in the American Film Institute's 100 Years...100 Movies 10th Anniversary Edition. [2]

The rest of the characters are so complex that to describe them would merely dampen everyone elses opinion on the film. I know it was nominated for some Academy Awards, and didn't win any, but it deserved more than Titanic!

It is didactic and its main theme is hope. In fact the last few lines of the film always bring tears to my eyes - "I hope to see my friend, and shake his hand. I hope the Pacific is as blue as it has been in my mind. I hope." These words, uttered by Morgan Freemon are truely inspirational words.

My opinion is watch this movie as often as possible, and learn from it.

The Shawshank Redemption - the best movie ever!!

Throughout his years in prison, we watch Andy go from some prisoners' boxing bag, to prison's librarian, to prison guards' personal banker. We experience with him the pain, the frustration, the sorrow. Tim Robbins gives a magnificent performance opposite Morgan Freeman's Red, maybe the only role outshining Mandela in Invictus.

If you haven't already watched this masterpiece of a movie, rush to the nearest DVD store. Every human being able of watching a movie should watch this movie at least once.

10.title: Best

The Shawshank Redemption is a powerful and moving film that explores themes of hope, friendship, and resilience in the face of adversity. It is also a scathing indictment of the American prison system, which is often portrayed as being corrupt, dehumanizing, and unjust.

What makes The Shawshank Redemption so special?

There are many things that make The Shawshank Redemption a special film. First and foremost, it is a beautifully told story with complex and well-developed characters. Andy Dufresne is a man of unwavering hope and determination, even in the darkest of circumstances. Red is a wise and compassionate man who has seen it all, but still maintains a sense of humanity. The supporting cast is also excellent, with memorable performances from Bob Gunton as the sadistic Warden Norton, William Sadler as the brutal Captain Hadley, and Clancy Brown as the menacing inmate Hadley.

Another thing that makes The Shawshank Redemption so special is its realistic portrayal of prison life. The film does not shy away from the harsh realities of incarceration, but it also shows that there can be moments of joy and even friendship behind bars. The film's message of hope is ultimately one of its greatest strengths.

The Shawshank Redemption as a social commentary

The Shawshank Redemption is also a powerful social commentary on the American prison system. The film shows how the system can be corrupt and dehumanizing, and how it can chew up and spit out innocent people. Andy Dufresne's wrongful conviction and subsequent incarceration is a prime example of the injustices that can occur within the prison system.

The film also explores the issue of rehabilitation. Andy Dufresne is a model prisoner who uses his skills and intelligence to help others. However, the prison system is not designed to rehabilitate inmates. Instead, it is focused on punishment and control. This is evident in the character of Warden Norton, who is more interested in using Andy's skills for his own personal gain than he is in helping him become a productive member of society.

Conclusion

The Shawshank Redemption is a classic film that deserves to be seen by everyone. It is a story of hope, friendship, and resilience in the face of adversity. It is also a powerful social commentary on the American prison system. The film is beautifully told, well-acted, and thought-provoking. It is a film that will stay with you long after you have seen it.

In addition to the above, here are some other thoughts on the film:

The Shawshank Redemption is a masterclass in storytelling. Darabont's screenplay is perfectly paced and structured, and he builds suspense and tension beautifully. The film is also visually stunning, with Roger Deakins' cinematography capturing the beauty and despair of Shawshank Prison.

The performances in The Shawshank Redemption are all top-notch. Tim Robbins is simply brilliant as Andy Dufresne, and Morgan Freeman gives one of the best performances of his career as Red. The supporting cast is also excellent, with Bob Gunton, William Sadler, and Clancy Brown all delivering standout performances.

The Shawshank Redemption is a film that stays with you long after you have seen it. It is a film that makes you think about the importance of hope, friendship, and resilience. It is also a film that challenges you to think about the American prison system and its flaws.

Overall, The Shawshank Redemption is a masterpiece of cinema. It is a film that everyone should see at least once in their lifetime.

10.title: Filmmaking Redemption
10.content:
It's hard to find a decent picture nowadays. Our screens are polluted by the filthy and unimaginative trash that we in the modern age, and ages of recent late, call remakes, reimaginings, and, if you're referencing the gaming industry, remasters. But here is a film that couldn't in any way be reimagined, remade, or remastered. As well, films based on books, in my opinion, often fail to convey the thoroughness and whole-heartedness of the written word. But here is a film that [I'd say] is the exception.

Here is a film whose actors portray their characters with such imagination of their own that it's hard not to like them and relate to them. You may think that Tim Robbins, wearing that sneaky grin and sometimes straight face throughout the film, is a lifeless individual, but in reality, it's that muck-eatin grin he dons on occassion that let's you know, yeah this guys up to something. I knew it from the moment Andy Dufraine presented a simple exploit to the prison guard, Byron Hadley, allowing him to could keep his money instead of having it taken by the IRS, those bloodsuckers. In the days following, as Andy watched his "co-workers" sip cold beers, he simply sat there, grinning facade, basking in the glory of his deviousness and the formation of what would become his master escape plan.

It's the simple things like that that made this film such a pleasurable viewing experience for me. The minute successes and acts of kindness and the subsequent feeling of pride and accomplishment from the two main characters gave me, in a way, my very own sense of accomplishment.

This is a rare feat. It's difficult to create a film that actually allows the viewer to feel as if they are living the life of the character, in whatever moment of said character's life said film is taking place in. By the end of the movie, I had a renewed feeling. The only other time I can recall having this reaction is when I saw The Silver Linings Playbook (2012), another excellent and good-feeling film in which the main character undergoes a traumatic experience and we see his continued suffering, post incident. I felt as though I was with him through every moment of his struggles.

In conclusion, and this seems to have become the theme of my review, it's thr simplest things that give this film its great vibe, and compells me to continue watching all the way through to that very last scene in which Andy and Red (Morgan Freeman) share a distantly viewed hug alongside the lightly rolling waves of the Pacific. Simple, yet beautiful, and heartwarming.

10.title: The best movie I 've ever seen
10.content:
Prison is a scary place. It changes people, breaks and cripples their body and soul. For many, getting into such a place is worse than death, or at least the end of a past life forever. This film shows that even in such a terrible place, a person is able to survive, adapt and, having overcome all the trials, break free.

Escape from Shawshank is the best film adaptation of the works of Stephen King. If the horror adaptations of the famous author are somehow unlucky, then this is on the contrary - a wonderful film.

The main character is an accountant, innocently convicted of murdering his wife, who ends up in Shawshank Prison, filled with villains and scoundrels of all stripes both inside and outside the cells. From the first days, all the unbearable weight of this place falls on the hero, capable of breaking even the most persistent, but he accepts all this and endures, adapting to the terrible reality, and later begins to hatch an escape.

The film very accurately conveys the prison world of the USA with all its unsightly sides and gloomy details. This place is able to scare no worse than monsters from other books by Stephen King, and the more you admire the hero, who, when faced with these horrors, is able to overcome them and emerge victorious thanks to his will, intelligence and ingenuity. Due to the competent narration, saturation of actions and tension, the picture is very interesting to watch and the story of Andy Dufresne's escape from his personal hell captures and does not let go until the very end. The picture is complemented by excellent actors who perfectly fit into their images and competent camerawork and directing.

10.title: A Classic

This film was adapted from a short story, 'Rita Hayworth and The Shawshank Redemption,' written by Stephen King. Perhaps it is because it's adapted from a short story as to why this works so well as there are only minor changes and nothing essential is left out, leaving the film makers with the ability to strengthen and stretch out the main focus, which is the bond created by the two main characters. In my personal opinion I would say this film is one of the most successful book to script adaptations in film history. The direction is brilliant in the way it is almost not noticeable as it relies on the actors and their interactions with each other to keep the audience interested. Cinematography is worth a mention also as each shot is captured beautifully. In summary, Shawshank is a must see and a well deserved film classic.

10.title: Hope
10.content:
There's 2 kinds of people who watch this film - this who get it and those who don't.

Of the latter category, yeah OK, it is just a film about a couple of guys in prison. It's excellently acted, scripted, directed and filmed. And yeah it does have a great ending.

But there's something more than that. And this is where former category of people come in.

The film is about hope, and living with hope. "Andy Dufrenes" (Tim Robbins) is imprisoned wrongly. Where many people would have given up, he refuses to do so and throughout his time in prison, clings to that hope. A journey of 1000 miles is taken one step at a time.

Contrast this to "Red" (Morgan Freeman). He's become used to being in prison, he's institutionalised, his repeated parole refusals have meant he's give up hope. And like Brooks before him he knows that he wouldn't survive on the outside.

"Get busy living, or get busy dying", says Andy. It's the hope that Andy has carried throughout that provides the salvation, the redemption, for both himself and Red.

I can't recommend this movie highly enough.

It could have just whithered away on the store shelves, like Andy Dufresne could have in his own cell. But the characters prevailed, because Andy -- And Shawshank -- stayed true. Now, these movies are right up there as the most popular films of all time.

Anyone who has yet to watch Shawshank may be so jaded of movies, or the film's title, or how a 2-1/2- hour movie set inside the walls of a prison can manage to tap the soul of such a wide range of people. Shawshank has not one explosion. I wonder if it even has a single special effect or digitally- enhanced frame.

10.title: The Timeless Triumph of "The Shawshank Redemption"
10.content:
This compelling 1994 film provides a poignant exploration of human resilience, friendship, and hope.

The storyline revolves around Andy Dufresne, a banker wrongly convicted of murder, and his fellow inmate Red. The narrative is captivating, keeping audiences glued to the screen as the story unfolds over the years within the Shawshank penitentiary. Darabont's adept direction is evident in the attention to detail, remarkable performances, and the creation of an atmosphere laden with both tension and optimism.

Morgan Freeman delivers an unforgettable performance as Red, the story's narrator and Andy's steadfast friend. Tim Robbins, portraying Andy, masterfully embodies the determination and dignity of a man who refuses to bow to injustice.

Roger Deakins' cinematography is superb, capturing the monotony of prison life and highlighting moments of freedom and hope with extraordinary visual finesse. Thomas Newman's soundtrack significantly contributes to creating the film's emotional atmosphere.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is more than a mere prison drama; it's a celebration of the inner strength of humanity, redemption, and the possibility of finding freedom even in the most oppressive circumstances. This film continues to inspire and touch the hearts of viewers with its powerful storytelling and profound humanity.

10.title: Master piece
10.content:
I don't know what to tell about this film.I just know this is the best film i watched in my entire life.t is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

From Andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - Red, who becomes his best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'."

The key to the film's structure, I think, is that it's not about its hero, but about our relationship with him - our curiosity, our pity, our admiration. If Andy had been the heroic center, bravely enduring, the film would have been conventional, and less mysterious. But we wonder about this guy. Did he really kill those two people? Why does he keep so much to himself? Why can he amble through the prison yard like a free man on a stroll, when everyone else plods or sidles?

Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'."

10.title: Nice movie

The Shawshank Redemption is a 1994 drama film that tells the story of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a man wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. Sentenced to life in Shawshank prison, Andy befriends fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman) and embarks on a long journey of hope, perseverance, and ultimately, redemption.

Strengths of the film

Powerful performances: Both Robbins and Freeman deliver exceptional performances. Robbins portrays Andy's quiet determination with strength, while Freeman narrates the story with a sense of weary wisdom. Their friendship is the heart of the film.

Thematic depth: The Shawshank Redemption is more than just a prison escape story. It's a meditation on hope, friendship, and the importance of finding meaning even in the face of adversity. The film explores the corrupting influence of power and the resilience of the human spirit.

Pacing and suspense: Despite its long runtime, the film is never slow. Director Frank Darabont masterfully builds suspense and slowly reveals Andy's plan, keeping the audience engaged throughout.

10.title: Excellent
10.content:
Stephen King's books have a distinctive voice - warm, sincere, inviting - that probably accounts for the appeal of his fiction just as much as his macabre imagination.

Yet none of the many movies adapted from King's work have managed to capture his singular, light, immediately recognizable tone.

Until now, that is: "The Shawshank Redemption," a first feature written and directed by Frank Darabont, finds the perfect cinematic equivalent to King's style. Based on the nonhorror novella "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption," this is an engagingly simple, good-hearted film, with just enough darkness around the edges to give contrast and relief to its glowingly benign view of human nature.

Like much of King's work, "The Shawshank Redemption" is about an exceptional individual at odds with society, picked on or persecuted for the gifts that set him apart. In this case, the gift isn't supernatural, like Carrie's telekinetic powers, but moral and spiritual.

Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is a gangly young banker when he enters Maine's fortresslike Shawshank State Prison in 1946, accused of killing his unfaithful wife and her lover. Though his protestations of innocence don't carry much weight, his shy manner and decency does. Befriended by Red (Morgan Freeman), a veteran con who is the prison fixer, he soon draws a circle of other boyishly likable prisoners around him, including William Sadler as a sweet- tempered thug and James Whitmore as a cuddly old man who is the prison librarian.

10.title: The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Masterpiece
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption," directed by Frank Darabont, stands as a cinematic masterpiece that has etched itself into the annals of film history. Adapted from Stephen King's novella, the movie is a timeless exploration of hope, resilience, and the enduring power of friendship.

Tim Robbins delivers a compelling performance as Andy Dufresne, a banker unjustly imprisoned for murder, while Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is nothing short of iconic. The chemistry between the two actors forms the heart of the film, providing an emotional resonance that lingers long after the credits roll.

Darabont's direction, coupled with Roger Deakins' evocative cinematography, creates a visually stunning and narratively rich experience. The deliberate pacing allows the characters to unfold organically, drawing the audience into a world where the human spirit triumphs over adversity.

With a poignant exploration of institutionalization and a hauntingly beautiful score by Thomas Newman, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic triumph that transcends its genre. Its enduring appeal lies in its ability to resonate universally, making it a must-watch for cinephiles and a timeless classic that continues to captivate audiences worldwide.

10.title: The best movie ever seen
10.content:
Amazing movie, the magic of cinema.

The director, Frank Darabont, paints the prison in drab grays and shadows, so that when key events do occur, they seem to have a life of their own.

Andy, as played by Robbins, keeps his thoughts to himself. Red, as Freeman plays him, is therefore a crucial element in the story: His close observation of this man, down through the years, provides the way we monitor changes and track the measure of his influence on those around him. And all the time there is something else happening, hidden and secret, which is revealed only at the end.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is not a depressing story, although I may have made it sound that way. There is a lot of life and humor in it, and warmth in the friendship that builds up between Andy and Red. There is even excitement and suspense, although not when we expect it. But mostly the film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything. If the film is perhaps a little slow in its middle passages, maybe that is part of the idea, too, to give us a sense of the leaden passage of time, before the glory of the final redemption.

10.title: best movie ever
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair.

The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest busload of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

But Andy does not cry, and Red loses the cigarettes he wagered. Andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in Shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. Andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. He's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

Red is also a lifer. From time to time, measuring the decades, he goes up in front of the parole board, and they measure the length of his term (20 years, 30 years) and ask him if he thinks he has been rehabilitated. Oh, most surely, yes, he replies; but the fire goes out of his assurances as the years march past, and there is the sense that he has been institutionalized -- that, like another old lifer who kills himself after being paroled, he can no longer really envision life on the outside.

Red's narration of the story allows him to speak for all of the prisoners, who sense a fortitude and integrity in Andy that survives the years. Andy will not kiss butt. He will not back down. But he is not violent, just formidably sure of himself. For the warden (Bob Gunton), he is both a challenge and a resource; Andy knows all about bookkeeping and tax preparation, and before long he's been moved out of his prison job in the library and assigned to the warden's office, where he sits behind an adding machine and keeps tabs on the warden's ill-gotten gains. His fame spreads, and eventually he's doing the taxes and pension plans for most of the officials of the local prison system.

There are key moments in the film, as when Andy uses his clout to get some cold beers for his friends who are working on a roofing job. Or when he befriends the old prison librarian (James Whitmore). Or when he oversteps his boundaries and is thrown into solitary confinement. What quietly amazes everyone in the prison -- and us, too -- is the way he accepts the good and the bad as all part of some larger pattern than only he can fully see.

The partnership between the characters played by Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman is crucial to the way the story unfolds. This is not a "prison drama" in any conventional sense of the word. It is not about violence, riots or melodrama. The word "redemption" is in the title for a reason. The movie is based on a story, Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption, by Stephen King, which is quite unlike most of King's work. The horror here is not of the supernatural kind, but of the sort that flows from the realization than 10, 20, 30 years of a man's life have unreeled in the same unchanging daily prison routine.

The director, Frank Darabont, paints the prison in drab grays and shadows, so that when key events do occur, they seem to have a life of their own.

Andy, as played by Robbins, keeps his thoughts to himself. Red, as Freeman plays him, is therefore a crucial element in the story: His close observation of this man, down through the years, provides the way we monitor changes and track the measure of his influence on those around him. And all the time there is something else happening, hidden and secret, which is revealed only at the end.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is not a depressing story, although I may have made it sound that way. There is a lot of life and humor in it, and warmth in the friendship that builds up between Andy and Red. There is even excitement and suspense, although not when we expect it. But mostly the film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything. If the film is perhaps a little slow in its middle passages, maybe that is part of the idea, too, to give us a sense of the leaden passage of time, before the glory of the final redemption.

Though the film is set in Maine, the Ohio State Reformatory in Mansfield, Ohio, served as the fictional Shawshank State Penitentiary. Although a large portion of the prison was torn down after filming, the main administration building and two cell blocks remained; the site was revisited for filming parts of the film Air Force One.[12] Several of the interior shots of the specialized prison facilities, such as the admittance rooms and the warden's office, were shot in the reformatory. [12] The interior of the boarding room used by Brooks and Red was located in the administration building, though exterior shots were made elsewhere.[12] The prison site is a tourist attraction.[12] Internal scenes in the prison cell blocks were actually filmed on a soundstage built inside the nearby shuttered Westinghouse factory.[12] Downtown scenes were also filmed in Mansfield, as well as neighboring Ashland, Ohio. The oak tree under which Andy buries his letter to Red is located at 40°39′14″N 82°23′31″W, near Malabar Farm State Park, in Lucas, Ohio. The tree was heavily damaged by straight-line winds in a thunderstorm on July 29, 2011; officials were unsure if the tree would survive.[13] However, due to rally groups and inspections by forestry organizations, the tree was found to be alive and well and still stands today.[14]

Just as a prison in Ohio stood in for a fictional one in Maine, the beach scenes shown in the final minutes of the film meant to portray Zihuatanejo, Mexico, were actually shot in the Caribbean on the island of St. Croix, one of the U.S. Virgin Islands. The beach at 'Zihuatanejo' is Sandy Point National Wildlife Refuge, a two-mile crescent of sand just south of Frederiksted on the southwestern tip of the island. The refuge is a hatching ground for leather back sea turtles, and open only at limited times (10 am to 4 pm on Saturdays and Sundays), and not at all during the breeding season.[15]

10.title: Capra-esqe Prison Yarn A Huge Cult Hit
10.content:
A Prison Movie. An all-male cast (except for Rita Hayworth). Violence. A title guaranteed to sprain your jaw. When Shawshank hit theatres in 1994, odds were decidedly against it becoming a huge success. It would be nice to think that an ultimately upbeat, earnest, modernist take on the films of Frank Capra would immediately find a sympathetic and appreciative audience. But that would be a fairy tale, and life, like prison, is no fairy tale.

The film has the cheek to ask Which is worse, being a murderer, or being a lousy husband? Certainly the audience must ask itself this of the main character, Andy, played by Tim Robbins, who is sent to Shawshank Prison in 1947 for the murder of his wife and her lover. Introverted, bookish, proud, his fate is uncertain until he attracts the attention of the prison "finder" Red, played by Morgan Freeman. Together the two men must find emotional healing, spiritual redemption, and hope, if they are to survive.

Adroit and expertly manipulative, the film's pace is dictated by the deathless narration of Freeman, who could hold an audience spellbound while reciting phone book listings; or, suspend utter disbelief at a patently preposterous storyline. Nor are characterizations any less preposterous, from the sociopathic Warden, to the sadistic Head Guard, to the grandfatherly Librarian, to the manic-youthful Young Punk. But if the characters seem too archetypal to be true, it is a necessary, and tolerable evil in this fairy-tale set in a prison.

As I said, life is no fairy-tale, and prison movies rarely get to top-ten status. But sometimes some good does prevail, and redemption often stands in wait for those who dare reach out to it. As a first-run cinematic release Shawshank was not a great success. But as a commercial video, the film has achieved high status, and is voted year after year as a top consumer favorite. Cinematically near-perfect, visually breathtaking, Shawshank is a state-of-the-art example of the power of film to tell stories, and is rightly considered a must-see by most film reviewers.

10.title: overall great movie
10.content:
It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption is a novella written by Stephen King from the collection Different Seasons in 1982. This novella was also published as a short, standalone book. This story is entirely a story within Red's story, from a narrative that King claims to have written from September 1975 to January 1976, with additional chapters in the spring of 1977.

This story was adapted for the screen as The Shawshank Redemption by Frank Darabont in 1994, which received seven Academy Awards nominations in 1994, including the Best Picture category . In 2009, the story was adapted into a stage play entitled The Shawshank Redemption.

10.title: Great movie!
10.content: The Shawshank Redemption is a movie about two best friends finding hope in their condemned lives. Andy is a banker who was wrongly convicted of killing his wife. His wife was cheating on him and murdered during her affair. Andy befriends Red a fellow inmate. During their time in prison together they become best of friends. They work through their hardships together. Throughout their story this group of inmates lives an unordinary prison life. This is shown from drinking beer while tarring the roof to doing the officers taxes. This is a remarkable story of the ups and downs of prison life and the new people they become. Andy states that in his free life he was a law abiding man, but he had to come to jail to become a criminal. This is commented on when he begins laundering money for the warden. Towards the end the camera shows Andy slumped on the ground leaning up against the prison, which is very neat. This view is from far away up above and gives the feeling of Andy being rather small. This is an amazing angle as it helps show how he is confused about escaping because he will miss his friends. The lighting throughout this movie allows us to see everything appropriately, but helps to set the mood of each scene. This can be seen when Andy is in the movie room about to be attacked the lighting is very dark. This is just one example of the many great lighting choices. This has been my favorite movie for a long time. This movie allows the viewer to look into the men's hearts and minds. Perhaps one of the classic themes to this movie is the narration throughout the movie that is performed by Morgan Freeman. I believe it is clear how great this movie is as it is ranked #1 on IMDb for all time movies. This movie will always be one of the greats, and will withstand the test of time.

10.title: A Genuine Classic

From the opening sequence to the memorable finale, this is filmaking at its finest hour. Yes, the overall message may be simple, but the study of human nature throughout the film relays the complexities and frailties of the human race. I dont think there is one fault in this film and I have watched it many times now. I have seen many film opinion polls at this stage and I cannot remember shawshank being outside the top five in any of them. So we all cant be wrong. What it all boils down to is whether or not a film can move you, or leave a profound effect on you. Films like Shawshank, Seven, Braveheart, American History X and Jaws had a hugh effect on me, these films to me are what makes movies magical. For someone else it might be pulp fiction, the godfather or its a wonderful life. The magic of the movies is the effect that a particular film has on the particular person. I think the shawshank redemption had a profound effect on so many people, because we can identify so well with the point its trying to put across (Hope is a good thing, even when all seems lost) and that true friendship can get us out of the worst of times. Films will always have their critics, thats the nature of the business, but I was always told they dont make them like they used to, this film is proof that they still can. P.S. Stephen King is a genius.

10.title: Best Movie

Can Hollywood, usually creating things for entertainment purposes only, create art? To create something of this nature, a director must approach it in a most meticulous manner, due to the delicacy of the process. Such a daunting task requires an extremely capable artist with an undeniable managerial capacity and an acutely developed awareness of each element of art in their films, the most prominent; music, visuals, script, and acting. These elements, each equally important, must succeed independently, yet still form a harmonious union, because this mixture determines the fate of the artist's opus. Though already well known amongst his colleagues for his notable skills at writing and directing, Frank Darabont emerges with his feature film directorial debut, The Shawshank Redemption. Proving himself already a master of the craft, Darabont managed to create one of the most recognizable independent releases in the history of Hollywood. The Shawshank Redemption defines a genre, defies the odds, compels the emotions, and brings an era of artistically influential films back to Hollywood.

The story begins with the trial of a young banker, Andy Dufrense, victimized by circumstantial evidence, resulting in a conviction for the murder of his wife and her lover. After a quick conviction, Andy finds himself serving a life sentence at Shawshank prison, with no hope of parole. He exists in this prison only in appearance, keeping his mind free from the drab walls around him. His ability to do this results in the gaining of respect from his fellow inmates, but most of all from Ellis Redding. Ellis, commonly referred to as Red, finds gainful use of his entrepreneurial spirit within the drab walls of Shawshank by dealing in contraband and commodities rare to the confines of prison. Andy's demeanor and undeniable sense of hope causes Red to take a deeper look at himself, and the world around him. Andy proves to Red and the other inmates that in the conventional walls of Shawshank prison convention will find no home in his lifestyle.

10.title: excellent movie
10.content:
One of my all time favorites. Shawshank Redemption is a very moving story about hope and the power of friendship. Out of the three genre-defining classics released in 1994, The Shawshank Redemption was the one that ended up bearing the maximum brunt. First commercially by failing to recover its budget for it debuted in theatres together with one of cinema's greatest watershed events; Pulp Fiction. And then at Academy Awards where it was nominated for seven Oscars yet failed to win any, thanks to the sweeping show by the critics' darling, Forrest Gump.

But life ever since has been very kind to this film, and both critics & viewers have embraced its uplifting story of hope & friendship with remarkable amount of respect, love & kindness. Today, The Shawshank Redemption enjoys a position that's arguably even higher than the two classics which eclipsed it back in 1994 and while it was discarded at its time of release, it is now rightly & universally acknowledged as one of the greatest films of all time.

The Shawshank Redemption tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a successful banker, who is wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife & her illicit lover and is ultimately sentenced to two consecutive life terms in prison where his coping with the brutal hardships of confined life slowly earns him the respect of his fellow inmates & prison staff, including that of "Red" in whom Andy finds a trusted ally. The remainder of the film explores their friendship over the next two decades.

Written & directed by Frank Darabont, this prison drama is a simple but profoundly moving tale of hope, friendship & redemption that'll manage to connect deeply with most of us in one way or another plus it also marks Darabont's directional debut and he couldn't have asked for a better start. All this film has is men in either prison or police uniforms talking to one another over the course of its runtime and yet it never looked dull or felt like dragging at any given moment.

Cinematography exquisitely captures the monotonous daily life inside prison and provides considerable depth & realism to the era this film is set in. Every moment of despair has a shadowy appearance while moments of hope gleam with light. Editing is spectacular too as the gradual progression of Andy's life, his friendship with Red, and his determination to not give in to the four walls containing him is effectively unfolded. And Thomas Newman's score beautifully blends with the film's tone & characters' lives, and is emotionally fulfilling.

Coming to the performances, Tim Robbins delivers a swashbuckling performance as Andy Dufresne, the banker wrongfully convicted for the crime he didn't commit. And if Robbins is at his best, then Morgan Freeman is even better as Red, Andy's friend who is also serving a life sentence & is notorious amongst the inmates for he can smuggle goods into the prison. Freeman also narrates the story to us at which he does an even better job. His work is grounded & can go easily unnoticed, but the character of Red is the soul of this story.

There is a reason why this film still connects with so many people & why many of them have latched on to it. There is a reason why even after two decades, its legacy keeps flourishing & viewers keep returning to it despite its low entertainment value. One major reason is that even though The Shawshank Redemption is a prison drama, its story of imprisonment goes far beyond the bricks & steel rods of a jail house. The entire picture is a reflection of our own imprisonment in the institutions of our daily lives; institutions like work, family, society etc & living up to the expectations of each one of them.

On an overall scale, The Shawshank Redemption stresses that based on the outlook of life, there are only two types of people: one who can be free even in prison while others who find themselves imprisoned even in freedom. The message it is trying to resonate is clear: Fear can hold you prisoner, Hope can set you free. And if we all give ourselves some hope, there is nothing we can't survive. Yes, it all seems preachy n everything, but then if there's ever been a motion picture that has earned this sort of right, it's The Shawshank Redemption. Strongly recommended.

10.title: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece
10.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece that transcends the confines of its genre, leaving an indelible mark on the landscape of cinema. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, this timeless classic is a poignant tale of hope, resilience, and the enduring power of the human spirit.

Set within the walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film follows the journey of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, and his unlikely friendship with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman). Against the backdrop of institutionalized corruption and brutality, Andy's unwavering determination to preserve his dignity and find redemption resonates profoundly with audiences.

One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its richly drawn characters, brought to life by stellar performances from the cast. Robbins delivers a nuanced portrayal of Andy, capturing the character's quiet strength and resilience in the face of adversity. Freeman's narration, with its depth and gravitas, serves as the film's emotional anchor, guiding viewers through the tumultuous journey of hope and despair.

Darabont's direction is masterful, skillfully weaving together themes of friendship, justice, and the pursuit of freedom. The film's cinematography, marked by its evocative imagery and atmospheric lighting, immerses viewers in the stark realities of prison life while underscoring moments of triumph and redemption.

At its core, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a story about the transformative power of hope. It reminds us that even in the darkest of times, hope can be a beacon of light, guiding us through the most harrowing of circumstances. The film's uplifting message and universal themes continue to resonate with audiences worldwide, earning it a well-deserved place among the greatest films of all time.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic tour de force that captivates and inspires in equal measure. With its powerful performances, compelling narrative, and timeless themes, it stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of storytelling in film. A must-watch for cinephiles and casual viewers alike, this extraordinary film will leave an indelible impression on the hearts and minds of all who experience it.

What makes this film one of the best ever made is the message it conveys. It is one of eternal hope. Andy Dufresne, played by Tim Robbins, has been sent to prison for a crime he did not commit. But he never loses hope. He never gives up his quest to become a free man again. His years of tenacity, patience and wits keep him not only sane, but it gives his mind and a spirit a will to live. This film has a different feel to it. There has never been anything like it before and I don't know if there will again.

I'm not going to say any more about this film, it has already been said, but just suffice to say that I am glad that Forrest Gump won best picture in 94. 10.title: A Masterpiece A Masterpiece
10.content:
This is a rare kind of movie. A movie about the development of a friendship under the hardest conditions.

Being a huge fan of Stephen King's original novella, and considering past attempts to make his stories into movies, I was very sceptical when entering the theatre. But I have never seen an adaptation of his work which moved me in the way this one did. Director Darabont even get away with turning Red into an African American. Actually I think the movie is superior to the written version.

The main reason for this movie's strength is the two leading characters, brilliantly brought to life by Tim Robbins, (should have been Academy Award winner) Morgan Freeman. Together with the director they make this into a universal story and the American movie of the decade.

The only drawback is the ending. In my opinion it should have ended with Red getting on the bus. In that way each of us could create the ending we preferred. Most of us would have chosen the same one as the director but as it is presented I think it is a bit over the top. And that is sad for a movie of this kind.

Still, if I had to go to a deserted island bringing only one American movie from the nineties this would be it.
