9.title: Only one thing lacking...
9.content:
Overall, this is one of the finest films I've ever seen. Frank Darabont's masterful screenplay rendering of Stephen King's marginal novella brought every possible human emotion into play. And, every actor in the film did a superb job of translating this fiction into a believable reality.

On a scale from 1 to 100, I'd rate this movie a solid 99. Only one thing was lacking in the film to raise that score to 100 ... but this is just a personal thing.

POSSIBLE SPOILERS FOLLOWS:

During his time in prison, Andy Dufresne learns the identity of the man who killed his wife - a man named Elmo Blatch. And, he learns enough information about Blatch to render him "trackable" by an investigator. If 2 brief scenes had been added to the film, I'd have rated it a perfect film:

ADDED SCENE #1 - Shortly before his escape, Andy is seen talking to another inmate who gives him contact info for a person on the outside who does contract murder.

ADDED SCENE #2 - Shortly before Red's release from prison, we see him reading a newspaper story on the murder of an ex-con named Elmo Blatch.

Between the time of Andy's escape and Red's release, there would have been ample time for Andy to hire a private eye to track down Blatch and, afterward, hire a contract killer to kill him. Had I been Andy, I'd not have felt truly free of the suffering I'd endured in prison unless I knew the real killer got his just due. What Andy did to the Warden and Hadley is all well and good. But Blatch's death would settle all scores once and for all.

9.title: Excellent: an inspiring tale of hope and redemption
9.content:
It's a shame that The Shawshank Redemption was never as critically or commercially successful during it's run in theatres, as perhaps it should have been. If it were, then maybe the travesty of having Forrest Gump take the 1994 Best Picture Oscar could have been avoided, the award collected, instead, by either by this film or by Tarantino's groundbreaking Pulp Fiction, which were both stronger efforts. But I digress.

Beginning in 1946, Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is convicted for the murders of his wife and her lover. He's sentenced to serve two life terms back to back in Shawshank Prison, ruled with an iron fist by the Warden Samuel Norton (Bob Gunton) and the foul-mouthed, violent Captain Byron Hadley (Clancy Brown). Shawshank, Andy soon discovers, is a place of corruption and injustice, which begins at the Guards and stretches to the Warden himself, and includes a group of sodomites known as "the Sisters". Amidst this, Andy finds himself part of an unlikely group of friends, Red (Morgan Freeman), the "man who knows how to get things" and Brooks (James Whitmore), the good-natured, aging old-timer and librarian, among them. As we watch these men through the next 20 years of prison life, a tragic subplot develops with the Brooks character which deals with the nature of spending too long behind bars, and how, eventually, the bars and walls of prison can influence even a man of Brooks' good nature.

When a young convict arrives at Shawshank with proof that Andy is innocent, injustice at the prison rears it's ugly head. Andy is faced with a choice to make  "get busy livin', or get busy dying"  and he does just that, propelling the film from that point forward into a rousing, uplifting climax which tests the bonds of friendship between himself and Red, and ultimately provides the audience with an important message about hope, salvation, and redemption.

Writer/director Darabont reclines in his role and lets Shawshank's modestly-paced, subdued screenplay flow through it's 142 minutes. The film achieves the rare state of never seeming to drag or feel rushed. There's no flashy action here; rather, Darabont allows his audience to be compelled by the dialogue and the array of terrific performances, from the assured conviction with which Robbins believes in his innocence, to the thoughtful grace of Freeman's Red.

9.title: The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Masterpiece
9.content:
What sets The Shawshank Redemption apart from other prison dramas is its ability to transcend the confined setting and delve deep into the human spirit. While the film portrays the harsh realities of prison life, it also explores themes of resilience, determination, and the indomitable nature of the human spirit. It reminds us that even in the most hopeless of circumstances, one can find solace, purpose, and ultimately, redemption.

The performances in this film are nothing short of extraordinary. Tim Robbins delivers a nuanced portrayal of Andy Dufresne, capturing the character's quiet strength and unwavering belief in his own innocence. Morgan Freeman's narration, with his rich and soothing voice, adds depth and introspection to the story. Freeman's portrayal of Red is a masterclass in acting, perfectly capturing the character's transformation from skepticism to unwavering loyalty.

Frank Darabont's direction is impeccable, balancing moments of tension and despair with instances of genuine warmth and friendship. The film's pacing is deliberate, allowing the story to unfold gradually, building emotional investment as we witness the characters' struggles and triumphs. The cinematography, combined with an evocative score by Thomas Newman, creates a melancholic yet hopeful atmosphere that lingers long after the credits roll.

Beyond its technical brilliance, The Shawshank Redemption resonates on a profound level due to its universal themes. It explores the human desire for freedom, both physical and emotional, and the lengths individuals will go to preserve their dignity. It also sheds light on the transformative power of friendship and the significance of hope in the face of adversity.

The Shawshank Redemption is a film that demands multiple viewings to fully appreciate its depth and intricacies. Each time, it reveals new layers of meaning and leaves a lasting impact on the viewer. It is a testament to the power of storytelling and the enduring capacity of the human spirit.

9.title: Friendship

Still ranked #2 on IMDb:s top 250-list, this is not one of those epic masterpieces like resident #1 "The Godfather". Rather this is a small and quite low-key film that brings up some of the biggest concepts in life. And that it certainly speaks to people can be seen from the grade if nothing else.

I had watched this movie a few years ago, and i didn't really understand then what all the fuss was about. I enjoyed it, surely, but not in the way that other people seemed to. But having recently watched it again i must say that the message finally drove home. For several reasons this is an amazing film.

First of all the concepts it touches. Justice, fairness, endurance, hope and of course above all friendship. Seldom have i seen a movie so filled with emotion and still it's not weighted down by it. The movie is one of the few i have seen where all this emotion truly feels justified. Not least because of the second reason why this is an amazing movie: the actors. Tim Robbins is one of my personal favorites, an amazing actor to say the least. He almost never fails to deliver and here he is mesmerizing. Morgan Freeman is another stable and dependable actor, but i don't think he has ever been as good as he is here. And they are supported by a very well balanced and well chosen supporting cast. Finally Frank Darabonts directing is done with the lightest touch and an amazing attention to detail. He never lets things slide out of hand as they often do when strong emotions are present.

While i find this to be an amazing film the high average score here at IMDb still surprises me somewhat. It's a great movie, but it's not the kind of movie i expected so many people would consider great. But maybe it's just because what we have here is a movie about the greatest thing life has to offer; friendship. And an unlikely friendship at that, simple to understand and simple to appreciate. This is a feel-good movie in the best way imaginable - one where you must first pass through fire before you reach redemption.

9/10

9.title: Review: The Shawshank Redemption
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a timeless masterpiece that transcends the traditional confines of the prison drama genre, offering a profound exploration of hope, friendship, and the human spirit. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, this 1994 film has rightfully earned its place as one of the greatest films of all time.

At its core, The Shawshank Redemption is a story about hope in the face of despair. The film follows Andy Dufresne (played by Tim Robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, as he navigates the harsh realities of life inside Shawshank Prison. Despite the brutal and oppressive environment, Andy maintains a quiet dignity and resilience, which ultimately inspires those around him, including his friend Red (played by Morgan Freeman).

Robbins delivers a career-defining performance as Andy, capturing the character's internal strength and unwavering optimism with subtlety and grace. Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is equally compelling, bringing warmth and wisdom to the role of a man who has become institutionalized by decades of incarceration. Freeman's narration adds a layer of depth to the story, guiding the audience through the emotional highs and lows of prison life with his iconic voice.

The film's cinematography, by Roger Deakins, is visually stunning, with Shawshank Prison itself almost becoming a character in the story. The bleak, gray walls of the prison contrast sharply with the rare moments of beauty and freedom, such as the memorable scene where Andy plays Mozart over the prison's loudspeakers, momentarily lifting the spirits of every inmate.

Thomas Newman's hauntingly beautiful score further enhances the film's emotional impact, perfectly complementing the narrative's themes of redemption and hope. The music swells at just the right moments, evoking a sense of yearning and transcendence that stays with the viewer long after the credits roll.

What makes The Shawshank Redemption truly extraordinary is its exploration of the human spirit. The film delves into the complexities of life behind bars, showing how hope and friendship can survive even in the darkest of places. Andy's relentless pursuit of freedom, both physical and spiritual, serves as a powerful reminder that the human spirit can endure and overcome even the most daunting of circumstances.

The Shawshank Redemption is more than just a prison drama; it is a meditation on the power of hope and the resilience of the human soul. Its universal themes resonate with audiences of all backgrounds, making it a film that transcends time and place. In the end, it is a story about redemption-not just for Andy, but for everyone who has ever felt trapped by the circumstances of life.

In a world filled with fleeting entertainment, The Shawshank Redemption stands as a beacon of cinematic excellence, a film that will continue to inspire and uplift generations to come. It is, quite simply, a triumph.

9.title: Awesome
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty - - not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair.

The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest bus load of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

But Andy does not cry, and Red loses the cigarettes he wagered. Andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in Shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. Andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. He's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

Red is also a lifer. From time to time, measuring the decades, he goes up in front of the parole board, and they measure the length of his term (20 years, 30 years) and ask him if he thinks he has been rehabilitated. Oh, most surely, yes, he replies; but the fire goes out of his assurances as the years march past, and there is the sense that he has been institutionalized -- that, like another old lifer who kills himself after being paroled, he can no longer really envision life on the outside.

Red's narration of the story allows him to speak for all of the prisoners, who sense a fortitude and integrity in Andy that survives the years. Andy will not kiss butt. He will not back down. But he is not violent, just formidably sure of himself. For the warden (Bob Gunton), he is both a challenge and a resource; Andy knows all about bookkeeping and tax preparation, and before long he's been moved out of his prison job in the library and assigned to the warden's office, where he sits behind an adding machine and keeps tabs on the warden's ill-gotten gains. His fame spreads, and eventually he's doing the taxes and pension plans for most of the officials of the local prison system.

There are key moments in the film, as when Andy uses his clout to get some cold beers for his friends who are working on a roofing job. Or when he befriends the old prison librarian (James Whitmore). Or when he oversteps his boundaries and is thrown into solitary confinement. What quietly amazes everyone in the prison -- and us, too -- is the way he accepts the good and the bad as all part of some larger pattern than only he can fully see.

The partnership between the characters played by Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman is crucial to the way the story unfolds. This is not a "prison drama" in any conventional sense of the word. It is not about violence, riots or melodrama. The word "redemption" is in the title for a reason. The movie is based on a story, Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption, by Stephen King, which is quite unlike most of King's work. The horror here is not of the supernatural kind, but of the sort that flows from the realization than 10, 20, 30 years of a man's life have unreeled in the same unchanging daily prison routine.

The director, Frank Darabont, paints the prison in drab grays and shadows, so that when key events do occur, they seem to have a life of their own.

Andy, as played by Robbins, keeps his thoughts to himself. Red, as Freeman plays him, is therefore a crucial element in the story: His close observation of this man, down through the years, provides the way we monitor changes and track the measure of his influence on those around him. And all the time there is something else happening, hidden and secret, which is revealed only at the end.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is not a depressing story, although I may have made it sound that way. There is a lot of life and humor in it, and warmth in the friendship that builds up between Andy and Red. There is even excitement and suspense, although not when we expect it. But mostly the film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything. If the film is perhaps a little slow in its middle passages, maybe that is part of the idea, too, to give us a sense of the leaden passage of time, before the glory of the final redemption.

9.title: The Shawshank Redemption | A brief review by a Film Making student
9.content:
*Contain Spoilers*

The Shawshank Redemption (1994) Director - Frank Darabont Cinematographer – Roger Deakins Writers – Stephen King and Frank Darabont Editor – Richard Francis-Bruce

Favorite Quote: "Hope is a good thing and good things never die." The Shawshank Redemption is about time, patience, hope and loyalty. In 1946, a banker named Andy Dufresne (protagonist) is convicted of a double murder, even though he stubbornly proclaims his innocence. He's sentenced to a life term at the Shawshank State Prison in Maine, where another lifer, Ellis "Red" Redding, picks him as the new recruit. The first part of the film deals with Andy, Red and their group of friends dealing with prison life.

Andy wants to be a freeman. He regrets his past and wants to move on with a new life and memories. But the ugly realities of prison life are quickly introduced to Andy. A corrupt warden, sadistic guards led by Capt. Byron Hadley and inmates who are little better than animals, willing to use rape or beatings to insure their dominance. But Andy does not crack. He has the hope of the truly innocent, which (together with his smarts) allow him to prevail behind bars. He uses his banking skills to win favor with the warden and the guards, doing the books for Norton's illegal business schemes and keeping an eye on the investments of most of the prison staff. In exchange, he is able to improve the prison library and bring some dignity and respect back to many of the inmates, including Red.

After almost a two decade stay, in 1966, Andy Dufresne escapes the Shawshank prison by tunneling through the wall with a rock hammer worn down to the nub. He sets off to a new country for a new life and is later accompanied by his prison mate Red.

Andy Duresne is a man of hope. He is a smart person and a loyal friend. The Shawshank Redemption is the journey of redemption of Andy and his fellow convicts. Redemption is found in many ways, by many characters, even by a bird named Jake. It's a story portraying the corruption and politics in a prison and the transformation of an investment banker to a smart con. It shows how the weak and innocent protagonist, who is often bullied and tortured during his early stay in prison, adapts and changes himself with the situation and out smarts the guards and warden to run away with their illegal money and starts a new life.

Review By – Mayank Bhattacharya

9.title: Great story, wondrously told and acted
9.content:
At the heart of this extraordinary movie is a brilliant and indelible performance by Morgan Freeman as Red, the man who knows how to get things, the "only" guilty man at Shawshank prison. He was nominated by the Academy for Best Actor in 1995 but didn't win. (Tom Hanks won for Forrest Gump.) What Freeman does so beautifully is to slightly underplay the part so that the eternal boredom and cynicism of the lifer comes through, and yet we can see how very much alive with the warmth of life the man is despite his confinement. Someday Morgan Freeman is going to win an Academy Award and it will be in belated recognition for this performance, which I think was a little too subtle for some Academy members to fully appreciate at the time.

But Freeman is not alone. Tim Robbins plays the hero of the story, banker Andy Dufresne, who has been falsely convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. Robbins has a unique quality as an actor in that he lends ever so slightly a bemused irony to the characters he plays. It is as though part of him is amused at what he is doing. I believe this is the best performance of his career, but it might be compared with his work in The Player (1992), another excellent movie, and in Mystic River (2003) for which he won an Oscar as Best Supporting Actor.

It is said that every good story needs a villain, and in the Bible-quoting, Bible-thumping, massively hypocritical, sadistic Warden Samuel Norton, played perfectly by Bob Gunton, we have a doozy. I want to tell you that Norton is so evil that fundamentalist Christians actually hate this movie because of how precisely his vile character is revealed. They also hate the movie because of its depiction of violent, predatory homosexual behavior (which is the reason the movie is rated R). On the wall of his office (hiding his safe with its ill-gotten contents and duplicitous accounts) is a framed plaque of the words "His judgment cometh and that right soon." The irony of these words as they apply to the men in the prison and ultimately to the warden himself is just perfect. You will take delight, I promise.

Here is some other information about the movie that may interest you. As most people know, it was adapted from a novella by Stephen King entitled "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption." Rita Hayworth figures in the story because Red procures a poster of her for Andy that he pins up on the wall of his cell. The poster is a still from the film Gilda (1946) starring her and Glenn Ford. We see a clip from the black and white film as the prisoners watch, cheering and hollering when Rita Hayworth appears. If you haven't seen her, check out that old movie. She really is gorgeous and a forerunner of Marilyn Monroe, who next appears on Andy's wall in a still from The Seven Year Itch (1955). It's the famous shot of her in which her skirt is blown up to reveal her shapely legs. Following her on Andy's wall (and, by the way, these pinups figure prominently in the plot) is Rachel Welsh from One Million Years B.C. (1966). In a simple and effective device these pinups show us graphically how long Andy and Red have been pining away.

Frank Darabont's direction is full of similar devices that clearly and naturally tell the story. There is Brooks (James Whitmore) who gets out after fifty years but is so institutionalized that he can't cope with life on the outside and hangs himself. Playing off of this is Red's periodic appearance before the parole board where his parole is summarily REJECTED. Watch how this plays out at the end.

The cinematography by Roger Deakins is excellent. The editing superb: there's not a single dead spot in the whole movie. The difference between the good guys (Red, Andy, Brooks, etc.) and the bad guys (the warden, the guards, the "sisters," etc.) is perhaps too starkly drawn, and perhaps Andy is a bit too heroic and determined beyond what might be realistic, and perhaps the "redemption" is a bit too miraculous in how beautifully it works out. But never mind. We love it.

All in all this is a great story vividly told that will leave you with a true sense of redemption in your soul. It is not a chick flick, and that is an understatement. It is a male bonding movie about friendship and the strength of character, about going up against what is wrong and unfair and coming out on top through pure true grit and a little luck.

Bottom line: one of the best ever made, currently rated #2 (behind The Godfather) at the IMDb. Don't miss it.

9.title: Survival and Triumph

A lot of The Shawshank Redemption points to one theme, never give up. We have a hero, will played by Tim Robbins, pitted against corrupt prison guards and an evil warden. We wonder how he will survive the oppressive prison system and the cruel inmates. This is pretty standard but what makes Shawshank special is the connection between the Robbins character and another inmate in the prison played by Morgan Freeman who also narrates much of the film. The relationship between these two is one of discovery not only of inner strength but also how strong a friendship can be.

Much of The Shawshank Redemption is mood and emotion. We feel terror, heat, boredom and anger. Every aspect of the movie is a quality piece of work to drive home the feelings of the story. The entire cast is very good in how they fit into this closed often horrible world.

Along with this praise comes some criticism. In the middle of Shawshank I thought that the pace was too slow. I know we are supposed to see bored inmates but boring the viewer isn't the way to go. I won't give away the ending but it has a fantasy quality about it that just doesn't fit the very real nature of most of the movie. It's a Hollywood ending tacked on to a more serious film.

The Shawshank Redemption is a quality effort and is a welcome change from the routine action, horror or romance junk food films that are mostly released today. It takes a hard view of life but also shows the unbending will of the human spirit.

9.title: simply, the best
9.content:
Spoiler Alert A few films can presume of the importance that a film like The Shawshank Redemption does. Shawshank Redemption is considered by some critics as one of the best movies in the story of American film (listed as #2 by the Internet Movie Data Base,http://www.imdb.com). For many other people the film is considered as one of those films which theme is universal and that transcends throughout the ages and decades. And this is because topics like freedom, justice and injustice, greed and honesty, and perseverance are mixed in a manner that specifies what the human condition is and will be.

The performances given by Tim Robbins and the always acclaimed Morgan Freeman give the film the emotional touch that is easy to get as a viewer. The story is centered in a person called Andy Dufrense who was convicted for the murder of his wife, him, being a young and intelligent banker was one of the most promising persons in his category, but all his potential was brought down with his conviction, undoubtely unfair since it is obvious a person like Dufrense wouldn´t be capable of such a thing like murdering the person he loved with all his heart. Also the story of the "institutionalized" Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding played wonderfully by Morgan Freeman, a man who lost all hope of ever going out even if he had already payed more than he had ever expected for his crime, until he met Dufrense, who as anyone could see teaches Red the meaning of what to have a dream is, even if it takes you 20 years to accomplish it.

Greed comes in form of Captain Byron Hadley played by lancy Brown, an unscrupulous man, who ironicly although he directed the place were the "bad" element of society is reformed he was no better than the ones he subdued. Hadley since he first met Dufrense sought in him his golden egg gouse and used him to fulfill a fraud becoming Dufrense now into a real criminal, which he wasn´t until he got to jail. When the opportunity to prove Dufrense´s innocence comes, Hadley makes everything as possible to avoid that even though the assesination of a young person was in the middle. At the end, Dufrense escapes from jail through a hole he had dug for 20 years covering the evidence with several posters from the hollywood divas from those times from Rita Hayworth to Jane Fonda.

But, let´s talk about Andy Dufresne for a while, let´s take the scene at the roof of the building in which Andy gets beers for his coworkers in exchange for work. At the end of the scene we can see the smile of Andy, a happy man, who was happy with small little accomplishments. Andy was someone who was talented and yet, all he wanted was a yat in Puerto Vallarta near by the beach and that would be the heaven for him. In a world full of intelligent people who use their talents to get to the top, andy was one who needed little to be happy.

Of course the success of this film is based on what most of the famous films do, an utopic idea of society or how the human being should have been. Andy is the prototype of how all of us should be, never loose the sense of hope, always fight for what you want, greed and money is not good, and of course, being like this you will always succeed. After all, a movie that should be seen by everyone.

Few movies capture the essence of hope and resilience like The Shawshank Redemption. What starts as a tale of injustice slowly transforms into one of the greatest prison break stories ever told.

Andy Dufresne, an innocent man, endures decades of cruelty at Shawshank, but beneath his quiet demeanor, he is always planning. The moment Warden Norton rips off the poster, revealing the escape tunnel, is nothing short of legendary! Andy crawling through 500 yards of filth to freedom remains one of the most iconic scenes in cinema history. And that final moment-Red walking toward Andy on the beach in Zihuatanejo-delivers the most rewarding, emotional payoff a film can offer.

It's a movie that demands uninterrupted viewing, and honestly, I was lucky enough to rewatch it on a platform with zero ads and no subscription hassle. With big-name streaming services now forcing ads, it's a relief to find better alternatives online. If you want to experience films like this without distractions, there are some hidden gems out there-worth checking out! 😉

9.title: A story of human tenacity and persistence
9.content:
It is not the first time that a movie presents the development of a drama in a U.S. prison. It contains elements of violence, depravity (of prisoners, their guards and the director), corruption, indifference, injustice, loneliness, solidarity, ingenuity developed by limitations, perseverance and tenacity to develop for more than two hours a good human story culminating in a happy ending "Hollywood-style".

It highlights the good performances of Morgan Freeman and Tim Robbins, the telling of the story from the point of view of one of the inmates (Freeman), the criticism of the prison system culminating in the desire of their oldest prisoners to stay there instead of the alternative of dealing with a hostile and unknown world as soon as they are released from this status to their new freedom (the Netherland's syndrome).

It is a message of perseverance, faith and strong commitment to a goal from inmates unfairly treated and judged as well as of indifference from a society that had created this scheme.

9.title: A truly iconic and classic film!
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is one of those films that the majority of people will love, and yet, it can be hard to pinpoint one particular reason why. The performances are stellar, in fact it's hard to think of any particular cast member who lets the team down, but that's not it. The set design is suitably bleak, the dialogue is just the right balance of realism and poetry, and we once again get to hear the dulcet tones of Morgan Freeman's narration, but again, these are not what make the film great.

Everything comes together with Shawshank, creating an instant and intense atmosphere that can be gritty, distressing, and at the same time, hopeful, humorous and beautiful. This film portrays the character's life and experience with frank honesty, with the undeniable quality of the production only serving to support this incredible story. Even the score is impressive, adding tension even when you don't even notice it's there.

The only reason I don't give this film a ten is because it is not usually a genre that I love, and although this film is definitely an exception, I cannot say it is outright perfect. But it's damn near close!

9.title: Stephen King's Masterpiece Comes To Life

9.title: Shawshan redemption review
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption: Accepting the bleak and harsh realities that present themselves in our lives is part of what it means to mature as a person. No film I have ever seen so deeply encapsulates this sentiment as Frank Darabont's Shawshank Redemption. Two convicted felons live out their life sentences in the Shawshank prison, usually by outfoxing guards with red's smuggling network or just rambling with old chums. The Shawshank Redemption is a masterfully crafted film because the excellent cinematography, engaging plot, and Tim Robbin's acting eloquently reflects the frustrations of a wrongly convicted man named Andy Dufresne, and his struggle to maintain one of the most valuable aspects of humanity: hope.

The outstanding cinematography and drab grey shading help convey a bleak setting at the beginning of the film. Tense moments were punctuated with dark shadows cast over the actor's faces, and intensified further with Morgan Freeman's dulcet narration. The establishing shots of the prison were dull and grey, akin to the monotonous lifestyles of the institutionalized convicts that had accepted their lot in life. The somber tone created by dull colors and shading slowly captivated my attention, leaving me with baited breath in anticipation for the events to unfold.

The majority of the story was set in Shawshank prison, where our main characters, 'Red', and Andy Dufresne stare the reality of a life sentence in the face. Throughout the film, the two main characters complement one another with their incongruent views of what being behind bars truly means. Red believed that they should accept their current situation and make the best of it, whereas Andy tried to busy himself with his hobbies: keeping his mind focused on things beyond the walls that caged him. I found this optimistic behavior incredibly inspiring as a viewer. There is truly a positive gem of wisdom to be found in a person who is thrusted into an impossible situation, and still finds a perseverance to escape it as Andy Dufresne did.

The actors in this film performed extremely well overall, and Morgan Freeman's narration enriched my experience of this film immensely, because it complemented Tim Robin's delivery of Andy's character. Tim Robin's acting during Andy Dufresne's first interaction with Red was so well done, I felt as though Morgan Freedman's narration was manifesting on screen rather than being acted out. The entire cast succeeded especially well in bringing their respective characters to life: not forcefully exuding emotion, but casually, and crisply conveying memorable character interactions.

The Shawshank Redemption is a powerful piece which stands in a class of its own: original, nuanced, and engaging. A great deal of care, time, and consideration was placed into the production of this film. I reflect back on the many other films have emerged in recent decades: films that tried to emulate Shawshank Redemption's sleek mature essence, to no avail. Truly this film stands without peer by my metric. I have enjoyed the viewing and critiquing process of this film immensely, it is truly a treasure which I would recommend anyone watch for their enjoyment as well.

9.title: Great
9.content:
It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

From Andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - Red, who becomes his best friend, Brooks the old librarian, the corrupt Warden Norton, guards and prisoners. Red is our surrogate. He's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is Red's. We've been shown by Andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells Red. "Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'."

The Shawshank Redemption is a 1994 American drama film written and directed by Frank Darabont, based on the 1982 Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption. It stars Tim Robbins as Andy Dufresne, a banker who is sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary for the murder of his wife and her lover, despite his claims of innocence. Morgan Freeman stars as Ellis "Red" Redding, a fellow inmate who becomes Andy's friend and confidant.

The film chronicles Andy's experiences in prison, including his encounters with guards and other inmates, his attempts to maintain his hope and dignity, and his eventual plan to escape. The Shawshank Redemption is a powerful and moving story about friendship, hope, and redemption. It has been praised for its performances, direction, and writing, and is considered one of the greatest films of all time.

Here are some of the things that critics have praised about The Shawshank Redemption:

The performances: Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman give career-best performances in the film. Robbins is particularly effective as Andy Dufresne, conveying his character's intelligence, resilience, and hope. Freeman is also excellent as Red, the wise and world-weary narrator of the story.

The direction: Frank Darabont does a masterful job of directing the film, creating a world that is both realistic and emotionally resonant. He uses the film's setting to great effect, contrasting the harshness of prison life with the beauty of the outside world.

The writing: The Shawshank Redemption is based on a novella by Stephen King, but the screenplay by Frank Darabont and Andrew Sean Dendrant is excellent in its own right. The dialogue is sharp and witty, and the story is both suspenseful and moving.

The Shawshank Redemption is a must-see film for anyone who has ever felt lost or hopeless. It is a story about the power of the human spirit and the importance of never giving up on hope.

Here are some of the awards and nominations that The Shawshank Redemption has received:

Academy Awards: Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Cinematography Golden Globe Awards: Best Picture - Drama, Best Director, Best Actor - Drama (Tim Robbins), Best Supporting Actor (Morgan Freeman) American Film Institute: 100 Years...100 Movies list The Shawshank Redemption is currently ranked #1 on the IMDb Top 250 list of all time. It has a 99% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, and an average score of 88 out of 100 on Metacritic.

If you are looking for a powerful and moving film that will stay with you long after you have seen it, The Shawshank Redemption is the perfect choice.

9.title: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story,
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair.

The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest bus load of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

But Andy does not cry, and Red loses the cigarettes he wagered. Andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in Shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. Andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. He's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

Red is also a lifer. From time to time, measuring the decades, he goes up in front of the parole board, and they measure the length of his term (20 years, 30 years) and ask him if he thinks he has been rehabilitated. Oh, most surely, yes, he replies; but the fire goes out of his assurances as the years march past, and there is the sense that he has been institutionalized -- that, like another old lifer who kills himself after being paroled, he can no longer really envision life on the outside.

9.title: Tells a powerful story well, but I wish it allowed more development of supporting characters
9.content: I watched "The Shawshank Redemption" last night with my husband, partly to see what the fuss was all about. I found it a well made moving film, but a little too sentimental. Red's character was complex. He was very noble (well, he is played by Morgan Freeman) but he was in prison for being a murderer, and the speech he made to the parole board at the end of the film showed his dilemmas and the darker side of his personality. Andy was complex too as the other prisoners saw. I thought the characters were too clichéd in the way that the warden and the guards were bad, the prisoners were good, except for a group of prisoners (the Sisters) who were bad. Aside from Andy and Red, the characters fit clearly on one side of the good/bad divide. I would have liked to see more sides of their personalities. The film delivers some surprises by the end: it was wonderful not to have any inkling of Andy's escape, his plans for revenge, or his gift to Red, providing Red with his freedom. The script develops the story skillfully and makes the audience care deeply about the prisoners, not just Andy and Red. I would have liked to know what happened to the prisoners after the corrupt warden and the bullying guards were arrested. "The Shawshank Redemption" tells a powerful story well, but it would have an even more powerful punch if it allowed more time to discover the prisoners' inner natures: the darker tone of the "fishing" scenes at the start really isn't returned to. I loved Banks' pet crow and the nod to "Birdman of Alcatraz". That film was a strong portrait of both the Birdman and the experience of being in a prison. Ultimately, I didn't feel that "The Shawshank Redemption" gives a picture of what it's like to be a prisoner locked away in a corrupt institution for decades. For one thing, I can't see an entire population of a prison reacting to Mozart on the loudspeaker with awe: surely there must have been more prisoners who prefer Hank Williams.

For other uses, see The Shawshank Redemption (disambiguation). The Shawshank Redemption ShawshankRedemptionMoviePoster Theatrical release poster Directed by Frank Darabont Produced by Niki Marvin Screenplay by Frank Darabont Based on Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption by Stephen King Starring Tim Robbins Morgan Freeman Bob Gunton William Sadler Clancy Brown Gil Bellows James Whitmore Music by Thomas Newman Cinematography Roger Deakins Edited by Richard Francis-Bruce Production company Castle Rock Entertainment Distributed by Columbia Pictures Release dates September 10, 1994 (Toronto) September 23, 1994 (United States) Running time 142 minutes[1] Country United States Language English Budget $25 million[2] Box office $58 million[3] The Shawshank Redemption is a 1994 American drama film written and directed by Frank Darabont, and starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. Adapted from the Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption, the film tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary for the murder of his wife and her lover, despite his claims of innocence. During his time at the prison, he befriends a fellow inmate, Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding, and finds himself protected by the guards after the warden begins using him in his money-laundering operation.

Although the film was a box office disappointment, it received multiple award nominations (including seven Oscar nominations) and highly positive reviews from critics for its acting, story, and realism. It is now considered to be one of the greatest films of the 1990s. It has since been successful on cable television, VHS, DVD, and Blu-ray. It was included in the American Film Institute's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition).[4]

In 2015, the United States Library of Congress selected the film for preservation in the National Film Registry, finding it "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".[5]

9.title: Inside and out, a beautifully sculpted movie with great life lessons.
9.content:
I think that I am a little late to the party on this one. This movie has rightfully been acclaimed as a cinematic masterpiece for quite some time now. The naked viewers eye may not have caught everything that this sentimental film has to offer.

On the upper level of film analysis, we find the film very appealing to our physical senses. The basis of every great film is great writing. The film's dialogue rarely came out as cheesy, yet still carried an impactful punch. The conversations between characters always felt ernest. I found it easy to share the characters sentiments. Being someone who has worked in lock down systems such as prison, I can testify that the dialogue and writing was spot on. Something that should definitely be appreciated. 9.5/10 for writing.

Still on the upper level of film analysis, the cinematography was amazingly put to use. I have never liked it when strong color tints, over done close ups and wide outs, or crazy angles are used in film. Shawshank Redemption avoids the overuse of anything too drastic with its filming style. Perhaps a smidgen overuse of the slow-paced close up technique; however, for the most part this technique really works for the films dialogue. Most conversations in the movie tend to boil down to a simple thesis put at the end of the scene. It only makes sense that the cinematography matches the flow of conversation, by narrowing in to what the audience should specifically take away. 9.9/10 for cinematography

Set design is another component which was important to this particular story. It was important that there was a transition of color and feeling between each location in the film. This film truly puts the audience in locations of freedom and entrapment. 10/10

Editing and directing was spot on. The film felt well paced.

Now, for the lower level of film analysis (the deeper meaning). This film is a field of gold when it comes symbolism and life lessons if you ask me. This film is not only about redemption, hope, judgment, trial, captivity or freedom; it is also about the world we are uncontrollably born into. The film is sprinkled with symbolism towards birth into situations beyond our control. The film is also a symbol of the life of Christ-- Andy being that sort symbol. For example, he is a sinless man put into suffering conditions for a crime someone committed. He is depicted as soft spoken and humble lamb who is led to slaughter. He creates his first service to his fellow inmates by supplying alcohol, a parallel to how Christ began his earthy ministry, turning water into wine at a wedding. He teaches others, he helps those who are his enemies, and he suffers at the hand of his rulers. One morning we find that his cell, the place he is to die someday, is empty- much like the tomb of Christ. He then finishes the movie by redeeming Red, the "only guilty man in Shawshank prison".

I could go on and on about these lower level film analytics. This movie is filled with all sorts of lessons which will shine through for different audience members.

Side note, I watched this movie on a editing system which took out F bombs and other foul language. For those who would only ever see this movie if edited, it is definitely worth it.

9.title: Hope and beauty masterfully depicted in a timeless classic for years to come
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption was likely going to be good. Nothing outstanding to timestamp on the history of film, but by 1995 it had suddenly grown a cult following and understandably so. It took a few years to become to cinematic phenomenon it is but in 1994 it was still recognised by the Academy with a best picture nomination, but it could not contend with big players such as the likes of Pulp Fiction and eventual winner Forrest Gump. Whether or not it should have won that year's Oscar award is still highly debated due to the quality of film from that year, but by no doubt it has aged the best, even better than Tarantino's acclaimed and admired Pulp Fiction.

Does the Shawshank Redemption have great cinematography? Yes. But is it monumental to film like Stanley Kubrick's Barry Lyndon or Akira Kurosawa's Seven Samurai? No. It's not specifically outstanding. Is it an artsy and classy film with technical detail to inadvertently sway the audience's emotions? To an extent yes, but not quite as artsy or technical as Francis Ford Coppola's Godfather trilogy or Martin Scorcese's Raging Bull. It is simply an excellent film with excellent technique made into a timeless film because it is so rewarding to the viewer. For starters, the plot is excellent. It is often a very underrated factor of a film but your plot is so important to a viewer. It is a tale of a man wrongfully convicted of murder who uses his wit, integrity, patience and most of all hope to persevere. It instills a reason to watch the film, to watch the protagonist struggle under such odds. Like said before, the camera work is excellent with them utilising the shot variation to convey the emotion of the scene. And next I would like to mention the sub plot. One often failed thing in films. They try too hard to build the sub charachter and in the end it does nothing in the long run. The main sub plot of an old man who owns a library in the prison is such a great contributor not only to the story but to the circumstances and environment. Not to forget the excellent acting and narration by Morgan Freeman and Tim Robbins. It has absolutely fantastic antagonists as well.

As well as this, it acts quite like a David Fincher film in that it rewards you more whenever you watch it a second time around. There are little details and smart lines of dialogue which you can pick up on. It is just so fantastic how every minute of that film gets tied in a neat little bow. Everything comes full circle. Perhaps nothing so unexpected would turn out to be so excellent. I only take issue with the ending which with the beginning is the most important part of the film. I hear one of the Castle Rock producers insisted on a complete conclusion with the ending, but if that little knot had just stayed untied then that film would have been even better. In spite of this, it is with no doubt in the top 10 (and likely top 5 films ever made). Afterall, it hasn't been IMDB's top film for so long for nothing. Pure excellence.

Set in the harsh environment of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film follows the story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is wrongfully convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison.

What sets this film apart is its powerful storytelling and character development. The audience is drawn into Andy's plight, rooting for him as he navigates the brutal world of Shawshank and befriends fellow inmate Red. 9.title: Shawshank Redeems Hollywood
9.content:
"Shawshank Redeems Hollywood" is not just a movie; it's a cinematic triumph that continues to captivate audiences with its timeless tale of hope, friendship, and redemption. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," this film stands as a testament to the power of storytelling and the resilience of the human spirit.

Set within the confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film follows the journey of Andy Dufresne, a mild-mannered banker wrongly convicted of murder, and his unlikely friendship with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding. Played with understated brilliance by Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman, respectively, Andy and Red form the emotional core of the film, anchoring its narrative with their compelling character arcs and nuanced performances.

What sets "Shawshank Redeems Hollywood" apart from other prison dramas is its unwavering commitment to authenticity and emotional honesty. Rather than relying on gratuitous violence or sensationalism, the film opts for a more introspective approach, delving deep into the psyche of its characters and exploring themes of guilt, redemption, and the quest for meaning in a harsh and unforgiving world.

Central to the film's success is its impeccable pacing and narrative structure. Through a series of carefully crafted flashbacks and plot twists, Darabont keeps viewers on the edge of their seats, gradually unraveling the mystery of Andy's innocence while simultaneously deepening our understanding of the characters and their motivations. Each scene is imbued with a sense of purpose and significance, driving the story forward with relentless momentum towards its cathartic climax.

However, come Academy Award time the film received several nominations, and although it won none, it stirred up interest in the film for its home entertainment release. The rest, as they say, is history. For the film finally found an audience that saw the film propelled to almost mythical proportions as an endearing modern day classic. Something that has delighted its fans, whilst simultaneously baffling its detractors. One thing is for sure, though, is that which ever side of the Shawshank fence you sit on, the film continues to gather new fans and simply will never go away or loose that mythical status.

It's possibly the simplicity of it all that sends some haters of the film into cinematic spasms. The implausible plot and an apparent sentimental edge that makes a nonsense of prison life, are but two chief complaints from those that dislike the film with a passion. Yet when characters are this richly drawn, and so movingly performed, it strikes me as churlish to do down a human drama that's dealing in hope, friendship and faith. The sentimental aspect is indeed there, but that acts as a counterpoint to the suffering, degradation and shattering of the soul involving our protagonist. Cosy prison life you say? No chance. The need for human connection is never more needed than during incarceration, surely? And given the quite terrific performances of Robbins (never better) & Freeman (sublimely making it easy), it's the easiest thing in the world to warm to Andy and Red.

Those in support aren't faring too bad either. Bob Gunton is coiled spring smarm as Warden Norton, James Whitmore is heart achingly great as the "Birdman Of Shawshank," Clancy Brown is menacing as antagonist Capt. Byron Hadley, William Sadler amusing as Heywood & Mark Rolston is impressively vile as Bogs Diamond. Then there's Roger Deakins' lush cinematography as the camera gracefully glides in and out of the prison offering almost ethereal hope to our characters (yes, they are ours). The music pings in conjunction with the emotional flow of the movie too. Thomas Newman's score is mostly piano based, dovetailing neatly with Andy's state of mind, while the excellently selected soundtrack ranges from the likes of Hank Williams to the gorgeous Le Nozze di Figaro by Mozart.

9.title: A Tale of Freedom and Redemption Masterfully Told
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption redefines what a cinematic experience can be. Delivered with humility, honesty, and powerful performances, it weaves a captivating tale about freedom and hope that leaves an indelible mark on the hearts of viewers. Released in 1994, it may not have lit the box office on fire, but its flame continues to burn in the heart of cinema lovers.

The movie, adapted from Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption", pulls you into the bleak walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary. It follows the story of a banker, Andy Dufresne, played by Tim Robbins, who is wrongfully accused of murdering his wife and her lover, and receives a double life sentence. As he navigates the brutal reality of prison life, his friendship with Ellis 'Red' Redding, a long-term inmate, portrayed by Morgan Freeman, takes center stage. This friendship and their shared dreams of freedom form the crux of the plot.

The movie presents an array of brilliantly portrayed characters and themes, with each element skillfully contributing to the story's overall grandeur. Andy's unwavering hope and resilience against the brutal backdrop of Shawshank and Red's skepticism, which slowly transforms into belief, create a perfect on-screen balance. A curious trivia: The role of Tommy Williams, eloquently brought to life by the young Gil Bellows, was initially offered to Brad Pitt. He, however, had to turn it down due to scheduling conflicts.

The Shawshank Redemption showcases cinematic storytelling at its finest. Director Frank Darabont uses the camera to immerse us fully into the harsh environment of the prison, while Thomas Newman's score brings a distinctively emotive layer to the narrative. Not to mention, the film is interspersed with witty dialogues and philosophical insights, that further enrich the viewing experience. The famous dialogue, "Get busy living, or get busy dying", remains one of the most quoted lines in movie history.

On the critical front, The Shawshank Redemption does not falter. Its depiction of prison life is unflinchingly real yet avoids excessive pessimism. The plot does not rush but allows the characters and their relationships to evolve naturally. While some may argue that the movie's ending is overly optimistic, others would say that it perfectly encapsulates the film's prevailing theme of hope and redemption. An interesting note: while the movie ends on a different note from the novella, Stephen King has publicly stated that he prefers the film's ending.

In conclusion, The Shawshank Redemption is more than a movie; it's an experience, a life lesson wrapped in the garb of a prison drama. It delivers a powerful message about friendship, hope, and perseverance that resonates long after the end credits roll. Watching Andy and Red carve their path towards redemption is like witnessing a silent rebellion against fate. Despite being set within the confines of a grim penitentiary, it leaves you with an unconfined sense of freedom and an urge to embrace life with renewed vigor. As Red states in the movie, "Hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies". Indeed, The Shawshank Redemption is one such good thing, a cinematic masterpiece, that refuses to fade away.

9.title: An Unforgettable Masterpiece - The Shawshank Redemption
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic gem that transcends the boundaries of time and genre. Frank Darabont's 1994 adaptation of Stephen King's novella delivers an emotionally charged, thought-provoking narrative that has cemented its place as one of the greatest films in cinematic history.

The heart of the film lies in the friendship between Andy Dufresne, played brilliantly by Tim Robbins, and Ellis "Red" Redding, portrayed by the incomparable Morgan Freeman. Their on-screen chemistry is a true cinematic marvel, delivering performances that are nothing short of remarkable. Tim Robbins' portrayal of a man wrongfully convicted and his unwavering hope is a testament to the human spirit's resilience. Morgan Freeman's narration and portrayal of Red, the seasoned inmate, provide a soulful anchor to the story.

The plot is meticulously crafted, keeping the audience engaged throughout the film's 142-minute runtime. It weaves elements of hope, friendship, and the indomitable human spirit into a complex tale of redemption within the bleak confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary. The screenplay beautifully balances moments of despair and triumph, making the viewer's emotional journey a truly cathartic experience.

Cinematographer Roger Deakins captures the prison's stark, foreboding atmosphere and the transformative beauty of freedom with striking visuals. The film's timeless cinematography, along with Thomas Newman's evocative score, complements the storytelling in a way that deepens the emotional impact of every scene.

The supporting cast, featuring actors such as Bob Gunton, William Sadler, and Clancy Brown, contributes to the film's rich tapestry of characters, each with their own compelling stories and arcs.

What sets "The Shawshank Redemption" apart is its universal message of hope and redemption. It reminds us that even in the darkest of circumstances, the human spirit can endure and find its way back to the light. The film's profound themes resonate with audiences of all ages and backgrounds.

Ultimately, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of cinema. It's a timeless story of friendship, hope, and the resilience of the human spirit. A true classic, it will continue to inspire and touch the hearts of generations to come. If you haven't experienced this cinematic triumph, don't miss the opportunity to watch a film that will stay with you long after the credits roll.

9.title: The Best Film I ever seen
9.content:
Why do I want to write the 234th comment on The Shawshank Redemption? I am not sure - almost everything that could be possibly said about it has been said. But like so many other people who wrote comments, I was and am profoundly moved by this simple and eloquent depiction of hope and friendship and redemption.

The only other movie I have ever seen that effects me as strongly is To Kill a Mockingbird. Both movies leave me feeling cleaner for having watched them.

I didn't intend to see this movie at all: I do not like prison movies and I don't normally watch them. I work at a branch library and one day as I was checking The Shawshank Redemption out to one of our older patrons, she said to me, "Whenever I feel down or depressed, I check out this movie and watch it and it always makes me feel better." At the time, I thought that was very strange. One day there was nothing on TV except things I absolutely would not watch under any circumstance or things that I had seen too many times already. I remembered what she said, so I watched it. I have watched it many many times since then and it gets better with every showing.

No action, no special effects - just men in prison uniforms talking to each other.

The Shawshank Redemption and To Kill a Mockingbird are the best movies I have ever seen. I do not judge it by it's technical merits - I don't really care about that. I have read that Citizen Kane or The Godfather or this or that movie is the best movie ever made. They may have the best technique or be the most influential motion pictures ever made, but not the best. The best movies are ones that touch the soul. It takes a movie like The Shawshank Redemption to touch the soul.

9.title: The story about men
9.content:
It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne "Tim Robbins", the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding Morgan Freeman. It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy "looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over", and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

Nor again is there anyone who loves or pursues or desires to obtain pain of itself, because it is pain, but because occasionally circumstances occur in which toil and pain can procure him some great pleasure. To take a trivial example, which of us ever undertakes laborious physical exercise, except to obtain some advantage from it? But who has any right to find fault with a man who chooses to enjoy a pleasure that has no annoying consequences, or one who avoids a pain that produces no resultant pleasure?

On the other hand, we denounce with righteous indignation and dislike men who are so beguiled and demoralized by the charms of pleasure of the moment, so blinded by desire, that they cannot foresee the pain and trouble that are bound to ensue; and equal blame belongs to those who fail in their duty through weakness of will, which is the same as saying through shrinking from toil and pain. These cases are perfectly simple and easy to distinguish. In a free hour, when our power of choice is untrammelled and when nothing prevents our being able to do what we like best, every pleasure is to be welcomed and every pain avoided. But in certain circumstances and owing to the claims of duty or the obligations of business is will frequently occur that pleasures have to be repudiated and annoyances accepted. The wise man therefore always holds in these matters to this principle of selection: he rejects pleasures to secure other greater pleasures, or else he endures pains to avoid worse pains.

9.title: Andy and Red get busy...
9.content:
Never underestimate America's fascination with outlaws and criminals. Few can forget that band of revolutionaries who founded this country. Theirs was a heck of a gamble, which, in the case of proving unsuccessful, would have found them all hanging gallows high. So it should come as no surprise that many members of present society find cause to cheer outlaws and criminals of every stripe. The more intellectually resourceful, inventive and philosophical these characters prove to be, the more they seem to charm their audiences. Perhaps this partly explains the appeal of PULP FICTION (1994), with its hit men playing a faux version of students of Life, pondering the verities of Divine Intervention and the unsuspected temporary triumph of the so-called strong over the weak before chaos overcomes them in the out-takes. The strangest things can re-enforce this original archetype of free thinkers pugnaciously operating outside the strictures of the known and accepted Law.

Enter Tim Robbins as banker Andy Dufresne sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary. Ostensibly guilty for the murders of his wife and her lover, he claims innocence and is sticking to his story. But what else is new? He's merely declaring the party line. Later in the narrative, Morgan Freeman as fellow inmate Ellis Redding, demonstrates that everyone in Shawshank can claim innocence, so he happens to be in good company.

The relationship between Andy and Red is interesting to compare with that of John Travolta as Vincent Vega and Samuel L. Jackson as Jules Winnfield. I believe it was Roger Ebert who alluded to an echoing of the relationship between Huckleberry Finn and Jim in Tarantino's Indie masterpiece PULP FICTION (1994). You might also find it of value to compare the relationship between Max Durocher as played by Jamie Foxx and Vincent as played by Tom Cruise in Michael Mann's COLLATERAL (2004) for good measure. It might explain the appeal of these kind of buddy movies where one character is white and the other black.

Now Huckleberry Finn was moving down a river of Space with an escaped slave called Jim on a raft, and at times this involved trading incidents about their life experience. Doing time together, Andy and Red find themselves riding down a river of Time toward a destination that appears to be unknown. Vincent Vega and Jules Winnfield find themselves moving down a river of Time and Space past points of chaos to some kind of paradigm shift beyond their current professional duties. Tom Cruise's take on the philosophical assassin, also curiously named Vincent, is also moving down a river of Urban angst with Jamie Foxx as Jim to his Huckleberry Finn. Examine these pairings closely and you will see that the African American male tends to serve as the moral conscience for the tale while the so-called Anglo-American tends to do the kind of resourceful thinking that resolves the narrative. This is less true for PULP FICTION (1994), where Jules Winnfield does most of the quick thinking AND serves as the moral conscience for the piece, and this alteration of the paradigm is further echoed in Max Durocher's seismic relationship with his Vincent in COLLATERAL (2004).

American society is so thoroughly saturated with the atmosphere of race consciousness that these kind of relationships between black and white males are a source of endless fascination and enormous appeal to audiences everywhere. White males traditionally demonstrate greater access to the machinations of a system primarily designed to favor them with opportunities, while the black males they are paired with tend to watch their backs, because, in the words of the immortal Sachel Paige, something might be gaining on them. It could be the hound dogs or the lynch mob or anybody else with their finger on the trigger.

Morgan Freeman gently and gradually grows on you, narrating the story until he comes to a near hero worship of Andy Dufresne, but as you'll see when you get near the end; it is evidently not without good reason. Director Frank Darabont give a nice elegiac flow to the entire proceedings peopled with as fine a motley crew of character actors as you could ask from anywhere. These include William Sadler as Heywood, a long standing member of Red's gang, James Whitmore as Brooks Hatlen, the elderly prison librarian, Clancy Brown as the brutal captain of the guards, and Gil Bellows as Tommy Williams, a young convict who gives and gets an education from Andy Dufresne. Bob Gunton as Samuel Norton, the sanctimonious warden of Shawshank prison, puts a supercilious smiley face on prison corruption, as Andy Dufresne finds himself reduced to playing ball and cobbling out his own chess pieces from rocks in the yard.

Just as Andy and Red evolve a relationship between each other that one could consider harkens back to Huckleberry Finn and Jim, so too does the final convolution of plot startle and surprise us with its faint resonances to Alexander Dumas' novel THE COUNT OF MONTE CRISTO. We recall later how Dumas the writer was mentioned earlier in the prison library. That being said, Morgan Freeman gets to utter one of the great lines in all of cinema before he enlarges his role to give us a taste of the Nelson Mandela he will play fifteen years later in Clint Eastwood's film INVICTUS (2009). Tim Robbins as Andy Dufresne gets to join Freeman on the narration as the vivid cinematography of Roger Deakins and the hauntingly endearing music of Thomas Newman takes us out of the closing scenes. We are left with a lot to digest about the roles of fear and hope as it relates to the vindication of faith beyond the confines of Shawshank Prison...

9.title: "Get busy living, or get busy dying"

I don't know what more I can add to all the reviews already out there, but the truth is, this will probably serve more to let IMDb's algorithm know what's good and what I want to watch.

A truly timeless film. Made in 1994, but you could easily tell me it was produced in 2024. In 2 hours and 22 minutes, we get a story with a clear beginning, middle, and end, with no details left out, summing Morgan Freeman's narration, guiding us through the thoughts of the prisoners, keeps the narrative alive and the viewer fully engaged.

The film made me see prison life through a different lens, highlighting the stark difference between the term "rehabilitated" and what Red and Brooks truly feel, as "institutionalized." After so many years living within the same four walls, in a "community" where he had a place and purpose, prison became the life he knew. As Red tells Andy, "They send you here for life, and that's exactly what they take," meaning that even if released early, the life waiting on the outside will never be the same as the routine you've been "indoctrinated" into.

I'm honestly amazed. I don't know exactly what makes a 10/10 film, but if one exists, I feel this would be it. Thank you.

9.title: Terrific Film Based on a short story by...
9.content:
When I was a teenager, I read a book called Different Seasons which, at the time, was a series of short stories by a man named Richard Bachman.

Richard Bachman, as it turns out, was actually Stephen King.

King was apparently worried that having his name on this book would cause people to have preconceived notions and possibly judge the work by his name alone, rather than by it's contents.

Among the short stories in this book was one titled, Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption, on which the film was based.

There are a lot of memorable characters and happenings throughout, and in the center of all of them is Andy Dufresne, who was accused of killing his wife for sleeping with a golf pro at the local country club.

Andy claims he is innocent, but is convicted and sent to prison for the murder.

This film does a very good job of staying true to the story, with only a few minor changes that do not effect the outcome.

Without giving too much away, I will just say that this film is the highest rated on IMDb for a reason. It is about so many different things that it would take some time to list them, would have to contain spoilers and would not do the film justice.

This movie will elicit many different emotions and is definitely worth the viewing.

9.title: The whole atmosphere of the film is soaked through with injustice and cruelty.

The film tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a former vice president of the bank, who got into Shawshank prison, from which no one has ever managed to escape. Dufresne was sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of his wife and her lover, since all the witness statements and evidence are against him, but he does not admit his guilt. But did he commit this crime? Maybe he ended up in prison because of an unfortunate set of circumstances? We won't get answers to these questions right away. Everyone has to decide for himself what to believe.

The whole atmosphere of the film is soaked through with injustice and cruelty. But in every dark kingdom there is a ray of light, here it is hope. A hope that won't let us go until we die. Whatever happens, we continue to hope for the best. And Thomas Newman, the composer of the film, managed to feel all this, to convey to the viewer the right atmosphere. His music draws us into what is happening on the screen. And only with the onset of the credits, I bitterly acknowledged the fact that the film was over, and I would so like to know what will happen next...

9.title: Get busy living, or get busy dying
9.content:
Escape from Shawshank is a film that rightfully considers the timeline as irrelevant, making it a classic. It teaches us various lessons, prompting contemplation on whether one's societal position truly reflects one's character's quality. Is absolute truth provable, and do all individuals seek it?

In the harshness of the prison guards and the warden, a deep-rooted arrogance is evident, coupled with a satisfaction derived from their superior positions. Bob Gunton, portraying the Warden, becomes an all-powerful figure upon assuming his role, seemingly indifferent to fulfilling his duties. His exaggerated egotism reaches its peak in the final scene when he decides that taking his own life is more valuable than continuing as a prisoner, considering his existence and worth insignificant.

On the contrary, the protagonist, Andy, suggests that, despite appearing insignificant, the situation he found himself in was an opportunity to find hope. As he puts it, hope is a very good thing, perhaps the best of things. Andy demonstrates the importance of living meaningfully, asserting that a static existence devoid of progress renders life insignificant.

In essence, the film presents a simple choice: get busy living or get busy dying. This dichotomy serves as a powerful message, urging viewers to reflect on the profound themes of hope, purpose, and the significance of one's choices in the face of adversity.

9.title: Greatest film of all time?
9.content: Perhaps the greatest challenge of the AMPAS is determining what defines a "Best Picture." I have heard it defined from some forgotten source directly tied to the AMPAS that a Best Picture is one that holds itself superb in the following three categories: Direction, Writing, and Acting, not necessarily in that order. A good example would be Citizen Kane, arguably the most worthy winner of these three categories (Kane lost to How Green and never picked up the Best Picture statue). However, it is certain that the greatest film of all time would need to excel especially in one field: Originality. How many people would even go bother to see another interpertation of Titanic? However, if this particular film had come out before the Cameron version, it would certainly be hailed with critical acclaim. Shawshank is one that meets the AMPAS standards of excellence, and most certainly would have taken the Best Picture title, if not for Forrest Gump, a film which many members perhaps found it impossible to not vote for due to the momentum it had gained. If Shawshank had been nominated almost any other year of this decade, the statue would have been a lock. However, we must look at Shawshank not as the year's Best Picture, but as a film in the long timeline of movie history, a film which tells an original story with original acting style and original directing. Can we look at Shawshank and with all sincerity call it the greatest film ever? Before deciding, a prerequisite should be to see at least 50 of the best films of this century. In this way, Shawshank loses the advantage of being fresh in our memory, losing the emotional effect, and must bow to the annals of time as do all the other superb films of history. Shawshank is not the Best Picture of all time nor the greatest film of all time. This is a fact we must face and learn to live with, no matter how much the storyline touched us all.

9.content: The reason this movie is ranked number one is that it is a tale of hope. It's the story of a man, who claims to be innocent, on the inside of a jail. We witness the cruelties.
