9.title: Breaking Free: A Deep Dive into The Shawshank Redemption
9.content:
Hey there, fellow cinephiles and casual movie-goers! Have you ever found yourself pondering the grim realities of life behind bars for a crime you swear on your grandma's grave you didn't commit? Well, put down that stale popcorn and grab a fresh bucket because we're about to plunge headfirst into the labyrinthine walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary. This isn't just any prison; it's a fortress of despair with sky-high walls and even higher stakes. Today, we're dissecting the 1994 cinematic masterpiece known as "The Shawshank Redemption," directed and adapted for the screen by the one and only Frank Darabont. Why, you ask, should you care about a movie that's almost three decades old? Because it's not just another run-of-the-mill prison drama; it's a timeless narrative that delves into the complexities of friendship, the enduring power of hope, and the indomitable resilience of the human spirit. So buckle up, because this is going to be a ride you won't want to miss!

The Plot - No Spoilers, I Promise!

Imagine it's the 1930s, and you're Andy Dufresne, a banker played by Tim Robbins, who's just been handed a double life sentence for the murder of his wife and her lover. The catch? You're innocent. Welcome to Shawshank, a prison that makes Alcatraz look like a summer camp. From the get-go, the place is a nightmare. On his very first night, Andy witnesses the guards' brutality as they beat an inmate to death. It's a harsh wake-up call to the realities of prison life. But Andy is a survivor. He keeps his head down, mouth shut, and ears open. One day, he overhears a guard complaining about taxes. Seizing the opportunity, Andy offers his financial expertise, and just like that, he becomes the unofficial financial advisor to the guards and eventually even the corrupt Warden Norton. But here's where the plot thickens: a new inmate arrives, someone who could potentially exonerate Andy. But will Warden Norton let that happen? Not if his greed has anything to do with it.

The Characters - More Layers Than an Onion Andy Dufresne: "The Banker Behind Bars" At first glance, Andy Dufresne seems like a fish out of water-a quiet, almost timid individual who you'd think would never survive a day in Shawshank. But as the story unfolds, we see layers of his character peel away to reveal a man of incredible resilience, intelligence, and hope. His transformation from a meek newcomer to the prison's financial guru is not just a testament to his ingenuity but also an inspiring narrative of human potential.

Red: "The Narrator Who Knows How to Get Things" Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is nothing short of iconic. He's the narrator, the philosopher, and the moral compass of the story. His friendship with Andy offers a heartwarming contrast to the bleakness of Shawshank. Through his eyes, we get a panoramic view of life behind bars-from the mundane to the miraculous. His narration isn't just a storytelling device; it's the soul of the movie, offering profound insights into the human condition.

Warden Norton: "The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing" Warden Norton is the epitome of hypocrisy-a man who hides his corrupt and malevolent nature behind a veneer of Christian piety. He quotes the Bible, but his actions are far from Christ-like. He's a master manipulator who knows how to play the system to his advantage. His character serves as a stark reminder that sometimes the real criminals are the ones running the show.

The Guards: "The Real Criminals?" Speaking of running the show, let's talk about the guards. These guys are the foot soldiers of Warden Norton's corrupt regime. Their brutality is not just physical but psychological, serving as a constant reminder to the inmates that they're at the bottom of the food chain. But as Andy rises in prominence, we see subtle shifts in their behavior, adding layers of complexity to their characters.

The Director & Screenplay - Frank Darabont's Masterpiece Frank Darabont took Stephen King's novella and transformed it into a screenplay that's a masterclass in storytelling. The pacing is impeccable, the dialogue is crisp, and the character development is so well-executed that you forget you're watching a movie; you're living it. As film critic Roger Ebert eloquently put it, "The film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything." Darabont crafts a narrative that transcends the confines of its prison setting to explore universal themes of humanity, making you question your own moral compass along the way.

Cinematography & Music - A Symphony of Shots The film's cinematography and music are characters in their own right. The camera work captures the stark contrast between the oppressive walls of Shawshank and the liberating vastness of the outside world. The score by Thomas Newman is a symphony that perfectly complements the highs and lows of the narrative. Peter Travers of Rolling Stone summed it up best when he said, "It's Darabont's accomplished storytelling that makes Shawshank compelling." The visual and auditory elements of the film work in harmony to create an immersive experience that stays with you long after the credits roll.

Themes - Not Just a Prison Break Friendship: "The Bromance That Survived Shawshank" The friendship between Andy and Red serves as the emotional core of the movie. It's not just a bromance; it's a deep, platonic love story that transcends the grim realities of prison life. Their friendship offers a glimmer of hope and humanity in a world that often seems devoid of both.

Hope: "The Thing With Feathers That Perches in the Soul" Hope is a recurring motif in the film. It's what drives Andy to seek a better life, even within the confines of Shawshank. It's what keeps Red going, despite decades of imprisonment. Hope is the light at the end of a very long, very dark tunnel, and it's what makes the story universally relatable.

Justice: "The Long Road to Redemption" The film raises poignant questions about justice and redemption. Is the legal system truly just? Can one find redemption in a place designed to strip you of your humanity? These themes resonate on a deep, existential level, making the film much more than a simple prison drama.

The Impact - Why It's Still Relevant Despite being nearly three decades old, "The Shawshank Redemption" has left an indelible mark on pop culture. It continues to top IMDb rankings and is frequently cited in discussions about the greatest films of all time. Its themes of friendship, hope, and justice make it a timeless classic that resonates with audiences of all ages.

Conclusion If you've made it this far and still haven't seen "The Shawshank Redemption," then I have to ask: what on Earth are you waiting for? An engraved invitation from Warden Norton himself? This isn't just a movie; it's a transformative experience that challenges your perceptions, tugs at your heartstrings, and leaves you pondering long after the credits have rolled. It's a cinematic journey that you owe it to yourself to take.

9.title: Wonderful
9.content: Wonderful movie, based on determination, hard work and intelligence. Use of time at it best In 1946, a banker named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is convicted of a double murder, even though he stubbornly proclaims his innocence. He's sentenced to a life term at the Shawshank State Prison in Maine, where another lifer, Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), picks him as the new recruit most likely to crack under the pressure. The ugly realities of prison life are quickly introduced to Andy: a corrupt warden (Bob Gunton), sadistic guards led by Capt. Byron Hadley (Clancy Brown), and inmates who are little better than animals, willing to use rape or beatings to insure their dominance. But Andy does not crack: he has the hope of the truly innocent, which (together with his smarts) allow him to prevail behind bars. He uses his banking skills to win favor with the warden and the guards, doing the books for Norton's illegal business schemes and keeping an eye on the investments of most of the prison staff. In exchange, he is able to improve the prison library and bring some dignity and respect back to many of the inmates, including Red. Based on a story by Stephen King, The Shawshank Redemption was the directorial debut of screenwriter Frank Darabont. ~ Mark Deming, Rovi

9.title: Before Watching: The Shawshank Redemption (1994)
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" (1994) is both an excellent drama and the highest rated movie on IMDb, and for a good reason. If you want to get as much out of it as possible, there are a few things you need to keep in mind before watching:

This movie is a prison movie. There are harsh language, a lot of profanity, violence (although not too graphic), and some psychologically intense moments. The opening scene features some very sensual elements, and the subject of rape is heavily present in the first half of the movie as well. Overall, it is easy to see why this is a R-rated movie.

Nevertheless, all of that can be derived from the Parents Guide. What the Parents Guide doesn't necessarily tell you is how impactful this movie is. It requires an additional half an hour after the credits have rolled to really be appreciated and soaked in, and make sure to take that into consideration. One should never put him- or herself in a stressful situation before, during or after watching this.

The Shawshank Redemption is brilliant, and treat it as such. Respect its voice over, its mood and atmosphere, and its music! Let it resonate. Enjoy it.

9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that has solidified its place as one of the greatest films ever made. Released in 1994, directed by Frank Darabont, and based on Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," this film beautifully captures the human spirit, showcasing the power of friendship, resilience, and the pursuit of freedom.

Set within the walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the story revolves around Andy Dufresne (played by Tim Robbins), a quiet and intelligent banker who is wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. From the moment he steps foot into the prison, Andy's transformation and journey begin.

What sets "The Shawshank Redemption" apart is its ability to evoke a wide range of emotions. It seamlessly balances moments of despair, heartache, and darkness with hope, humor, and triumph. The screenplay is meticulously crafted, drawing viewers into the harsh realities of prison life while simultaneously highlighting the indomitable human spirit.

The performances in this film are exceptional. Tim Robbins delivers a nuanced portrayal of Andy, capturing his quiet determination and inner strength. Morgan Freeman, in one of his most memorable roles as Ellis "Red" Redding, narrates the story with a soothing and wise voice, infusing it with warmth and depth. The chemistry between Robbins and Freeman is magnetic, forming the heart and soul of the film.

"The Shawshank Redemption" not only explores the dynamics of life behind bars but also delves into broader themes such as friendship, loyalty, and the quest for redemption. It portrays the power of human connection, illustrating how even in the darkest of places, genuine bonds can form and transform lives.

Visually, the film is captivating. The cinematography captures the essence of Shawshank State Penitentiary, with its towering walls, claustrophobic cells, and the contrasting beauty of freedom beyond. The score by Thomas Newman complements the narrative perfectly, intensifying the emotions and creating a hauntingly beautiful atmosphere.

The story unfolds at a deliberate pace, allowing the audience to truly immerse themselves in the characters' lives. The twists and turns keep you engaged, and the climax is both satisfying and cathartic. "The Shawshank Redemption" leaves an indelible mark, reminding us that hope can thrive even in the most hopeless of situations.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece that stands the test of time. Its poignant storytelling, outstanding performances, and profound themes make it a must-watch for any film enthusiast. It serves as a powerful reminder that hope, friendship, and the pursuit of redemption can transcend the darkest of circumstances.

9.title: Not your usual Stephen King story
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is based on a story by Stephen King, but if you know what King usually writes about, you will be totally surprised by this film. There are no monsters or creepy crawlies at all. No, instead we are given a story about prison life that involves our two central characters, Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) and Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), both of whom are convicted of multiple life sentences in Shawshank Prison.

Andy is a banker whose life is turned upside down when he is convicted of murdering both his wife and her lover. Sentenced to 2 life prisons, Andy does his best to survive by using his skills as a banker and accountant to move up in the prison world. He soon gains respect from his fellow inmates, especially Red, and not long after both he and Red become good friends. I was never sure what Red was imprisoned for, and though the story is mainly about Andy, Red's role is just as important. Kudos to Morgan Freeman, who gives one of his best performances ever.

The movie is well over two hours long, but I was never bored. Frank Darabont, the director and writer of the screenplay, keeps things interesting throughout. The pacing is perfect, and the actors, all of them, kept me engaged in the story. The movie also has some twists and turns which when finally revealed are perfect and add to the film's excitement.

The dialog is one of the most important aspects of the film and one of the films strongest points. We may have never learned much about the prison guards or the warden, but we got enough of an idea about them to be satisfied because of the dialog and because of the actors who played those parts. Also dialog is vital in Andy and Red's friendship. Without it, and the great work by the two actors, the film wouldn't have been quite as strong.

The only flaw I could find in the story would be in the prison terms for both men. If they are both imprisoned for multiple life sentences, how come they never seem to age over the years? It is a small problem, but it takes away some of the reality of the movie, and so I can't quite give it the perfect rating. Other than that, this is still and incredible movie going experience.

Note: I see that Shawshank Redemption is sitting pretty at #2 on IMDb's top 250. I'm not sure it deserves to be that high, but that doesn't stop it from still being superior to many other films on that list.

9.title: This movie is timeless.
9.content: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece of cinema that is timeless and essential to watch whatever ages you are. It defies description and portrays a timeless story of friendship, hope, and the victory of the human spirit. This film, which is based on the Stephen King novella and was directed by Frank Darabont, is an excellent examination of the human experience in a prison environment. This movie is an incredible character study at its core. In his role as Andy Dufresne, a man wrongfully imprisoned for a crime he did not commit, Tim Robbins gives an outstanding performance. Andy's strength, intelligence, and quiet will to take back his life and find redemption is symbolised by Robbins. As Ellis "Red" Redding, Morgan Freeman gives the story a strong narrative voice that leads us through it while delivering perceptive commentary on life and the human condition. Also, the story develops with the right amount of suspense and thought. Inspiring and heartbreaking, Andy's journey from an innocent guy imprisoned for a crime he didn't commit to a glimmer of hope inside the forbidding walls of Shawshank Penitentiary. The rebirth of the supporting cast, sparked by Andy's everlasting optimism and friendship, gives the story depth and emotional impact. The bond that forms between the prisoners, especially Andy and Red, provides the emotional foundation of the movie. The sincere relationship they share as well as tiny acts of compassion show how even in the worst of situations, human connection has the potential to alter. Red is portrayed by Morgan Freeman as developing from a pessimistic institutionalized prisoner to a hopeful believer in the possibility of redemption. Moreover, Roger Deakins' expert cinematography in the movie shows the sharp contrast between Andy's message of optimism and the brutalities of jail life. The concepts of darkness vs faith and prison versus independence are reinforced using light and shadow as well as the contrasting color palette. A rich and vivid experience is created by the visuals and Thomas Newman's moving musical composition, which improves the emotional effect of the narrative. A story that defies goals, "The Shawshank Redemption" overcomes its prison setting to become an inspiring reflection on life, resolve, and the possibility of change. It challenges conventional ideas about right and wrong, forgiveness, and the capacity for personal development. The film's storytelling is compelling and real, leaving viewers feeling emotionally affected and reflective. The movie's attractive scenes, like Andy's deep escape or the dramatic ending in Zihuatanejo, will go down in movie history. These scenes highlight the victory of hope and the fulfilment of long-awaited redemption, and they are not only technically outstanding but also emotionally impactful. In the end, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a consistently excellent work of cinema. For anyone looking for a fascinating and thought-provoking film experience, it is a must-watch due to its themes of optimism, friendship, and the indestructible human spirit. This movie is a prime illustration of how storytelling can move us, bring us up, and serve as a constant reminder of the inherent goodness we all possess.

"The Shawshank Redemption," directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," stands as a cinematic magnum opus that has left an indelible mark on audiences since its release in 1994. With a rating of 9 out of 10, this timeless classic has earned its place among the greatest films ever made.

At its core, the film is a tale of hope, friendship, and the enduring human spirit set against the backdrop of Shawshank State Penitentiary. Andy Dufresne, played by Tim Robbins, finds himself unjustly convicted of the murder of his wife and her lover. The narrative unfolds as Andy adjusts to the harsh realities of prison life, maintaining his innocence amidst a system fraught with corruption and brutality.

One of the film's key strengths lies in its meticulous storytelling. Darabont weaves a narrative that seamlessly combines elements of drama, suspense, and redemption. The pacing is deliberate, allowing the audience to immerse themselves in the intricacies of the characters' lives. The script, filled with memorable lines and poignant moments, adds depth to the storytelling, making it a masterclass in cinematic narrative construction.

The cinematography by Roger Deakins is another standout feature. The visual language of the film is evocative, capturing the starkness of prison life while also conveying the underlying themes of hope and freedom. The use of lighting, framing, and camera angles enhances the emotional resonance of key scenes, creating a visual tapestry that complements the narrative with precision.

Tim Robbins delivers a career-defining performance as Andy Dufresne. His portrayal is nuanced, capturing the quiet strength and resilience of a man wrongly accused. Robbins infuses Andy with a sense of dignity that transcends the confines of Shawshank. Morgan Freeman, as Red, the seasoned inmate and narrator, provides a soulful performance that serves as the emotional anchor of the film. The chemistry between Robbins and Freeman is palpable, elevating their characters' friendship to a level of authenticity rarely seen in cinema.

The film's exploration of the human spirit's capacity for hope is perhaps its most enduring theme. Despite the harsh realities of prison life, Andy maintains an unwavering belief in the power of hope. This theme is encapsulated in the iconic line, "Hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies." The gradual unfolding of Andy's plan to escape and the eventual realization of his dreams underscore the triumph of hope over despair.

The supporting cast, including the ensemble of inmates and prison staff, contributes to the film's richness. Each character is meticulously crafted, adding layers to the narrative and providing a glimpse into the complex dynamics of life behind bars. The film humanizes its characters, forcing the audience to confront the moral ambiguities that define the prison environment.

The score by Thomas Newman further enhances the emotional impact of the film. The hauntingly beautiful music complements the narrative, underscoring key moments and eliciting a range of emotions from the audience. The use of classical pieces, combined with Newman's original compositions, creates a soundtrack that lingers in the viewer's memory long after the credits roll.

Beyond its technical and artistic achievements, "The Shawshank Redemption" resonates on a deeper level due to its universal themes. The film explores the innate human desire for freedom and the resilience that allows individuals to endure even the harshest circumstances. The portrayal of friendship as a source of solace and strength adds a layer of emotional depth, making the film relatable to audiences across cultures and generations.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic triumph that transcends its genre. With its compelling narrative, stellar performances, and thematic richness, the film has earned its place as a classic. Its enduring popularity and critical acclaim are a testament to the power of storytelling to connect with the human experience. With a rating of 9 out of 10, "The Shawshank Redemption" stands tall as a timeless masterpiece that continues to inspire and resonate with audiences worldwide.

9.title: GOOD
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" emphasizes Andy's inner strength and unwavering hope in the face of daunting prison conditions. Universal themes such as criticism of the prison system, the yearning for inner freedom, and the healing power of friendship provide the audience with profound contemplation.

The film excels with its flawless screenplay, compelling performances, and unforgettable moments. The prison atmosphere serves as a poignant backdrop, unraveling the complexity of human nature and highlighting the resilience of the human spirit. Additionally, the film's ending is both surprising and thought-provoking, leaving a lasting impact on the viewer.

Over the years, "The Shawshank Redemption" has achieved cult status and is widely regarded as one of the greatest films in cinematic history. Beyond the confines of prison drama, the movie resonates as a testament to the indomitable strength of the human spirit and its ability to persevere with hope. It has earned a special place in the hearts of audiences, solidifying its reputation as a timeless classic.

9.title: "Put your trust in the Lord  your ass belongs to me"
9.content:
So says the warden of Shawshank prison, though Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) finds it belongs to a lot more people in this often-harrowing tale.

The Shawshank Redemption is a very, very clever film in that it takes its call from elder cinema, meaning it can net not only acclaim but also a wider audience. It's surely no coincidence that the first sound we hear  before the titles have even begun to roll - is that of The Ink Spots singing "If I Didn't Care". The shot pans out to Tim Robbins in an old-fashioned automobile and then to a courtroom where his last words to his wife were "I'll see you in Hell". No profanity from a bitter man in 90's cinema, though expletives do flavour the piece, with 24 uses of the f-word and 48 minor swearwords.

A few minutes into the film and part of the reason is given: the setting is 1947. However, the oldstyle trappings of the piece never leave it: violence and sexual activity are never laboured on. Beatings are delivered in shadow, or, in the case of Andy's first, the camera discretely pulls back and turns a corner while we just hear the sound. Note we are never shown that Andy is raped, we are just told that he is by Morgan Freeman's narration. That's another strong point of the film, and also an historical device, that of first person narration. Freeman adds a constant magnetism to the film; his voice-over a necessity considering it takes place over 20 years. Refreshingly, the ageing process is used subtly, if at all, rather than using unconvincing prosthetics. A little grey to Morgan's hair and the power of persuasion is all that is needed to carry out the illusion of time passing.

Another interesting point is that of race. Someone once told me they didn't like the film because they saw the black/white male bonding between Robbins and Freeman as too contrived and worthy. I told them that this showed a suspect attitude on their part as Ellis Redding's skin colour hadn't occurred to me, nor is it ever mentioned throughout the film. It isn't an issue that Redding is black, he just IS.

Ultimately, the redemption of the title comes from Robbins' humanitarian intellectualism against the warden's fundamental religious beliefs. But the ultimate testament to erstwhile cinema is that of two things: plot and character. It's this strength of character, not to mention two superb understated leads, which mean you can watch it again and again, even when one viewing reveals the twist in the tale. All the characters are three-dimensional, breathing human beings that get not lines, but emotions and beliefs. Occasionally some  not much, but some  of the dialogue can strain towards the overly sentimental. Perhaps this is what produced the nauseating tagline "Fear can hold you prisoner  hope can set you free". Yuck! But generally this pleasantly paced, well-told tale hits the target in it's own relaxed way. Far from pedestrian, the timing of the film is like that of drinking a cool beer on a hot summer's roof, or a whole yardful of inmates standing stock still to the beauty of Mozart.

The Shawshank Redemption was released the same year as Pulp Fiction, yet both of them were disgraced at the Oscars by the forgettable Forrest Gump. A great oversight.

9.content: In 1946, a banker named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is convicted of a double murder, even though he stubbornly proclaims his innocence. He's sentenced to a life term at the Shawshank State Prison in Maine, where another lifer, Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), picks him as the new recruit most likely to crack under the pressure. The ugly realities of prison life are quickly introduced to Andy: a corrupt warden (Bob Gunton), sadistic guards led by Capt. Byron Hadley (Clancy Brown), and inmates who are little better than animals, willing to use rape or beatings to insure their dominance. But Andy does not crack: he has the hope of the truly innocent, which (together with his smarts) allow him to prevail behind bars. He uses his banking skills to win favor with the warden and the guards, doing the books for Norton's illegal business schemes and keeping an eye on the investments of most of the prison staff. In exchange, he is able to improve the prison library and bring some dignity and respect back to many of the inmates, including Red. Based on a story by Stephen King, The Shawshank Redemption was the directorial debut of screenwriter Frank Darabont. ~ Mark Deming, Rovi

9.title: A True Movie of Character
9.content:
The story that emerges from from this unlikely source is hope and inspiration. I say unlikely source because the story comes from the pen of horror master Stephen King. This is not a story you can easily envision coming from his tortured soul. But perhaps King is in his element when words like prison, solitary confinement, torture and unrealistic all spring forth to describe the story of Andy Dufresne and his years at Shawshank prison.

Narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), Shawshank Prison has become his captive home of customers since he is able to procure certain items like cigarettes, candy and so on. For a self proclaimed innocent victim of the system, new comer Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) "Red" is asked for a most unusual item - a rock pick. Andy is an amateur geologist. Andy and "Red" gradually become friends as people come and go, one way or another, from Shawshank as time passes them by.

What on the surface might seem like a depressing story and situation is filled with personal challenges and one's will to overcome impossible odds. The prison is speckled with interesting characters such as the oldest convict Brooks the librarian (James Whitmore) or the bible thumping man at the top of Shawshank, Warden Norton (Bob Gunton). Whether doing time like Andy or finally being release like Brooks or being torn between beliefs like Warden Norton, each man faces their own challenges while all of them endure the ravages of time.

Everything about this movie is done with the backdrop of the prison even though it is nothing like any typical prison film. The movie is based on Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption by Stephen King. There is no horror that is normally found in King's work. Instead this is more of an inner character struggle like is found in another of King's work, Stand By Me. Like that story the two main character are linked in partnership with Tim Robbins giving a moving and powerful performance next to a solid character study by Morgan Freeman.

Director Frank Darabont delivers a solid film adding lots of life to what could have been a dreary background. The story flows evenly with a genuine care given to each character and each actor's performance. Shawshank is an instant classic and puts Robbins in the lead to play any every-man role aside the likes of Jimmy Stewart.

9.title: Wiki
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is a 1994 American drama film written and directed by Frank Darabont, and starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. Adapted from the Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption, the film tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is sentenced to life in Shawshank State Penitentiary for the murder of his wife and her lover, despite his claims of innocence. During his time at the prison, he befriends a fellow inmate, Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding, and finds himself protected by the guards after the warden begins using him in his money-laundering operation.

Although it was a box office disappointment, the film received multiple award nominations (including seven Oscar nominations) and outstanding reviews from critics for its acting, story, and realism. It has since been successful on cable television, VHS, DVD, and Blu- ray. It was included in the American Film Institute's 100 Years...100 Movies 10th Anniversary Edition.[4] It is considered to be one of the greatest films of all time.

In 2015, the United States Library of Congress selected the film for preservation in the National Film Registry, finding it "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".

9.title: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities,
9.content:
Stephen King Crime, Drama

Rated R

142 minutes

| Roger Ebert September 23, 1994 | Print Page

"The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair.

WATCH NOW

The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

But Andy does not cry, and Red loses the cigarettes he wagered. Andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in Shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. Andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. He's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

9.title: A keeper
9.content:
I've never read any Stephen King. For reading, I don't do novels, I prefer non-fiction.

I do novels via movies.

I really liked this movie, but I read a few 10 star reviews, (and a few negative reviews) and I was pretty incredulous about how much intense gushing went on about this movie, as well as some very interesting philosophies written out & even waxing poetic. It seemed the mid to low stars were given just tryin' to add balance, lol.

Allegedly, The Godfather was once the number one movie of all time . . . ? (currently ranks 2 these days) I was a kid when that came out, and all I really remembered about it was that horse head. So I recently rewatched all 3 Godfather movies - and tried to consider the era/technique, etc they were produced in - but I gotta say - I was unimpressed. The Godfather was just 'ok' to me. It wasn't that compelling to me. I've much more enjoyed the endless parodies of it over the decades.

Shawshank is a different animal - I'll just briefly touch on what I like; Cast, direction, sets, & production, are all excellent. The fact that it's set in the late 40's, aside from just feeling like a classic movie, also gives credence to pulling off a carefully calculated planned escape - but the brilliant thing is, they captured the fact that much has stood still - very little 'updating' occurs in prison life, and that element is portrayed visually & it 'felt' still stuck in the 30s, even the 20s.

Some noted the prison 'cliches' - well, these 'cliches' ARE prison life. That's the picture. Nothing changes. What would you expect?

One cannot help but like the intended and compelling meaning of the story being played out which is this; the tables of justice turned on those who abused the wielding of justice - the tables turned on the power-drunk who twisted & perverted justice, and knowing their own guilt, tried to hide it, feared their exposure.

It's a running theme - I think the judge & the lawyers in the courtroom identified with Andy - but their fear condenmed him, they wielded their power to cover their own similar thoughts & fears. Of course, 'the sister's represented another kind of fear that must be overcome with power. The abusive guard also, and the warden being the biggest victim of his own crime, & fear of being found out.

Prison guards, even wardens, are basically doin' time too. Here we get to see some coping mechanisms of good & bad guards, which explore the concept that many of the free men portrayed, as a primary example, captain Hadley, are as much criminals as any inmate.

And this movie creates the questions; How does it get to be like this? How are some criminals free & their crimes are 'ok' or easily hidden because in their freedom they can abuse the power of their position of authority?

The fact that Andy, is innocent, and WANTS the truth exposed, is the juxtaposition, AND uses his powers of intelligence & patience, to improve his position, and expose THE paradox of criminality is what is so compelling about this movie, combined with the fact that all this was done/told/portrayed on screen so well.

Bottom line; this is an interesting, immersive movie portraying life inside bars, and what some of those lives looked like outside bars, whether free or incarcerated.

This is definitely a keeper movie.

If you have it on DVD you'll enjoy the special features too.

9.title: Perfect
9.content: My first inspirational movie of my entire life... In 1947 Portland, Maine, banker Andy Dufresne is convicted of murdering his wife and her lover and sentenced to two consecutive life sentences at the fictional Shawshank State Penitentiary in rural Maine. Andy befriends prison contraband smuggler, Ellis "Red" Redding, an inmate serving a life sentence. Red procures a rock hammer and later a large poster of Rita Hayworth for Andy. Working in the prison laundry, Andy is regularly assaulted by the "bull queer" gang "the Sisters" and their leader, Bogs. In 1949, Andy overhears the brutal captain of the guards, Byron Hadley, complaining about being taxed on an inheritance and offers to help him legally shelter the money. After a vicious assault by the Sisters nearly kills Andy, Hadley beats Bogs severely. Bogs is sent to another prison and Andy is never attacked again. Warden Samuel Norton meets Andy and reassigns him to the prison library to assist elderly inmate Brooks Hatlen. Andy's new job is a pretext for him to begin managing financial matters for the prison employees. As time passes, the Warden begins using Andy to handle matters for a variety of people including guards from other prisons and the warden himself. Andy begins writing weekly letters to the state government for funds to improve the decaying library.

9.title: Meticulously powerful film
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is something of an oddity. Based on a Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption, it has dominated IMDb's Top 250 list for years now and has often been regarded as one of the best films ever made. Almost every adult Westerner has seen the movie at some point during their lives, yet not all that many people talk about this film, at least in my experience. It's not often recommended to others like The Godfathers, it's not quoted as often as The Dark Knight or Fight Club, it's not regarded as inherently cool as Pulp Fiction. So what makes it so great then? In my opinion the answer lies in its quality as a whole. It's not a flashy film. The pacing is slow as time itself - fitting for a prison film, admittedly - the conversations are often quiet and thoughtful, the prison setting never changes, but rather builds up in intensity and while there are emotions and deep themes displayed, they're not over the top or hammered in. Rather they're subtle, real if you will.

It's not a film that you will talk about a lot, but it's a movie that will stick with you. It's not a film that will leave you puzzled for days as you try to work through it's meanings, it's not a hard movie to understand, but you'll find yourself returning to it from time to time. And there are a lot of things to return to. The quiet dignity of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the friendship between him and Red (Morgan Freeman), the other inmates, the brutality of the warden and the guards, that brilliant moment in the rain, the ending, the callbacks, the overarching and complex plot.

The Shawshank Redemption is the jack of all trades of films. Not a single element in it is the absolute best within cinema, but they're all way above average. Everything from the slightest camera angle to the main actors is up to par and beyond. Personally it's not my favourite movie of all time, I admit as much, but it's a masterpiece in its own right. I have nothing against it being the number one.

9.title: Simply excellent
9.content:
There is a scene early in the movie when the viewer is introduced for the first time to Shawshank prison. The camera takes us on an extraordinary panorama, beginning at ground level and rising up until we see the inmates crowding around like ants. It must have been shot with a sky-crane or something because there is no break in continuity. The view just goes on, up and around in a breathtaking cycle. The effect is reminiscent of the 360 degree battlefield panorama of Rod Stieger's Napoleon in 'Waterloo'. It is almost arrogant, except that it's wonderful. From this point on, I knew I was about to watch something very, very special.

The film depicts the institutional brutality that sadly continues to be the hallmark or imprisonment, and how one comes to terms with it, or not. We quickly discover what happens to those who don't. Some hysterical white-collar inmate cracks-up and is beaten to death on his first night. It is a monstrous example of the ironically named 'correctional facility' at work.

Morgan Freeman is another actor as remarkable for his voice as his other abilities. He is perfectly chosen as narrator.

For almost 2 hours we endure the gloomy, threatening claustrophobia that makes up much of prison time, and what inmates do to gain some little respect and make life endurable. In this regard it has a lot in common with 'Midnight Express'. Except that here we are dealing with an innocent man.

Music scores are perfectly chosen. The sound effects equally well matched. The viewer is taken upon a journey so complete and plausible - assisted by strong acting and excellent script - that when the extremely unlikely escape is discovered, we are left believing that too.

The idea that a thunderstorm should fortuitously arrive at the very hour of need to mask the sounds of hammering, and that it would be possible to find sufficient air in the enclosed sewer-pipe, both stretch our credence a little.

My favourite moment features the abscondment-on-parole of Red, who goes in search of a certain Field with a certain tree. After so long steeped in the dank, evil reek of prison one can almost smell the scents of summer, the mown hay. All is silent except for the whir of insects and distant birdsong as soft sunlight filters down through trees. The contrast is perfect, the ambiance tangible. These are surely the things to savour most when freed from permanent brutality.

This, and the movie 'Fried Greeen Tomatoes' seem to perfectly counterpoint each other. They are both of equal quality and address parallels of endurance and relationships from male or female perspectives. I love 'em both as much.

I'm told that each bombed at the box-office. Not enough pyrotechnics and CGI effects I guess.

If you haven't seen either of them; get busy. But watch them on a decent telly with a quality independent sound-system.

9.title: Brilliant
9.content:
The first time I viewed Shawshank Redemption I didn't find it to be anything special. Sure, stars Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman were good BUT their performances weren't anything special...or so I thought at the time.

Frank Darabont directs Shawshank Redemption with a gentle, guiding hand allowing the actors to discover the essence within their characters. Some actors, undoubtedly, would not be up to the task. Robbins and Freeman, however, are not "some actors." They are consummate actors and masterful in their portrayals here.

Based upon Stephen King's novella, Darabont creates a film that never buys into the drama of its story, instead choosing to present the lives of the characters involved without histrionics. I have long felt, in fact, that the film may even improve upon the novella by bringing it into focus and providing it with a pacing that allows a more explicit character development.

I have noticed that many of my favorite films are ensemble pieces, and while Robbins and Freeman shine here it is actually the entire cast that brings this story to life with such grace and beauty. Supporting performances by the likes of James Whitmore, William Sadler, Gil Bellows and others who take what could be caricatures and give them in-depth personalities and thoughts and feelings.

Thomas Newman's score is supremely divine and changes along with the characters. It further enhances Darabont's pacing, as well. There are so many memorable scenes in Shawshank Redemption, however, the closing scene is certainly among one of the best closing scenes ever witnessed.

It is hard to fathom that a "prison" movie could be a source of tremendous hope, light and inspiration. Yet, to call Shawshank Redemption a prison movie is to minimize its greatness. It is a brilliant film, a study of humanity in all its wonder AND it happens to take place within the confines of a prison.

Moving, brilliant, inspirational, hopeful and empowering are all words that describe "The Shawshank Redemption." With outstanding performances from its ensemble cast and a work of tremendous cinematic poetry by director Frank Darabont. "Shawshank Redemption" creates a stellar vision that teaches, challenges, inspires and evokes a wide array of emotions and thoughts that serves to remind us that in the darkest moments of our lives there is always a light that shines within.

9.title: Just a Beautiful movie

I'm a guy that takes pride on the fact of being quite open-minded when it comes to appreciating different genres and kinds of stories. I love movies that faithfully and movingly depict the ugly side of humanity, but every now and then I also like something that tells us that not everything is lost.

The Shawshank Redemption introduces us to Andy Dufresne. A gentile yet emotionally estranged banker who's wrongfully accused of murdering his wife and her lover. This brings him to a gruesome prison were his will to maintain his humanity will be put to the test by the corrupt and abusive authorities of the prison, and also by some of his fellow inmates. In this bleak scenario he will find hope in the guise of friendship. Which will push him to rise above the situation.

This movie is all about hope. About the power of friendship and the reluctance to give up on life, even under the darkest circumstances. Even locked in a pit of pure evil, human spirit can be enough to lift you up.

Tim Robbins is convincing and moving in his performance, although he is outshone by a brilliant Morgan Freeman, who always seems to effortlessly touch the soul of the audience with his performances. The bad guys also generate the right amount of repulsion, with a good job from Bob Gunton as the morally questionable warden and Clancy Brown in the memorable role of the violent and vicious captain Hadley.

I've seen some reviews questioning the placement of this film as #1 for IMDb users. I don't think any of us can put a movie above all the rest or below them. Art is subject to personal appreciation and there will never be a single opinion more valuable than the rest. What's undeniable is that Shawshank caused what it intended. Moving the majority of people that have seen it through a beautiful story that aims to the human spirit and it's power to shed light in the darkest moments.

9.title: Excellent
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Exploration of Hope and Friendship

Released in 1994, Frank Darabont's adaptation of Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption" has become a cornerstone of cinematic excellence, transcending its initial box office performance to achieve iconic status over the decades. The film stars Tim Robbins as Andy Dufresne, a banker wrongfully imprisoned for the murder of his wife, and Morgan Freeman as Ellis "Red" Redding, a lifer who becomes Andy's closest friend.

Set against the bleak backdrop of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film expertly navigates themes of hope, friendship, and the human spirit's resilience. From the outset, viewers are thrust into the harsh realities of prison life, marked by brutality and despair. Andy's arrival at Shawshank is a pivotal moment that sets the tone for the film. His calm demeanor and quiet intelligence quickly draw the attention of other inmates, particularly Red, who serves as the film's narrator. Freeman's portrayal of Red adds depth and gravitas, capturing the weariness of a man who has long given up on hope.

One of the film's most compelling elements is its exploration of hope. Andy's unyielding belief in a better future contrasts starkly with the environment around him. He finds solace in small acts of rebellion, such as playing opera music over the prison's loudspeakers and starting a library program. These moments highlight his defiance against a system designed to break spirits. The iconic scene where he plays "Duettino - Sull'aria" from Mozart's "The Marriage of Figaro" resonates deeply, symbolizing the liberation of the human spirit even within the confines of a brutal institution.

Darbont's direction is masterful, employing a careful balance of bleak realism and moments of profound beauty. The cinematography by Roger Deakins is stunning, using light and shadow to reflect the characters' emotional landscapes. The prison itself, with its imposing walls and cold concrete, serves as a character in its own right, representing both confinement and the possibility of redemption.

The relationship between Andy and Red is at the heart of the film. Their bond evolves from cautious camaraderie to a profound friendship that sustains both men through the darkest of times. The dialogue is rich with meaning, underscoring the themes of trust and loyalty. Red's narration adds layers to the story, as he reflects on their experiences with wisdom and poignancy. The moments of levity shared between them-such as their discussions about hope and the nature of freedom-contrast sharply with the grim realities they face, offering viewers a glimmer of optimism amid despair.

The film also delves into the consequences of institutionalization, a poignant theme explored through characters like Brooks Hatlen, who struggles to adapt to life outside prison after decades of incarceration. This aspect of the story serves as a sobering reminder of the challenges faced by those who lose their freedom, amplifying the film's emotional weight.

The climax of the film delivers a powerful message about perseverance and the triumph of the human spirit. Andy's escape is not just a physical act; it symbolizes a reclamation of his identity and agency. His meticulous planning and unwavering resolve demonstrate that hope is not merely a passive wish but an active choice.

The Shawshank Redemption ultimately culminates in a profound statement about friendship, freedom, and the indomitable nature of hope. Its final scenes are both uplifting and cathartic, leaving audiences with a sense of resolution and the belief that redemption is possible, no matter how dire the circumstances.

Despite its initial lukewarm reception, the film has since garnered critical acclaim and a loyal fan base, frequently topping "greatest films" lists. Its blend of exceptional storytelling, strong performances, and emotional depth cements The Shawshank Redemption as a timeless classic that continues to inspire and resonate with viewers around the world. In an era where narratives of despair often dominate, this film stands as a testament to the enduring power of hope and friendship in the face of adversity.

9.title: Greatest movie i ever saw
9.content:
The Shawshank Redemption is an uplifting, deeply satisfying prison drama with sensitive direction and fine performances. The Shawshank Redemption is a 1994 epic American drama film written and directed by Frank Darabont and starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. It is ranked #1 in IMDb's "Top 250" list based on over a million votes (9.3 out of 10) and is considered one of the best movies of all time.

Adapted from the Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption, the film tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is sentenced to life in Shawshank State Prison for the murder of his wife and her lover despite his claims of innocence. During his time at the prison, he befriends a fellow inmate, Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding, and finds himself protected by the guards after the warden begins using him in his money laundering operation.

Despite being a box office flop (that barely recouped its budget), the film received multiple award nominations and outstanding reviews from critics for its acting, story, and realism. It has since been successful on cable television, VHS, DVD, and Blu-ray. It was included in the American Film Institute's 100 Years...100 Movies 10th Anniversary Edition.

9.title: hope vs. certainty
9.content:
Interpretation, spoilers:

Brooks represents complete complacency with life, so much so that any disturbance causes anxiety and suicidal ideation. Red also, for a time, represents this complacency. This movie is not simply a prison story, its message is generalized to mankind in general and it can be assumed that this complacency also represents modern man's need for routine - to the detriment of authentic living.

It takes an unjustly imprisoned man, Andy, to demonstrate to Red the life-or-death importance of hope and the freedom allowed by hope. As shown, hope entails slight fear because it necessarily interferes with order in life. Andy illustrates that this fear is a part of living, and renunciation from it results in an ingenuine sort of living.

Red soon realizes - given the rock hammer, the poster, and the mexico plans - that Andy had never given up his hope despite 19 years in prison. Hope and a sense of freedom and allowed even in prison, but not to all (music scene). For Red, it takes an actual physical freedom to live with a sense of hope. Andy, by exuding auras of hope from the beginning - though he would be expected to despair the most given his innocence - helps Red reach an epiphany of sorts; certainty and hope are mutually exclusive, and hope is always to be preferred. The Brook's path is shirked, and Red chooses life in all of its confusion, because true hope is omnipotent.

But let me perhaps add that what I find so fascinating about Shawshank is that Stephen King wrote it.

King is one of the best writers in the world. Books like IT and the Castle Rock series are some of the greatest stories ever told. But his best adaptations are always done by the best directors. ***Spoilers ahead***

It's a poignant tale of an innocent man (banker) wrongfully convicted for committing a crime of passion (killing his wife and her lover).When he is sent to jail (Shawshank prison)for the aforementioned reason,he develops a special bond with a jail mate "Red" ( played by Morgan Freeman) supposedly the only guilty one at Shawshank.During his time in prison he comes across many harsh realities such as the dull eerie life in prison,the atrocities on prisoners and most importantly the real culprit behind the crime (the one who actually killed his wife).To exact his revenge he develops a master plan using his banking knowledge and outwits the jail guards by a surreptitious escape from prison to lead a new life in another part of the world.

The movie scores in following aspects Dialogue:Witty , memorablejust simply great..and yeah not to mention the smart,strong and powerful narration by Morgan Freeman.

Character formation:Every character carried some background information.

Background score:That's the USP of this film..The background theme during the scene where Andy dufresne is brought into the Shawshank prison and the camera rolls high above the prison is just so mesmerizing.

Acting: Top notch acting by the lead actors and backed well by the support cast.

Story: Powerful,thought-provoking,tear-shedding and most importantly not a clichéd one.

To sum up this movie gives a powerful message of hope and redemption .something we all seek in life.

9.title: Fantastic Movie
9.content: It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shaw shank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shaw shank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope. Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

This movie is the highest movie on IMDb and deservedly so. At first when I saw it, I thought "how good can this movie be? and does it deserve all the praise?" yeah, well, it's that good and it deserved all the praise now I know.

One thing that strucked me while watching this movie is the similarity between SR and Prison Break, yes, prison break, especially the first season, the similarities are:

°Calm, calculating and clever protagonist, Michael Scofield and Andy Dufresne,

°the Warden likes the protagonist and make them to do job for their personal use

°Elderly men keeping pet in the their pocket

°Tough and cold-hearted head of security

° The protagonists escape at the end

°Both wrongfully convicted etc

I found it similar and I think Prison Break must be inspired by Shawkshaw Redemption,but the thing they never mentioned it, which is weird.

I love that the escape plan was kept a secret until the last minute, we were made to believe Dufresne just want to adjust to the prison life and make life better for himself while making friends and acquaintances but he actually had a grand plan all along. it is well done and it's one of the most interesting and thought-provoking use of plot twist I've seen in a movie.

9.title: Corruption at Shawshank
9.content:
This movie is fantastic in it's build up and execution of what finally happens. With Andy and red going through so much, for both of them on their own to get redemption. In that it also points out an excellent point for the crappy us prison system, which only institutionalizes criminals. And makes you see the flaw of their failure to rehabilitate people. In this movie the acting is expressive and realistic from most people, but natural as something based off Steven king, the antagonist and alot of other bad characters come off as 2d and dry in terms of emotion, over the course of the film you get to see the warden in more depth, but the rest you don't besides maybe a quick glimpse into their life through dialog, which is an extremely strong point of this film. I feel all the conversation are written very well, and even reds narration is written very well if not a bit cliche. The story is very slow, and paints a beautifully sad picture of all of it throughout the course. And the story on its own is a really powerful one, which is a great combination with actually having been well done. The sets are great, of course as it almost exclusively takes place in one location. But even outside they're convincing. The way this movie presents back stories I can't feel if it's good or bad, but I like it and it's very unique. The music in this movie is extremely simple, but does it effectively. And the rest of the sound design is done fine too. The acting of red, Andy, Tommy, haywood, the warden, and brooks are all very fantastic performances. They all feel like real humans. And I feel like this could be a study of humans, it shows everything in so much detail while not being super long it's impressive. The ending is just iconic, and is one of the best endings for a movie. The long narration of what happens after while showing is so well done. This movie feels very grounded into reality which makes the satisfaction by the end all the more satisfying.

The camerawork in this movie isn't the best, but feels effective and never feels like it isn't conveying the mood or theme.

Overall though; even though I don't feel like it's the best movie ever, it's a fantastically written, with very efficient music and timing. And is a must see to anyone who likes good movies. Overall a 8.7/10 from me.

9.title: An excellent movie.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is one of my all time favorite movies. It tells the story about one man's journey through prison and his struggle to find a purpose in his life, in prison he meets a new good friend , Andy Dufresne, a man wrongfully accused of viciously murdering his wife.

In a way this movie is two movies rapped up into one. It not only tells the unfortunate story of a normal man in prison, and what he does there. But it also is about a man rightfully accused of murder, and does his time in prison, we find he only committed this crime as a young, stupid kid, and is full of regret, he has become wise in prison and becomes rehabilitated for normal life, he is no longer a danger to society.

His struggle to be free and search for meaning in his life is his main passion. He is convinced that hope can destroy a man, hope is not a good thing. While Andy believes that hope is the only friend one can have in prison, in solitary, hope is the only way out. Andy acts as Red's mentor and guides him to the right way of thinking. This all leads up to Andy's need of Red, and finally one of the most moving endings in movie history.

Tim Robbins is excellent in the movie. He gives the performance of his life and plays Andy Dufresne to perfection. Morgan Freeman is also very good. It shows the ups and downs in Red's life, and the way of life for a prison inmate. While also showing the meaning of hope and how hope can keep a man's faith, and as a result, himself, alive. Don't miss this, you really need to see this movie several times to completely appreciate it. But even seeing it once is heart-warming enough.

9.title: Finding Redemption: A Timeless Journey of Hope and Resilience
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences worldwide since its release in 1994. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, this film is a poignant tale of hope, friendship, and the indomitable human spirit.

Set within the confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the story follows Andy Dufresne, a banker wrongly convicted of murder, and his journey over two decades of imprisonment. The film intricately weaves together themes of redemption, resilience, and the power of inner freedom.

One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its impeccable storytelling and character development. Andy, portrayed brilliantly by Tim Robbins, embodies quiet strength and unwavering determination, while Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, a fellow inmate and narrator of the story, is both compelling and deeply moving.

The cinematography of "The Shawshank Redemption" is breathtaking, capturing the starkness of prison life juxtaposed with moments of transcendent beauty. The score by Thomas Newman adds emotional depth, enhancing the film's impact on the audience.

What sets this film apart is its ability to resonate with viewers on a profound level. It reminds us of the resilience of the human spirit in the face of adversity and the transformative power of hope. "The Shawshank Redemption" is not just a film; it's an unforgettable journey that leaves a lasting impression on all who experience it.

9.title: Overhyped and Overrated: The Shawshank Redemption Falls Short of Its Reputation
9.content:
This film is absurdly overrated, with many praising it for its sentimental narrative and lush score, as if that automatically equals artistic brilliance. The direction is unremarkable, and the cinematography is, frankly, average at best. The script feels like a typical Stephen King tale, filled with melodrama and overwrought dialogue, laden with heavy-handed metaphors. For instance, the moment when the script explicitly states the prisoner's interest in geology-"It's all about TIME and PRESSURE"-feels like it's catering to the less attentive audience members.

While Morgan Freeman brings his usual excellence to the role, Tim Robbins' performance is inconsistent, especially as his character transitions from a newcomer to an experienced inmate. Though the film's liberal political leanings are praiseworthy, it certainly doesn't elevate the movie to the level of a great work of art.

9.title: A captivating, well made film.

I first watched it when I was 10 years old, and my mind immediately discarded it, but once I started to watch films for what they represent, I can honestly say that this film has all the qualities a great film will have: Great screen writing, great actors, a great director, a captivating story and a plot that swings you towards a great end.

This film represents what the whole film industry now a days has at times forgotten: You don't have to make a saga of films for people to remember your work, all you need is a great story that, despite being so complex, explains itself during the whole film, and doesn't need to be 3 or 4 hours long for you to understand the characters or empathize with the situations.

All in all this film will forever be the perfect example of how any film should be made, in order for it to be remembered.

9.title: We've Got to Get Out of This Place!
9.content:
At this writing I see that there is already 6,329 reviews of "The Shawshank Redemption" on IMDb so what the heck, I'll throw in my two cents worth.

"The Shawshank Redemption" was adapted from a Stephen King novelette about a wrongly convicted murderer's 19 year odyssey through Shawshank prison in Maine. Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is sent to prison for the murder of his wife and her lover. We don't learn until later that he really was innocent. Andy is taken under the wing of veteran lifer Red Redding (Morgan Freeman) who shows him the ways of prison life.

Warden Norton (Bob Gunton) is a strict Bible thumper who together with his sadistic Captain of the Guards Captain Hadley (Clancy Brown), maintain order within the prison. A convict named Bogs (Mark Rolston) sets his sights on Andy for homosexual purposes. Andy is continuously attacked by Bogs and his friends. While working on a roof top, Andy overhears Hadley's complaints over taxes on a small inheritance. Andy tells Hadley of a way in which he can avoid any taxes. As his "fee" Andy asks for beer for his co-workers which puts him favor with the group. Later, when Bogs and his gang rough up Andy, Hadley beats Bogs to a pulp and renders him a parapalygic.

Warden Norton sees possibilities in Andy and re-assigns him to the prison library being run by lifer Brooks Hatlen (James Whitmore). Andy through an exhaustive letter writing campaign, manages to gain funding from the state to expand the library along with a supply of used books. Andy does Income taxes for the guards and tutors some prisoners as well. Norton is impressed Under a scheme where prisoners are loaned out to the community for work on public projects, Norton develops a kick back scheme and employs Andy to keep the books for him.

A young convict named Tommy (Gil Bellows) comes to the prison and after gaining the confidence of Andy and Red, tells a tale of a prisoner that he had shared a cell with who admitted to killing Andy's wife and lover. Andy goes to Warden Norton to seek a new trial. Norton not wanting to lose Andy because of his accounting skills, refuses to help him. An argument ensues and Andy is thrust into solitary.

When he is released from solitary, Andy becomes distant and becomes a loner. What he is really doing is hatching an elaborate frame-up of Norton and his cronies while also planning to escape. One morning g at roll call Andy does not answer and......................................................................................

This film deservedly was nominated for seven Academy Awards. The acting is superb. Robbins and Woodward are tremendous as the two main characters. Gunton and Brown are great as the main villains. But veteran James Whitmore almost steals the movie with his sympathetic portrayal of the paroled lifer who tries to adjust to society after 50 years in prison.

A great movie.

9.title: Human again!
9.content:
Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is tall, lean, and a very successful Vice President for a bank in Portland, Maine. Andy's wife (Renee Blaine) is a beautiful and slim brunette who finally breaks her silence about her love affair with Glenn Quentin (Scott Mann) a golf pro. She informs Andy that she wants a divorce in Reno which he denied her. Now Andy finds himself facing a judge and jury as he flashes back to a dark and drunken night sitting in a wooden area at the end of a driveway in his car with a trusty bottle of Rosewood liquor in one hand, a musical tone "If I didn't care" (Jack Lawrence) playing in the background as a reaches for his six shooter from the glove compartment. Andy's blank face tells his version of his innocence; however, the neighbors plus two dead bodies tell the other side of the story. The dead body of Andy's wife and the golf pro give him two life sentences in the big houseShawshank Prison!

Andy arrives at Shawshank with the same blank facial expression that granted him the bus ride to the prison. As the welcoming committee provided a grand opening to the bus load of "Fresh Fish" inmates. This single file march of leg irons clanking, feet shuffling across the dusty prison yard, as fresh fish pass by the thunderous claps, and yelling voices which intimated some of the new fish. Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman) placed a bet of 10 cigarettes on the new fish named Andy Dufresne. Andy has a naive way of thinking, along with his new normal routine of strolling the prison yard in search of smooth rocks while keeping to himself. Andy finally breaks his silence after a month and engages in a conversation with Red.

Andy's life sentence was almost cut short while eavesdropping on a conversation of the brutal Captain Hadley (Clancy Brown). Since Andy befriends Red and his crew of intimates Brooks Hatlen (James Whitmore), Heywood (William Sadler), Jigger (Neil Giuntoli), Floyd (Brian Libby), and Skeet (Larry Brandenburg), he placed a request for a bottle of suds after the rigged roof job is completed by this team of inmates. Andy was able to do his "Real Job" again by performing banking services for every prison guard in Shawshank. Although he longed for this new freedom Andy still has to fight off his predator Boggs Diamond (Mark Rolston).

Andy is on the verge of losing his freedom due to his overzealous attitude toward Warden Norton (Bob Gunton). The Warden provides Andy with a few options while he spends two months in solitary confinement to reset his mind and his mouth. This melodramatic crime film will have your emotions racing as you cook up a new avenue for Andy to travel down.

The actors in "The Shawshank Redemption" have a more boisterous tone compared to the relaxed spoken actors in "The Green Mile" John Coffey (Michael Clark Duncan), Paul Edgecomb (Tom Hanks), Brutus "Brutal" Howell (David Morse), "Wild Bill" Wharton (Sam Rockwell), Eduard Delacroix (Michael Jeter), and Dean Stanton (Barry Pepper). The lighting for these two melodramatic crime films are different. Both John Coffey and Andy Dufresne are in prison for murder. Andy has more of a dark shadow over his face at times probably due to depression and when harm is coming his way. The lighting changes for him when he is able to accomplish a "normal / human" side of his past. John Coffey has a brighter atmosphere when is able to arouse those around him to think outside the box and have a more positive attitude in their heart toward life. John and Andy have to figure out which way to go in order to have freedom while in prison.

9.title: What makes this movie special
9.content:
What makes this movie special is how it handles themes of hope and friendship. Andy's resilience and cleverness in the face of a grim situation are inspiring. He finds ways to improve the prison for everyone, and his relationship with Red evolves beautifully throughout the film.

The acting is top-notch, with Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman giving standout performances. The story unfolds at a perfect pace, with moments of intense drama balanced by the quieter, more reflective parts. The ending is both satisfying and uplifting, leaving you with a sense of hope and redemption.

Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a powerful, moving film that's well worth watching. It's a classic for a reason and definitely a must-see if you haven't caught it yet.

9.title: lovely movie
9.content:
There are standard ways to stage a prison film and standard ways to tell a story by Stephen King. But "The Shawshank Redemption," based on a King novella and set in the correctional institution of the title, succeeds in avoiding the familiar.

Without a single riot scene or horrific effect, it tells a slow, gentle story of camaraderie and growth, with an ending that abruptly finds poetic justice in what has come before. The writer and director, Frank Darabont, tells this tale with a surprising degree of loving care.

There are times when "The Shawshank Redemption" comes dangerously close to sounding one of those "triumph of the human spirit" notes. But most of it is eloquently restrained. Despite an excess of voice-over narration and inspirational music, Mr. Darabont's film has a genuine dignity that holds the interest. It is helped greatly by fine, circumspect performances from Morgan Freeman as a rueful lifer named Red and Tim Robbins as Andy, the new kid on the cell block. The film spans nearly 20 years of friendship between these two.

When Andy is convicted of his wife's murder, the judge pronounces him "a particularly remorseless and icy man." He sustains that chill when he first arrives at Shawshank, remaining aloof from other inmates even when those inmates threaten him with physical harm. "I wish I could tell you that Andy fought the good fight," says Red, who knows Andy has been gang-raped by fellow prisoners, in one of the film's only halfway-brutal episodes. "I wish I could tell you that, but prison is no fairy-tale world."

By : JANET MASLIN The New York Times Published: September 23, 1994

9.title: The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Tale of Hope and Redemption"
9.content:
"The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of its genre, captivating audiences with its compelling narrative, exceptional performances, and profound themes. Directed by Frank Darabont and adapted from Stephen King's novella, this film stands as a testament to the power of hope, friendship, and the indomitable spirit of the human soul.

Set within the confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film introduces us to Andy Dufresne, portrayed brilliantly by Tim Robbins. Wrongfully convicted of a crime he didn't commit, Andy endures the relentless hardships of prison life. Yet, even in the face of injustice and despair, he remains a beacon of unwavering hope. Robbins masterfully portrays Andy's resilience, transforming him into a symbol of strength and determination.

Morgan Freeman delivers an iconic performance as Ellis "Red" Redding, a longtime inmate who becomes Andy's closest friend. Freeman's narration adds a layer of introspection and wisdom to the story, guiding us through the depths of the human experience. The on-screen chemistry between Robbins and Freeman is simply electrifying, elevating the film's emotional impact.

"The Shawshank Redemption" captivates viewers with its meticulously crafted storytelling. Frank Darabont's direction is nothing short of brilliant, as he weaves together various narrative threads with precision and finesse. The film's pacing is deliberate, allowing the story to unfold naturally and building anticipation for its powerful climax.

At its core, the film explores universal themes of hope, redemption, and the innate desire for freedom. It reminds us that even in the darkest of circumstances, the human spirit can triumph over adversity. Through Andy's resilience and his quest for justice, the movie leaves an indelible mark on the audience, inspiring us to seek hope and find solace in the power of the human spirit.

Visually, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a marvel. The gritty and oppressive atmosphere of the prison is juxtaposed with moments of breathtaking beauty, symbolizing the potential for transformation and finding redemption in the most unlikely places. The cinematography captures both the claustrophobic nature of the prison walls and the vastness of the human spirit, creating a visual tapestry that resonates long after the film ends.

Supported by a stellar ensemble cast, including the likes of Bob Gunton, William Sadler, and Clancy Brown, each character adds depth and nuance to the narrative. They reflect the complex web of humanity found within the prison walls, with performances that are both powerful and haunting.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is a cinematic gem that has withstood the test of time. Its timeless story of friendship, hope, and redemption continues to touch the hearts of audiences across generations. With its exceptional performances, impeccable storytelling, and profound themes, this film stands as a testament to the transformative power of cinema.

In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a must-watch for any film enthusiast. It weaves together a compelling narrative, outstanding performances, and a profound exploration of the human spirit. Prepare to be captivated, moved, and inspired by this extraordinary masterpiece that will leave an indelible mark on your soul.
